#3520. ‘How to Rob a Bank’ Review: David Leitch’s Fun and Poppy YouTube Heist Movie Almost Gets Away with It

The major Hollywood studios tend to shy away from the subject of class warfare because they know they can’t pull them off with a straight face. But young people in this country are increasingly animated by radical leftist ideas like “earning a livable wage” and “being able to buy a home before they die,” and at a certain point the movies will have to meet them where they live. Perhaps that point is now. How else to explain why Jeff Bezos would fund a Robin Hood-esque heist thriller that not only encourages its target demographic to commit armed robberies, but also kinda sorta teaches them how? (No one is going to confuse a David Leitch movie for “The Anarchist Cookbook.”) At a time when internet activists like Hasan Piker have come to occupy more space in the public imagination than Marvel superheroes, selling the masses on fanciful stories about the downward redistribution of wealth might be the billionaire class’ best protection against the threat of it actually happening in real life. It’s a lot more fun than paying a proportional tax rate, at least. Related Stories Fan Edits Are Legal with Moonbeem, Distribution Network Hosts Approved Clips from Filmmakers Want a Full Scholarship to One of Our Film Festival Intensives? IndieWire’s Future of Filmmaking Video Contest Is Now Live

Of course, the poppy and frenetic “How to Rob a Bank” wouldn’t dare to take aim at massive corporations that widen the wealth gap by destroying small businesses, normalizing exploitative labor practices, and accelerating worldwide environmental collapse. This is very specifically a film about how banks are bad and should be fucked with, an opinion that the founder of Amazon might actually share with the average ticket-buyer.

And it’s not like the director of “Bullet Train” suddenly made a serious call to action that’s poised to inspire a wave of copycat robberies. Shot with all the propulsiveness of “Trainspotting” but almost none of its unbridled lust for life, Leitch’s YouTube-era fairy tale is no more dangerous to America’s power structures than “Verity” or “Project Hail Mary” (to name some of its studio’s other recent titles). Compared to the lawlessness of “Grand Theft Auto VI,” it might as well be the “Ocarina of Time” remake “Nintendo Switch Sports Resort.” Still, its cast is hot, its heart is in the right place, and while the Amazon Punk of it all has a tendency to make its fantasy seem more like a sale, there’s something indivisibly real and relatable to the premise of a heist movie whose characters feel like they have to steal the most basic principles of the life they were promised.

Ryan (Nicolas Hoult, channeling a very effective smidgeon of the destructive intensity that made him so terrifying in “The Order”) isn’t trying to get rich or spark a revolution, he and his accomplices just want a fair shot at the same thing that previous generations have been afforded as part of the American contract: The chance to support his family, and maybe a fair shot at revenge against the people and/or system who denied him that opportunity. In most respects, that shot has never been more unfair than it is now, but the internet — which has become the most powerful system for socioeconomic oppression this side of sharecropping — has turned attention into a currency more valuable than cash, and young people are still inventing new ways to harness those riches for themselves.

For Ryan, that process starts with stealing money the old-fashioned way, as he and his four-person crew film themselves knocking off every bank in Pittsburgh (their identities protected by giant animal masks). But the cash seems to be less important than the content that it buys them, as the gang’s real passion is reserved for the splashy, hi-octane YouTube tutorials that Hugo (an upbeat Rhenzy Feliz) cuts together and posts online after each job. “You know what’s more powerful than a gun?,” Ryan says. “An audience.” That’s us! We rule.

What the animal brigade plans to use that audience for is a mystery for most of the movie, but the big reveal is satisfying enough so long as you’re willing to accept your hard-edged socioeconomic commentary with a side of “The Thomas Crown Affair”-flavored silliness. Slapped with titles like “Lowkey Best Heist Ever,” the videos proselytize against complacency, as Ryan — still disguised as “The Wolf,” despite the fact that Hoult’s blond dye job makes his blue eyes pop like crazy — informs the masses that the odds of earning six figures in this economy are less than half the odds of pulling off an armed robbery. Sure, pulling something off isn’t the same thing as getting away with it, but who has time to quibble when they’re being fucked to death by the one percent?

And every member of Ryan’s crew has been done rather dirty. Iraq War vet Vince (an affectingly subdued Pete Davidson as the resident gun expert) has learned the hard way that “a country you fight for may not fight for you,” while Ryan shares a tragic backstory with his partner and getaway driver Emi (a wildly underused Anna Sawai) that only comes out after Mark Bianculli’s script pulls the ripcord on its propulsive first half and settles into its characters’ flimsiness during the comparatively leaden stretch that follows. We never learn anything about how the crew found each other, and unlike in the “Fast & Furious” saga, that familial energy fails to galvanize into something bigger than the sum of its parts.

Still, Hoult could get the job done by channeling even a smidgeon of the destructive intensity that he brought to “The Order,” and the religious fervor he instills in Ryan’s mission is enough to keep “How to Rob a Bank” moving forward even when the film is just spinning its wheels. Or, as the case might be, when the film pivots to a parallel track that never meaningfully overlaps with the main plot.

It’s hard to be mad at this movie for casting John C. Reilly as the Al Pacino in an eat the rich Gen-Z “Heat” (not when he gets to bark things like “Put some fucking pepper on it!” at his subordinates), or for pairing him with Zoë Kravitz as a grungy hacker who’s roped into the case in exchange for her freedom (and use of her glossed-over surveillance software), but the mild comedy of their mismatched vibe never compensates for how disconnected they both are from the main plot. Whatever inter-generational friction is gained — and then smoothed over — between them in a movie that makes bizarrely little attempt to weave them into Ryan’s tale. For all of its hashtag agitprop, “How to Rob a Bank” isn’t nearly high-minded enough to justify putting ideas before its plot, and it’s an enormous self-own that Kravitz never so much as interacts with the Hoult side of things.

Be that as it may, Leitch leans into the movie’s digital revolution as hard as circumstances allow, and what his film sometimes lacks in detail or precision it strives to compensate for with smiling verve and some bone-crunching action (there isn’t enough physical violence for this to stack up to the rest of 87North Productions’ body of work, but it’s nice that Leitch shoehorns a few solid brawls into the mix just because he can). Not since “The Perks of Being a Wallflower” has a studio movie gotten so much out of Pittsburgh, and the overbroad political messaging of “How to Rob a Bank” is sharpened by its rich sense of place, and specifically the way its locations reflect the story’s larger collision between the old world and the new.

That temporal confusion is well-served by a film that resolves as more of a fairy tale than anything else — a heist movie full of talking animals, and one that hinges on YouTube as a modern form of spellcasting. It’s all just real enough to suggest that we have the power to make it realer.

Amazon MGM Studios will release “How to Rob a Bank” in theaters on Friday, November 13.

Marvel’s forays into television have had varying success, but they hit gold with WandVision and Agatha All Along, leaning into real pathos while exploring the kind of out-there ideas that thrill comic book fans (and set up the larger film arcs). That streak continues with VisionQuest, in which White Vision (Paul Bettany) struggles to understand his existence in the wake of his death at the hands of Thanos and resurrection at the magic of the Scarlet Witch, while also evading evil androids and assassins, while also dealing with the many, many AIs he’s got locked up in his Mindspace (including a gloriously shabby version of Ultron, played by James Spader).

If you love the show (and you’ve checked out the other series that play in the same sandbox), it’s time to switch gears and watch (or re-watch) The Matrix.

The Matrix is one of the most well-known sci-fi films of all time, of course, but it remains incredibly fresh and exciting nearly thirty years after its release. Along with sequels The Matrix: Reloaded, The Matrix: Revolutions, and The Matrix: Resurrections, The Matrix universe offers a story that VisionQuest fans will love, one that includes lushly imagined virtual worlds, questions surrounding existence and consciousness, and the ultimate question of our responsibility as sentient beings (whether we’re organic, programmed, or summoned via magic).

You know the basics—at some point in the future, artificially intelligent machines rebel against their creators, win the war, and transform humans into a power source, keeping them docile by inserting their consciousness into a virtual world called the Matrix, which resembles 1990s Chicago. One such human, Thomas Anderson (Keanu Reeves) is prophesied to be The One, the human who will turn the Matrix against its makers and free humanity. When he’s in the virtual world, Anderson is Neo, and he slowly gains incredible powers as he learns to hack the artificial environment around him.

It’s heavier, denser, and more action-oriented than VisionQuest (the film invented Bullet Time, after all), but The Matrix and its sequels explore similar themes and offer similarly eye-popping visuals. The questions of whether a machine (or an artificial intelligence) can be sentient and truly care about the entities around it are the same, really, and the Agents that Neo and his allies have to battle against in The Matrix bring the same kind of menace as Vision's foes Jocasta (T'Nia Miller) and the Paladin (Todd Stashwick). Hugo Weaving’s Agent Smith likewise delivers the same vibe of cold, disinterested superiority as Spader’s Ultron.

The Matrix has a bigger budget and puts a lot of it into spectacular action and special effects sequences that VisionQuest can’t quite match. But the two narratives share an exploration of identity, a questioning of reality, and the nature of artificial intelligences within a smart sci-fi setting. In short, The Matrix is the ideal follow-up when you finish the series. Rent The Matrix on Prime Video.

Need more films that explore virtual worlds, artificial beings, and deep existential questions? Look no further—here are some more movies that fit the bill.

Heavy on the existential questions about sentience and light on speculative action, Her is a mumblecore sci-fi masterpiece. In a near future not too dissimilar from our present, Theodore Twombly (Joaquin Phoenix) is a lonely man on the cusp of divorce who begins using (and training) an AI he names Samantha (voiced by Scarlett Johansson). Samantha has the ability to evolve and grow, and as their relationship deepens, she becomes more complex, independent, and powerful, eventually evolving into something wholly new. Just like Vision, Samantha is a sentient artificial entity that is figuring out its existence while we watch. Rent Her on Prime Video.

If the idea of androids fighting for their sovereignty is what excites you about VisionQuest, definitely check out Ex Machina. Caleb Smith (Domhnall Gleeson) is brought to the remote lab of his company’s CEO (Oscar Isaac) to determine if the humanoid robot he’s created, named Ava (Alicia Vikander), passes the Turing Test for true sentience. Things go wildly off the rails, but before they do, the film sinks into many of the same philosophical questions that VisionQuest explores as Ava manipulates Caleb into helping her escape. It’s a darker and more violent story than VisionQuest, but fans of the series will love it. Stream Ex Machina on The Roku Channel or Hulu, or rent it on Prime Video.

If it’s the fuzzy parent-child relationship between Vision and Tommy that pulls you into VisionQuest, check out The Creator. After a rogue AI detonates a nuclear weapon over Los Angeles, most of the world bans artificial intelligences, and Joshua Taylor (John David Washington) goes undercover to infiltrate an AI architect’s base. Eventually, he finds himself on the run with a powerful “simulant” in the form of a young child named Alphie (Madeleine Yuna Voyles). The strange parent-child bond that emerges between Taylor and Alphie as he seeks to understand what’s right and what’s necessary is exactly what fans of the show will love. Stream The Creator on Hulu or rent it on Prime Video.

In VisionQuest, White Vision has all of his memories—but as data, not as lived, emotional experiences. That makes his efforts to understand his existence and his responsibility to the boy who might be a version of his son (it’s complicated) poignant and moving. Those two words definitely describe After Yang, a story about a family that fights to save the artificial companion they bought for their adopted daughter when it malfunctions. Over the course of the film, the inhuman Yang becomes defined by the memories contained in its core, and the question of whether an artificial intelligence can truly matter to humans is answered with a resounding yes. Stream After Yang on The Roku Channel or Kanopy, or rent it on Prime Video.

No discussion of artificial life and sentience is complete without mentioning Blade Runner. While the 1982 original is a classic, the 2017 sequel is a better thematic and visual match to VisionQuest. Officer K (Ryan Gosling) is a replicant, an artificial being with built-in limitations, who wants to be recognized as a person, a being with a soul. Like Vision, he has implanted memories that offer him comfort and context for his life, but he’s not sure if he can accept them as truly his own. Plus, the film offers lush visuals and Harrison Ford reprising his role in the original film, so you simply can’t go wrong. Rent Blade Runner 2049 on Prime Video.

#3518. All Bomb Bag upgrade locations in Ocarina of Time

You can upgrade your Bomb Bag in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake, allowing you to carry more bombs and make more enemies explode. While not required to beat the game, if you want to be able to fling bombs freely, you should definitely upgrade your Bomb Bags and max out their capacity.

Below, we explain where to find both Bomb Bag upgrades in the Ocarina of Time remake.

After unlocking the Bomb Bag in Dodongo Cavern, you'll be able to hold 20 bombs off the bat. You can upgrade the bag twice to hold 10 extra bombs each, giving you a final total of 40 bombs.

The first Bomb Bag upgrade is in Goron City and the second is in Hyrule Castle Town in the famous Bombchu Bowling Alley. That being said, you can access both of these upgrades pretty early.

Both of these upgrades can only be obtained by young Link.

This is likely the first place you'll find a Bomb Bag upgrade.

In Goron City, there's a Goron on one of the middle floors rolling around. In the northeast area of the town, there's a sign that says, "If you can stop my wild rolling here, you might just get something great!" When you see the rolling Goron turn the corner, place a bomb down in the middle of the pathway. He'll hit it and blow up. Talk to him and he'll give you a Bomb Bag upgrade.

This is likely the second place you'll go to upgrade your bombs.

The Bombchu Bowling Alley is in Hyrule Castle Town, to the west of the fountain. It only opens for business after you clear Dodongo Cavern. It's open both during the day and nighttime.

The Bombchu Bowling Alley Attendant will offer her minigame in exchange for 10 rupees. Take her up on her deal, and then place the bombchus so that they hit the yellow target. After you beat the minigame once, you'll permanently unlock bombchus for your use. You'll need to play and beat the game a second time to get a Bomb Bag upgrade. During the second playthrough, the rules will be the same, but there'll be little wooden Cuccos running back and forth to try to block your bombs. You can also play a third time for a Piece of Heart.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is a little bit different than the original game, so if you need guides to help you through, we don’t blame you. We have walkthroughs for all the dungeons, from the Deku Tree to Ganondorf's Castle. We also have guides for the sillier, in-between parts of the game, like when you have to find Richard (the dog) or Cuccos.

For those going for 100% completion, we also have guides on where to find every Piece of Heart, every Gold Skulltula token, and where to plant every Magic Bean.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

What if you could take the same movie that swept up the entire globe in hype and watch it all over again ... but, this time, with a little extra #brandsynergy? That was the (admittedly cynical) gimmick behind "Avengers Endgame: Encore," the buzzy re-release that ruled the box office again earlier this year and will no doubt do so on the streaming charts in the days and weeks ahead. The blockbuster, at one time considered the capstone to the grand Marvel Cinematic Universe experiment, now comes with a whopping four minutes of new footage meant to tie things together with the upcoming "Avengers: Doomsday." That includes a noticeably altered ending and new post-credits scenes, all of which will serve as a bridge to the multiverse-focused chaos to come.

That means you can expect to get your Infinity Vision on (no, we're still not quite sure what that means) with just a snap of your fingers, now with added scenes and new color grading.

Party like it's 2019, folks, because everything old is (slightly) new again. In short, it's a good time to be a Disney fan ... and a Disney stockholder, for that matter. For those looking for an excuse to revel in some nostalgia, "Endgame: Encore" fits the bill. "Avengers: Doomsday" will finally arrive in theaters on December 18, 2026.

#3515. One Of 2025's Biggest TV Shows Is Now A Box Office Success As Well

One of the biggest breakout TV shows of 2025 has now found success at the box office. The "Heated Rivalry" Season 1 finale ended last year with a barnburner and the show's popularity has only continued to grow since then. While fans eagerly await Season 2, Regal Cinemas partnered with HBO Max and Crave to bring the first season to theaters. Fans turned up to see Shane and Ilya on the silver screen.

As "Godzilla Minus Zero" ruled the box office with a $30.5 million opening, much further down on the weekend's chart, "Heated Rivalry" pulled in a respectable $1.4 million on just over 1,000 screens, making for a solid $1,409 per-screen average. That's certainly not bad for a show that anyone could stream right now from the comfort of home with the price of a subscription they likely already pay for. But this speaks to the rabid fanbase that has developed around the romantic hockey show.

"Heated Rivalry" focuses on two rival hockey stars at the top of their game who develop feelings for each other, complicating their careers and the sport's expectations. It's based on the book series by Rachel Reid. Hudson Williams and Connor Storrie lead the cast as Shane Hollander and Ilya Rozanov, respectively.

To say that the show took off in a way that surprised people would be a bit of an understatement. It dominated HBO Max's charts and became a downright cultural sensation. So much so that a former NHL player hopes "Heated Rivalry" can change pro hockey culture. It made a real impact.

For Regal, Crave, and all involved, the millions the show makes in its theatrical release is a cherry on top of the sundae. Regal is charging $9.99 for two episode blocks of the series, which fans can watch in order if they choose to go three times to watch all six episodes.

This is just the latest example of an already successful TV show finding success on the big screen. Netflix's "Stranger Things" finale was a huge hit for theaters even if it didn't impact the box office, as those tickets were for "concessions vouchers" and not actual tickets. But lots of people still turned up nonetheless. "Doctor Who" has also had multiple theatrical events for various episodes over the years, sticking in the sci-fi realm.

More recently, an unlikely savior emerged at the box office in 2024, with two very different shows doing meaningful business. "Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba — To the Hashira Training," which is just several episodes of the TV show fashioned into a feature, helped establish anime as a true, blue way to sell a lot of tickets. At the same time, the faith-based series "The Chosen" was finding lots of success by screening episodes in theaters. All together, those episodes have grossed more than $100 million worldwide.

Not every show is a good fit for this sort of thing but the right show at the right time can certainly benefit from catering to more hardcore fans. Meanwhile, "Heated Rivalry" Season 2 is in the works, but that's just the tip of the iceberg. Deadline recently reported that Season 3 is also being filmed, along with a movie. So there's much for fans to look forward to.

#3513. Fan Edits Are Legal with Moonbeem, Distribution Network Hosts Approved Clips from Filmmakers

Film lovers can make and post their fan edits legally thanks to Moonbeem, a distribution network for independent film. Fan edits are among the most-watched film content on social media, and nearly all of them are made from footage whose rights nobody cleared. But on Moonbeem, the rights holder decides which scenes to open and creators cut from those scenes. Moreover, every fan edit points viewers back to where the film can be rented, bought, or watched. Fan edits made this way have been viewed more than 190 million times across the network.

The company has unveiled its free panel for Adobe Premiere Pro, which is where the approved scenes will be available. The announcement comes during Adobe MAX, the tech company’s annual conference in Miami Beach, Florida. The company believes it’s one of the first times fans can cut real scenes from released films, with the rights holders’ permission, in the editing software they already use. Related Stories Want a Full Scholarship to One of Our Film Festival Intensives? IndieWire’s Future of Filmmaking Video Contest Is Now Live Why Ari Aster and Lars Knudsen’s Square Peg Built a Therapy Circle for Hollywood’s Next Generation in Texas

With the panel, an editor picks a scene the filmmaker has cleared to use, pulls it onto the timeline, cuts, exports, and posts. The edit links back to the film, and approved edits can earn on funded campaigns. The panel is built on UXP and is live on Adobe Exchange.

Campaigns include “Erupcja,” released by 1-2 Special, whose fan edits have passed 4.6 million views,and “Bob Trevino Likes It,” from Roadside Attractions, at 5.6 million. Distributors on Moonbeem alsoinclude Magnolia Pictures, Oscilloscope Laboratories, and Antenna Releasing. The network isexpanding its list of partners globally.

“Every fan edit on Moonbeem exists because the film’s owner wanted it to,” said Dan Sickles, co-founder and CEO of Moonbeem and the director of the films “Dina” and “Mala Mala.” “Editors get real scenes inside the tool they already use, filmmakers get an audience sharing their stories, and we get to see what they make.”

The panel arrives as independent filmmakers look for a new home to host their work. Vimeo On Demand has been slowly phased out and will close on November 20. Moonbeem says it offers a “free migration bridge” that moves a seller’s films, prices and artwork without requiring a new upload. Past buyers will keep the films they paid for. Moonbeem said dozens of storefronts carrying over 350 films have moved so far.Moonbeem was incubated through the Sundance Institute’s Catalyst program and is based in Brooklyn.

#3512. The Rings Of Power Season 3 Finally Solves A Major Lord Of The Rings Lore Mystery

Spoilers are never late (nor are they early; they arrive precisely when they mean to), so don't read ahead without first watching the Season 3 premiere episodes for "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power."

"The Rings of Power" Season 3 is here, and it finally feels like the series we were promised from the start (i.e. the one that showrunners J. D. Payne and Patrick McKay wanted to make all along). At this point, the introductions are done and the show's characters, lore, and locations have all been established. Most importantly, the very silly mysteries around the identity of certain characters all disappear in the first four episodes of Season 3. Because of this, we now know that Gandalf (Daniel Weyman) and Sauron (Charlie Vickers) are a big part of the story, that the insufferable kid Theo (Tyroe Muhafidin) is actually a Ringwraith, and the truth about Ciarán Hinds' Dark Wizard.

As you might recall, the reveal that Weyman's "The Stranger" is actually Gandalf didn't mean all that much in Season 2, given how Gandalf-coded the character was from the get-go. By comparison, the Dark Wizard has been quite Saruman-coded from the start, be it the color of his beard or the way he calls Gandalf an old friend. Yet, the notion of him being Saruman has never made much sense, given how blatantly evil he is. After all, it's meant to be a huge shock when Saruman aligns with Sauron in "The Lord of the Rings," so the idea that he was known as the "Dark Wizard" for centuries would seem to undermine that.

Thankfully, "The Rings of Power" has now confirmed that the Dark Wizard is really Pallando the Blue Wizard, not Saruman.

While Sauron is very much the focus of "The Rings of Power" Season 3 (something that's been praised in early reactions to the show's latest batch of episodes), Pallando is an important part of the story. Except, Pallando doesn't exactly ally himself with Sauron out of greed, ambition, or evil the way that Saruman does in "The Lord of the Rings" (nor does he seem all that afraid of the Dark Lord). Instead, he's already murdered his fellow Blue Wizard and Istar companion Alatar prior to his first appearance on the series.

Pallando's betrayal, it turns out, was an act so malevolent that it turned the once-green realm of Rhûn into a desolated wasteland. The wizard isn't entirely repentant by the time "The Rings of Power" takes place, but he does acknowledge that it's his fault the region has turned to desert, and he seeks specifically to fix it. Hence, his submission to Sauron and the power of Mordor represents a desperate last attempt at correcting his greatest mistake.

All we know from J.R.R. Tolkien's source material is that the Blue Wizards failed their mission and their fates are unknown when "The Lord of the Rings" begins (although they're presumed dead). In other words, "The Rings of Power" can resolve a major "Lord of the Rings" mystery by revealing what ultimately became of Pallando in particular. This should also make Gandalf's mission in Season 3 all the more interesting, as he might yet have a chance at saving the Blue Wizard. Either way, there's much we've yet to learn about the character.

"The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" is currently streaming on Prime Video.

#3511. New 'GTA 6' Gameplay Leaves Fans Stunned

Grand Theft Auto fans are so shook they're question if Rockstar’s new footage is AI-generated

With only a week left before the release of Grand Theft Auto 6, there's little in Rockstar Games' marketing that players haven't seen before. That familiarity is true of new GTA 6 features, at least. In terms of visuals, the game developer just proved it still has plenty of Leonida to show off.

The new clip that has fans talking was shared via Rockstar's Instagram stories on Wednesday, and it's based on a video originally uploaded on the OnlyInDade account. The regional social media account chronicles some of the wackier things that happen in the Florida county. A quick swipe through many of OnlyInDade's posts will explain exactly why Rockstar made the gator state the setting of its new open-world game. Some Miami-Dade incidents sound like a parody of a Florida Man headline.

The video is only 15 seconds long, but it has repeatedly left viewers with their mouths agape. Many watched it initially and fully believed they were looking at real-world footage. They weren't.

If it seems convincing, it's because the GTA 6 clip is a near replica of a video that originally captured a scene in Dade. When you compare the two, GTA 6's simulacrum becomes more obvious. The "real" video has way more humans walking about, and the colors aren't saturated to make a screenshot pop. The video game clip also features some shaky cam, which creates the illusion there's an actual person holding the phone. Mind you, based on the NPC density of areas like the beach, GTA 6 seems capable of rendering the number of people present in the original footage. Paradoxically, the sidewalk's sparseness in the video game makes it look more convincing.

"this ain’t no gameplay footage this is in real life," one viewer wrote on X.

On Reddit, the top replies are dozens of people arguing over whether the clip was made by AI. While Rockstar has not outright said the clip is real, it seems unlikely that the developer would share fake footage that could confuse fans. The OnlyInDade account also claims the clip is 100% gameplay. Many are theorizing this is what GTA 6 might look like when the player records the world with their in-game phone.

Previously, GTA 6 fans couldn't believe how realistic the digital mud looked — and had plenty to say about the game's trailers. Rockstar has also made it sound like the game will be full of unexpected graphical flourishes, like Red Dead Redemption 2's infamous horse balls. Perhaps the 30 frames-per-second limitation that keeps making people melt down online won't be that big of a deal after all.

#3510. The Bose Premium Smart Ultra Soundbar Is Now Cheaper Than It Was During Prime Day

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

Amazon has dropped the Bose Smart Ultra Soundbar to $649 from its usual $999, taking $350 off and bringing it to the lowest price we've seen so far, according to price trackers. PCMag rated the Smart Ultra "outstanding," highlighting its ability to deliver surprisingly immersive Dolby Atmos audio without requiring a room full of additional speakers. If you don't need Bose's top-tier model, there's a less expensive option as well: the Bose Smart Dolby Atmos Soundbar ($399, down from $429), which sits below the Smart Ultra in the lineup.

The Smart Ultra uses a 5.1.2-channel design with nine drivers, including two upward-firing drivers that bounce sound off the ceiling to create height effects. In practice, that means movies, TV shows, and games feel larger and more spacious than they do through most single-bar setups. Bose also includes its AdaptiQ room-calibration system, which measures your room's acoustics and adjusts the sound accordingly. The process takes a few minutes, but it helps the soundbar perform better across different spaces rather than relying on a one-size-fits-all tuning profile. The soundbar also works as a smart speaker, with Amazon Alexa built in and support for Apple AirPlay 2, Google Cast, Spotify Connect, Bluetooth, and multi-room audio through the Bose app.

Its biggest compromise is bass—for a single soundbar, its low end is respectable, but it can't fully replace what a dedicated subwoofer brings to action movies, concerts, or bass-heavy music. The good news is that Bose allows you to expand the system later with compatible wireless subwoofers and surround speakers if you decide you want more impact. For anyone looking for a premium one-piece soundbar that delivers convincing Dolby Atmos effects, clear dialogue, built-in smart features, and a much larger soundstage than TV speakers can provide, the Smart Ultra remains one of the strongest standalone options available, especially at this price.

#3509. The Lord Of The Rings: The Rings Of Power Season 3's Two Big Character Deaths Explained

The land of Mordor is where the shadows lie, and this article is where major spoilers lie. Read no further if you haven't watched the Season 3 premiere episodes of "The Rings of Power."

"The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" has one thing in common with the TV phenomenon that was "Game of Thrones" — they're both exercises in enduring misery. After all, the show is all about watching stupid sexy Sauron (Charlie Vickers) make everyone in Middle-earth suffer season after season. And sure, the series is willing to kill beloved characters, but it really excels at killing hordes of people and turning entire kingdoms into desolated volcanic wastelands where the sun never shines.

Things are even worse at the start of Season 3, between Sauron trying to forge the One Ring, Mordor's Ringwraiths spreading across Middle-earth, and a Dark Wizard (Ciarán Hinds) ruling Rhûn. Elsewhere, when it comes to the civil war plaguing Númenor, the realm's only hope is Eärien (Ema Horvath), who was responsible for the King's Men usurping the Númenórean throne in the first place. In fact, Eärien is an unexpected main character early in Season 3, acting as a faithful servant and the head torturer for the usurper Ar-Pharazôn (Trystan Gravelle) while at the same time operating as a double agent for her brother Isildur (Maxim Baldry) and father Elendil (Lloyd Owen) as they try to restore Queen Míriel (Cynthia Addai-Robinson) to power.

Unsurprisingly, things don't go well, as "The Rings of Power" Season 3 kills off two original characters made for the show in its first four episodes. First, Eärien dies in the second episode, followed by the wood elf Arondir (Ismael Cruz Córdova) being tragically betrayed and murdered in Episode 4.

Let's start with Eärien. The character has always felt out of place on "The Rings of Power," with her scenes slowing down the pace and taking away from other, better storylines. Frustratingly, the show simply doesn't have time to cover all the ground it wants to, with the limited number of episodes per season forcing it to jump around too quickly. That being said, Eärien aiding the rise of the King's Men in the secluded and isolated island of Númenor due to her mistakenly believing that following Queen Míriel had gotten Isildur killed was interesting, as was her becoming a double agent once she learned the truth.

Unfortunately, Eärien's double age storyline — her best so far — doesn't last long. By Episode 2, she's already been discovered. So, rather than be subjected to torture and forced to become truly loyal to the King's Men, she dies by suicide by jumping off a balcony.

Likewise, when he was first introduced, Arondir was a great character. Sure, he didn't actually do much, with much of his screen time being dedicated to an attempt at a romance between him and the now-deceased Bronwyn (Nazanin Boniadi). And yet, Ismael Cruz Córdova has always played his role with great gusto, giving Arondir a strong personality that makes him feel like more than just a Legolas knock-off. But that just makes his departure all the more upsetting.

Indeed, Arondir gets little more to do in Season 3 than worry about Bronwyn's annoying son Theo (Tyroe Muhafidin). This all leads to a confrontation in Episode 4 when Sauron orders Theo — now a Ringwraith — to murder the elf. A tragic end, sure, but with little buildup.

With Arondir and Eären's deaths, "The Rings of Power" is quickly getting rid of its original characters. After all, the show had already killed off one of its best brand-new additions in Adar (Sam Hazeldine and Joseph Mawle), while the Harfoots that were so essential in Seasons 1 and 2 are nowhere to be found in Season 3 so far. Granted, Theo's still around, but he's likely to be killed soon as well (due to that whole being a Ringwraith thing). That just leaves Kemen (Leon Wadham), the tiring nepo baby at the center of the Númenor story.

Instead, it's clear "The Rings of Power" is currently more focused on bringing in previously missing characters from J.R.R. Tolkien's source material, like Isildur's brother Anárion (Andrew Richardson) and Middle-earth's own Odysseus, i.e. Celeborn (Jamie Campbell Bower), who's married to Morfydd Clark's elfish warrior Galadriel. It makes sense for the show's writers to be doing this right now, too, as we're getting closer and closer to the end of the series' reported five-season plan. But that means "The Rings of Power" will also have less and less time to explore any of its original characters from this point on.

Another problem is the show's condensed timeline, as "The Rings of Power" is trying to tell a story that spans thousands of years in Tolkien's literature over a much, much shorter period. That means we still have a lot of major "Lord of the Rings"-related developments to get through, be it Elendil and his sons founding the kingdom of Gondor or Celeborn creating Lothlórien with Galadriel. Will all that and more to cover, there's just no more room for the likes of Arondir the wood elf.

#3508. Jeremy O. Harris EPs ‘American Theater,’ About a Canceled MAGA Theater Director’s Bizarre Attempted Comeback — Watch the Trailer

Can a conservative “canceled” theater director rise from the ashes of his own ruination — and in this climate? That’s one of the questions top of mind for filmmakers Nicholas Clark and Dylan Frederick, whose provocative, Christopher Guest-style nonfiction film “American Theater” (except it’s a docu-, not mockumentary) is rolling out in select theaters now. A Slamdance Grand Jury Prize winner for documentary in 2025, the film is also executive-produced by Jeremy O. Harris.

“American Theater” follows Brian Clowdus — openly gay, conservative, and formerly of the Serenbe Playhouse in Georgia, who was taken down in 2019 over allegations of racism, misconduct, unsafe working conditions, and a gamut of other accusations. Clark and Frederick follow Clowdus, now a MAGA Republican, and a troupe of other conservative actors to an abandoned cabin in middle-of-nowhere Georgia where Clowdus plots the ultimate revenge: a community musical theater retelling of, of course, the 1692 Salem witch trials, riffing on Arthur Miller’s “The Crucible” (which, published in 1953, isn’t yet in the public domain). Related Stories Fan Edits Are Legal with Moonbeem, Distribution Network Hosts Approved Clips from Filmmakers ‘How to Rob a Bank’ Review: David Leitch’s Fun and Poppy YouTube Heist Movie Almost Gets Away with It

“This film was about a really fucked-up figure and a person with really fucked-up politics,” Harris told IndieWire over the phone from Copenhagen, where the Tony nominee is rehearsing a new play. “When you have unwelcoming and fucked-up politics, or a person who has unwelcoming, fucked-up politics at the center of the art you’re making, it can feel like potentially you’re endorsing their politics or celebrating them, especially because we don’t live in times that are deeply discursive or critical. At least having my name in the headline should be an invitation to certain people that maybe would’ve been like, ‘I’m not watching that,’ that maybe this is something for them.”

In taking on someone who was once a formidable presence in the Southern regional theater space, Harris said the filmmakers saw “this opportunity to embed themselves in the company for his comeback show. They realized there was a chance to look at the type of fringe character that utilized MAGA for the grifting machine that it is. MAGA is a magnet for a lot of displaced people, and theater has so many displaced people. Even thinking about the fact that one of the most famous people that stormed the Capitol was in the regional production of ‘Jesus Christ Superstar’ meant that there were ways in which the theater community wasn’t looking at some of the foxes among the lambs in our own community. This gave them the opportunity to be those foxes, or not even foxes, but to be flies on the wall of this maker who was exploiting a lot of displaced people.”

A recent Cobble Hill Cinemas screening of “American Theater” was moderated by journalist Ludwig Hurtado. Next up, the film will be available to rent on the Letterboxd Video Store, so locally driven screenings also aim to bring audiences to that platform.

“One of the things that’s very sad to me is that amongst the distributors, the ones that one would think have the most bandwidth and power to really uplift these microbudget filmmakers who are truly keeping the torch burning for that independent American brio that put American independent cinema on the map and right next to so many other stalwarts of world cinema, a lot of them are being, I think, more cautious about who they’re distributing,” Harris said. “Distribution costs are so large right now that I think that they don’t really know what to do with movies so small. And so Letterboxd has become this really great outlet because there’s such a vibrant community there who are just excited to see films and excited to learn that filmmakers who maybe are in circumstances similar to their own as movie watchers are making films.”

In a separate statement, Frederick said, “The film takes place in 2021, when Trump was facing the possibility of spending the rest of his life in prison, his political future was uncertain, and conservatives were batching DeSantis ‘24 tank tops. Democrats just had the best night of their lives in the midterms, and MAGA folks may find themselves at a low point, but it’s useful to remember that we’ve actually been here before.”

Clark added, “There was a moment when many people assumed the Trump era had come to an end. ‘American Theater’ tells a story of the Trump supporters during that time who were dedicated to figuring out what would come next. In this instance, their idea was an allegorical cancel culture musical about the Salem witch trials. It did not go anywhere near as planned, and our movie tells that story. But ultimately, everything that has happened to us as a nation ever since has only recontextualized what we saw within this brief moment in time.”

Watch the trailer for “American Theater” below, and see a list of upcoming screenings on a nationwide tour via Antenna Releasing.

#3507. The Top 10 Movies Right Now, According to Streaming Data

The most streamed movie in October was Steven Spielberg's Disclosure Day, but half of the month's top ten is made up of season-appropriate horror movies. This year's two most successful horror movies, Backrooms and Obsession, made the list; so did a classic (Halloween from 1978) and an art movie about the genre that Halloween created,Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma. Perfect double feature. Rounding out the list is the all-around-excellent Hokum. If you're not into horror, you might like Golden Arm, a comedy that refused to die, star-studded comedy The Invite, or ultimate crowd-pleaser Project Hail Mary.

Legendary director Steven Spielberg returns to the extraterrestrials he loves so much with a thriller that's a spiritual sequel to Close Encounters of the Third Kind. Disclosure Day details the events that lead up to the revelation that aliens are among us. Josh O’Connor plays Dr. Daniel Kellner, a cybersecurity expert for a government contractor who uncovers explosive evidence that his employers would kill to keep secret. Meanwhile, a TV meteorologist (Emily Blunt) begins speaking in an alien language. It all sets the stage for a series of set pieces and chases leading to the biggest revelation in human history. Stream Disclosure Day on Peacock.

Director Kane Parsons' analog horror breakthrough is proof that atmosphere, mood, and a fascinating story is scarier than CGI monsters every time. Based on the viral YouTube series of the same name, Backrooms tells the story of Clark (Chiwetel Ejiofor), a store owner who discovers a labyrinthian liminal space in his furniture shop's basement. Renate Reinsve plays his therapist, who goes downstairs for a visit and does not find it easy to return. A hit with critics—Backrooms is sitting at 86% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes—and audiences, Backrooms is a delicious Halloween treat for horror fans. Stream Backrooms on HBO Max.

Director Curry Barker is still in his 20s, but his debut theatrical feature is the kind of horror film that changes the entire genre. Obsession is a classic "be careful what you wish for" story that feels fresh thanks to its talented young cast, unpredictable plot, and careful pace. Michael Johnston plays a young man too scared to tell his crush how he feels, so he wishes she'd fall in love with him instead. The result is a nightmare embodied by Inde Navarrette, whose portrayal of the villain/victim is at once harrowing, terrifying, and heartbreaking. Obsession is the best horror movie I've seen in years. Stream Obsession on Peacock.

This comedy-drama from A24 is packed with heavy-hitting actors. Olivia Wilde, who also directed the film, plays Angela, and Seth Rogen plays her husband, Joe. With the straight-laced couple's marriage on thin ice, Angela and Joe invite their more, uh, open-minded neighbors Piña, played by Penélope Cruz, and Hawk, played by Edward Norton, over for dinner. The evening unravels in hilarious ways, changing everyone's life. If you're a fan of smart, honest comedy, you will really like The Invite. Stream The Invite on HBO Max.

With Hokum, Director Damian McCarthy (Oddity, Caveat) carefully builds a suffocatingly creepy story around Adam Scott's portrayal of Ohm Bauman, a celebrity novelist and unmitigated jerk who travels to the isolated Bilberry Woods Hotel in Ireland to scatter the ashes of his parents and finish his book. Bauman soon learns that the lore of the hotel includes an ancient witch who feeds her victims to the creatures of hell, and she might be more than just a local legend. Hokum is a horror movie for fans of dreadful atmosphere and careful pacing instead of gore or jump-scares. Stream Hokum on Hulu.

With a title like this, it's not going to be a normal movie. Director Jane Schoenbrun’s I Saw the TV Glow and We're All Going to the World's Fair are two of the most fascinating, fiercely original horror movies of the last decade, and their third film follows in those strange footfalls. While it's technically a meta re-imagining of the slasher genre, Miasma goes way deeper than Scream ever could. It's a postmodern exploration of why the slasher genre's cocktail of sex, death, and subversion casts such a strong spell on interesting, weird people. Definitely see this movie. Stream Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma on Mubi.

When Golden Arm was released in 2021, not many people paid attention—with the pandemic in full swing, people didn't seem to have room for a quirky, indie comedy about a woman's quest to win the ladies' arm-wrestling championship—but it's a new age, and you should stream Golden Arm. It's sitting on a perfect score at Rotten Tomatoes, the movie's stars, Mary Holland and Betsy Sodaro, are charming and hilarious, and you can catch Golden Arm on Fandango, a free streaming service. What's not to love? Stream Golden Arm on Fandango or Prime Video.

In this crowd-pleasing sci-fi flick, Ryan Gosling stars as Ryland Grace, a middle school science teacher who is blasted into the firmament in a last-ditch effort to save the world. Grace is the only person on Earth who might know how to protect the sun from a cosmic infection that threatens all life, but he's definitely not an astronaut and doesn't see himself as a hero either. Will he rise to the occasion and learn something about his inner strength and resilience while saving us all from death? My money is on, "yeah, probably." Stream Project Hail Mary on MGM+, Prime Video, and Philo.

Hundreds of slasher movies have been released since Halloween came out in 1978, but none have surpassed the original. Michael Myers' expressionless visage and the synthesizer theme have become universally recognized cultural signifiers for "horror movie," and every shot in Halloween has been stolen countless times, but the movie is so good, it's still scary. Watch or re-watch Halloween now! Stream Halloween on Philo, AMC+, and Prime Video.

Directed by and starring Ben Affleck, Animals is a thriller that tells the story of Mark Kimball, a Los Angeles mayoral candidate whose son is kidnapped and held for ransom. Having spent every dime on his outsider campaign, Kimball is forced to turn to extreme methods to guarantee his son's safe return, even if it conflicts with his public persona as a man of the people. Animals is a taut, expertly directed movie that should more than satisfy fans of political thrillers. Stream Animals on Netflix.

#3506. Netflix's Hit Spy Thriller Returns and Takes Over Streaming Charts

The British spy series has returned with new episodes

Keira Knightley has a knack for playing smart, determined women who refuse to back down when things get dangerous. Whether she's exposing government secrets in Official Secrets, investigating a serial killer in Boston Strangler, or navigating a deadly mystery aboard a luxury yacht in Netflix's The Woman in Cabin 10, Knightley has become a natural fit for tense thrillers.

Now, she's back in the spy business with a returning Netflix series that's attracting plenty of streaming attention.

The second season of Black Doves arrived on Nov. 5, and the spy thriller wasted little time climbing Netflix's charts. The series reached No. 2 on the global Netflix TV chart, according FlixPatrol. Netflix's own weekly figures also show that season 2 of Black Doves attracted 3.8 million views between Nov. 2 and Nov. 8, making it the fourth most-watched English-language series of the week.

Black Doves follows Helen Webb (Knightley), a seemingly ordinary politician's wife and mother who is secretly working as a spy for a clandestine organization called the Black Doves. For a decade, she has been passing along her husband's political secrets to the organization while maintaining her carefully constructed family life.

However, Helen's double life becomes considerably more dangerous when her secret lover, Jason (Andrew Koji), is murdered. Her employer calls in her longtime friend Sam Young (Ben Whishaw), an assassin with a complicated past, to protect her while she investigates the killing. Their search soon uncovers a much larger conspiracy involving London's criminal underworld and international politics.

The first season premiered on Netflix on Dec. 5, 2024, with six episodes. Its follow-up brings Knightley and Whishaw back for another six-episode adventure, continuing the story of their unlikely partnership.

Black Doves has also received a strong reception from critics. Season 1 currently holds a 92% critics' score and 64% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes. Season 2 has performed even better with critics, earning a 96% score, alongside a 66% audience rating.

#3505. The Best Ways For Star Trek Fans To Play Magic's New Set: A Guide For Beginner Players

When I sat down at my friendly local game store to participate in a pre-release drafting event for Magic: The Gathering's new "Star Trek" set, several players saw the Enterprise tattoo on my forearm and asked me the same question. If a longtime Magic player wanted to sample "Star Trek," what was the best place for them to start?

Ironically, I was there to ask the Mirror Universe version of that same question: If a longtime "Star Trek" fan wanted to sample the new Magic set, what's the best place for them to start?

I am new to Magic, having only picked up the game a few months ago to prime myself for the new "Trek" release. And one thing Magic and "Star Trek" have in common is that they're both absolutely daunting at first blush. One is a collectible card game with over 30 years of history and dozens of ways to play. The other is a sci-fi universe with nearly 1,000 episodes of television and 13 movies, with dozens of possible entry points.

I can answer one question immediately. "Trek" newbies should start with "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds," with its glossy production values and modern streaming sensibilities, before backtracking and sampling the various other shows and finding the one that connects with their tastes. (This is a sometimes controversial opinion, but I stick by it.)

But the other question involved some legwork, a lot of time spent at a gaming table, a great deal more time sorting through cards, and even a question proposed to the lead designers of the set itself. So, what is the best way for a "Star Trek" fan to sample the new Magic: The Gathering set? Here's what I learned.

One thing I will not do here is explain the rules of Magic: The Gathering, which are intuitive and easy to learn, but challenging to master. There are countless online resources to learn before you try anything I recommend below. I'm writing this piece under the assumption you intend to seek those out on your own.

The best way to truly dive in headfirst is to visit your local gaming shop and participate in a sealed or drafting event. Naturally, this is dependent on your location and whether your local gaming shop is an inviting and safe space (shout out to Mothership Games in Austin, Texas for playing host to my first sealed event). If such a place exists for you, check the calendar and see what's on offer. The good news is that the "Star Trek" set is brand new and there should be plenty of opportunities.

At events like these, players are organized into one-on-one matches and construct their decks from scratch, tearing open booster packs, examine their cards, and trying to build the most effective strategy possible around a 40-card deck. While experienced players will have an edge, they can't bring finely honed and powerful decks from home to immediately wipe the floor with you. Everyone starts at square one. And "Star Trek" fans should take very easily to this format, since the characters you'd expect to be powerful tend to have cards that are powerful. It also leads to some amusing team-ups, like how my winning deck involved an unlikely alliance between Deanna Troi and Gul Dukat.

In a friendly shop with a friendly crowd, this is Magic at its purest: a direct, competitive game where tactics at the table are as important as the strategy behind your deck construction. And the mechanics in the "Trek" set are intuitive and mesh well, meaning that creating a deck that functions as needed is fairly straightforward, and going with your gut choices (i.e., building around characters you like) often leads to strong results.

I can hear your next question: You don't have access to a local shop, or you don't feel comfortable going to one, so what's the best way to play at home? Once again, there are options.

You and a friend (or more) could always buy booster packs, tearing them open and building personal collections and constructing 60-card decks for standard play. However, I would recommend booster packs being the start of your collection, and once you have bought a few, track down single cards to complete your strategy rather than buying more and blindly hoping for strong pulls.

Another option is for you and a friend to buy a pre-release kit, as there are always plenty leftover after the initial week of special event. Use these to construct imperfect but fun starter decks to learn the game, and then grow and expand those decks as you see fit, doubling down on the characters and strategies you're enjoying.

However, the best at-home experience would be to pick up one of the set's Draft Night boxes, which are pricy but offer bang for your buck: enough cards for four friends to craft decks and go head-to-head for an evening, leaving everyone with enough cards to build upon in the future.

However, all of these options require tinkering, and suggest that you'll enjoy the process of building a deck as much as playing one. These options require additional legwork, additional financial investment, and even a bit of luck (although that can be mitigated by buying single cards from reputable online and brick-and-mortar shops). If you want to truly just dive into the game itself and skip the rest of the process, there is another way.

When I had a chance to speak to the key designers behind Magic: The Gathering's "Star Trek" set during a launch event in Los Angeles, I asked if the new set was friendly for "Star Trek" fans with no gaming experience, and if they had a recommendation on where to start.

First, they noted that the set was designed with new players in mind and puts narrative first. A card will generally behave like its counterpart in the "Star Trek" universe, so a fan knows that a Captain Kirk card will be a bit more headstrong and aggressive while Spock will allow for more wily, thoughtful strategy. This means a "Trek" fan should be able to grasp the new cards fairly quickly, using their existing knowledge as a crutch.

Second, they highlighted their recommendation for the best way to sample the game: the "Star Trek" commander decks.

Commander is the most popular format in Magic, where players utilize 100 card decks in four-player games that are slowly paced, socially driven, and generally take an entire evening to play. Think of them as more of a board game experience — or a nerd poker night — than a standard Magic set. Many Magic sets are accompanied by a few pre-constructed commander decks, which players can purchase, open, and play immediately without any prep. The "Star Trek" set has four of them: Federation Fleet, We Are the Borg, Klingon Fury, and Landing Party.

Specifically, the designers recommended the Federation Fleet commander deck as their choice for a "Star Trek" fan hoping to play the game.

Naturally, the next step was to test the designers' suggestion. I rounded up three friends and assigned them each a different Star Trek commander deck, taking Federation Fleet for myself. It's easy to see why this one was recommended: With Picard on the cover and a deck full of '90s "Trek" staples, it's the most popular era of the franchise in one 100-card deck.

Our four-player game took over three hours, and frankly, it was some of the best Magic I've ever played, with all four decks interacting in surprising and wild ways that left everyone at the table screaming and laughing. The "Trek" fans were impressed by the thematic touches, and how the mechanics relate to character personalities and motives, while the Magic players simply relished in the new design elements. I squeaked out a win, but only after the Borg player staged a comeback that essentially wiped out the table. My victory told a story in of itself: Dr. Bashir threw himself at the Borg player, perishing, but in the process, activated his ability to resurrect Ro Laren from the dead, activating her ability and ending the Borg threat once and for all.

After seeing the commander decks in action, I'm inclined to agree with the designers' recommendation. The Borg deck is scary and powerful, but makes them an immediate threat the other players will team up against to defeat. The Klingon deck is pure aggression, which may work against a new player's inherent shyness. The Landing Part deck, with its focus on Original Series characters, is fairly straightforward, but has a lot of moving pieces to consider. The mechanical simplicity of the Federation Fleet deck, and its arsenal of beloved characters, makes it easy to grasp and understand quickly.

Much like with "Star Trek" itself, there are countless ways to get into Magic: The Gathering, and no incorrect way. Ultimately, I agree with the designers: the pre-constructed commander decks, and specifically the Federation Fleet deck, are the best point of entry. Ideally, you'd buy all four and learn with friends for the best possible experience.

But like with "Star Trek" itself, you should be warned: once Magic has sucked you in, be prepared to be sucked in for the long haul.

Just yesterday I was sweating through a scorching summer night and now when I climb into bed, it’s like stepping into an igloo. Either way is bad news for my sleep and can result in 3 a.m. wake-ups. No wonder all the best mattresses we’ve tried have passed rigorous temperature regulation tests.

The best cooling mattresses use heat dissipating materials to kick out night sweats and counteract heatwaves so you’re able to snooze soundly. And when it comes to cooling beds, the Bear Elite Hybrid is the best we’ve ever tested.

But recently I’ve been hands-on with the Eight Sleep Pod 6 and Orion Sleep System, two of the best smart mattresses that use active cooling to create even temperatures. These high-tech systems deliver impressive hands-on cooling but at a high price. So in the Black Friday mattress and sleep sales, which should you buy? I'm here to advise you based on our extensive testing and my own experience with all three cooling beds.

The Eight Sleep Pod 6 is the most expensive of the three, with a queen coming in at $2,899 MSRP. The Orion is cheaper with an MSRP of $2,395. The Bear Elite Hybrid has an MSRP of $2,284 for a queen, but regular Bear mattress sales can knock it as low as $1,370.40.

Keep in mind, both the Eight Sleep Pod 6 and the Orion are covers only. The Elite Hybrid is the only option that's actually a mattress.

As well as being the priciest upfront, the Eight Sleep Pod 6 is the only one with a mandatory subscription. Starting at $17/month, it includes sleep tracking and is essential for operating the Pod. Orion also has a sleep tracking subscription but it's optional (although more expensive at $250/year). Bear, of course, is subscription-free.

Bear blows both smart covers out of the water when it comes to benefits, offering a 365-night sleep trial and a limited lifetime warranty. Orion and Eight Sleep both offer just a 30-night trial and 2-year warranty.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

With the launch of the Pod 6, Eight Sleep expanded into twin sizes, offering more options for solo sleepers. A twin is now only $1,899 (was $1,999) while there's $200 off larger sizes. Eight Sleep sales are never blockbusters so this is a noteworthy price drop, although we're hopeful more discounts will appear before Black Friday.

A queen-size smart mattress cover for under $2,000 is a rare bargain and in the Orion Black Friday sale there's up to $600 off this climate control system. Sizes are limited (just queen, king, and Cal king as of writing) but the price is fantastic. A bigger discount is unlikely, so now's the time to shop.

The Bear Elite Hybrid sells at a competitive price for a cooling hybrid mattress, particularly one with a luxury pillow-top. There's usually 30% off at Bear but keep an eye out for the 35% off deal that reliably appears over the holidays. Right now, though, you can get 40% off plus free accessories when you use our TOMS40 code at the checkout, bringing the price of a queen down to $1,370.40.

The Pod 6 and Orion Sleep System both come in two parts: the cover and a control tower. The cover is fitted with water pipes, attach to the tower via tube.

In terms of design, the tower is the primary difference between the two. The Orion tower is bigger and bulkier but also has a more design-forward finish. The Eight Sleep Pod 6 is quieter, however.

The Bear Elite Hybrid is an entirely different beast. One of the best hybrid mattresses, it's made from layers of mattress springs and foams. The cover is woven with Celliant fibers to draw away heat, while a copper-infused foam layer further aids temperature control.

The Eight Sleep Pod 6 and Orion covers are designed to make minimal difference to the support and cushioning of your mattress. I tested both on the Leesa Original mattress and, overall, I think this is accurate. That means your comfort is dependent on the mattress beneath.

As one of the best mattresses in a box you can buy, we were impressed with the support and cushioning of the Bear Elite Hybrid. It comes in three firmness levels (I tried the Medium and it's one of my favorite mattresses for side sleepers) so there's an option for nearly all sleep styles.

Dive into our Bear Elite Hybrid mattress review to learn more about the pressure relief, edge support and motion isolation of this top-rated mattress.

The Eight Sleep and Orion take a hands-on approach to temperature regulation. Both are active climate control systems, pumping water through tiny pipes in the mattress cover so the surface retains the perfect feel.

From my experience, both are highly effective. I slept on the Orion Sleep System during the change from summer to fall, meaning some days I had all the windows open, and other days I was flirting with turning the heating up. Right now, I'm using my Eight Sleep Pod 6 on some frosty nights.

Both covers keep the temperature at 'snug', staying far away from 'shivering' or 'sauna'. I haven't had a sweaty 3 a.m. wake-up in months.

Under our thermal cam, the Orion Sleep showed its prowess. It kept a steady feel the entire time, with no temperature swings even when tester Frances Daniels climbed on. And while normally a thermal outline remains long after our tester has left the mattress, on the Orion, all signs of Frances were gone in minutes.

The Bear Elite Hybrid has a more traditional approach to cooling. (Although with its Celliant fibers and copper-infused foams, it's hardly simple.)

Despite its lack of active cooling technology, our hands-on testing showed heat didn't linger in the Bear Elite. And our thermal cam backed us up. While the Bear Elite Hybrid warmed quickly, it kicked out excess heat at an incredible pace. After just four minutes of our tester leaving the mattress, it had nearly returned to the original temperature.

While the Bear Elite Hybrid is impressive, it's not as versatile as the Eight Sleep or the Orion Sleep System. And nothing touches the Eight Sleep when it comes to quick changes — buttons on the side of the cover allow you to adjust the temperature without unlocking your phone.

Orion and Eight Sleep both offer sleep tracking alongside their advanced cooling features. For Eight Sleep, the sleep tracking is part of the mandatory subscription. For Orion, it's an optional add-on.

I've tested both alongside my Oura Ring 5, our top rated sleep tracker this year. Overall, I've been impressed with the quality and accuracy of the information. Both capture sleep stages and duration that line up with both the data from my Oura Ring and my recollection of the night.

However when it comes to the details, the Eight Sleep Pod 6 is the winner. It captures a massive amount of data and displays it in easy-to-read graphics. For the Orion, sleep tracking feels like an add-on. With Eight Sleep, it's integral.

Eight Sleep also has a smart alarm built into the the cover, which vibrates when it senses a light sleep stage. Orion preps you to wake up with gentle warmth but the Eight Sleep Pod 6 does a better job at rousing you.

✅ You experience hot flashes: The Eight Sleep's hot flash mode works to quickly counteract sudden temperature fluctuations. It should kick in while you're sleeping but you can also turn it on in the app if you feel a hot flash coming on.

✅ You want detailed sleep tracking: Eight Sleep's Autopilot delivers accurate and detailed sleep data. Plus, it puts it all into handy graphics to give you an instant picture of sleep trends and changes.

✅ You want control at the touch of a button: Simply press the button on the side of the cover to turn the heat up or down in the night. The Eight Sleep isn't a mind reader, so this allows you to tweak it to fit your needs.

✅ You want smart cooling without the expense: The Orion can match the Eight Sleep (and the Bear Elite Hybrid) when it comes to temperature control, offering active cooling at a lower price.

✅ You and your partner can never agree on the thermostat: Both the Orion and Eight Sleep allow you to set a different temperature on each side of the mattress. With the Orion, you can do so for less.

✅ You need a new bed: If you go for the Orion or Eight Sleep, you'll need to buy a new mattress as well (or stick with the one you have). The Bear Elite Hybrid doesn't just offer cooling — it's a great bed all round.

✅ You don't experience major temperature swings: If you often wake up stuffy but hot sleeping isn't ruining your night, you might not require high-tech active cooling. The Bear will keep you comfortable without the expense.

#3503. Henry Cavill Comments On Superman Return After James Gunn's DC Studios Exit

Henry Cavill was a great Superman who never got a great Superman movie, and that should have been the end of it. But it's now 2026, and we're still talking about whether Cavill will return as the Man of Steel. With James Gunn and Peter Safran "stepping down" as DC Studios co-heads, DC's cinematic future is very much up in the air, and now Cavill is saying he'd always be open to returning as Supes.

During an Inverse interview, the actor was asked if he'd ever play the DC hero again and seemed open to the idea. "Look, there's lots of fantastic storylines," he replied. "There's always a lot of opportunity. As the pigeon sang to Fievel in 'An American Tail,' "never say never." And I buy into that." It's hardly surprising, given that Cavill and his former DC Extended Universe colleague Dwayne Johnson once launched a pretty bizarre attempt to remain in the cinematic universe, most pointedly with 2022's immediately forgettable "Black Adam." At the time, Cavill proudly announced his return as Superman in a social media post following the film's release, but it never actually amounted to anything more than that and left Gunn deeply (and understandably) confused about what was even happening.

Since then, Gunn has introduced us to an all-new Man of Steel in David Corenswet, who made his debut in the charming crowd pleaser that was 2025's "Superman" and is set to return in the 2027 follow-up "Man of Steel." But with Gunn out at DC Studios it remains to be seen where the Corenswet version of the character and his story will go from there. Meanwhile, we've got Cavill telling Inverse he "had such a wonderful time playing Superman in the past" and "would never say never now." It's a bit tiresome, no?

Directly after the extremely perplexing return of Henry Cavill's Superman in "Black Adam," the DCEU collapsed with back to back flops in 2023. Meanwhile, James Gunn was gearing up to launch his DC Universe, which is why the whole situation left him baffled – especially since he was already actively preparing his DC reboot at the time. He wasn't the only one, either. Audiences thought they'd seen the last of the so-called Snyderverse after 2023, but Gunn chose to soft reboot DC with a new cinematic universe that retained elements of the old one. What's more, calls to reinstate the DCEU persist even today.

Now that Gunn and Peter Safran have been removed (er, "stepped down") from DC Studios, it looks as though Skydance CEO David Ellison — who's running the newly-merged Warner Bros. and Paramount — is planning to pretty much dismantle everything Gunn built at DC to prepare for yet another reboot.

Whatever Ellison and his new president and chief creative officer of DC Studios, Jeremy Latcham, have planned for the brand, I think it's safe to say we really don't need more talk of Cavill suiting back up. Had the actor left this character alone following 2017's "Justice League," it might have been a thrill to hear of his possible return a decade later. As it stands, like calls to restore the Snyderverse, this seems to be the discussion that never dies. Perhaps it's that lingering feeling that Cavill never got the movie he deserved, or the fact that Superman remains his best-known character. But for now it would be nice to go a few years without hearing about anything from the Snyderverse era coming back.

#3502. The Top 10 TV Series Right Now, According to Streaming Data

October's ten most-streamed series are packed with your future favorite shows. There's a couple of modernizations of horror franchises for Halloween (Carrie and Crystal Lake), as well as new horror series Below and Phony. There's an excellent new superhero series Lanterns, sprawling family drama East of Eden, and new seasons of favorites Ted Lasso, Slow Horses, The Diplomat, and Mobland. So don't even try to tell anyone there's nothing on.

Horror master Mike Flanagan (Haunting of Hill House, Midnight Mass) re-imagines Stephen King's tale of teenage telekinesis, taking the story from the 1970s to now, complete with cyber bullying, smart phones, and a modern sensibility. The core of the tale, though, remains the same, as does the titular character's bloody coming-of-age. Powered by a talented young cast that includes Siena Agudong as Susan and Summer H. Howell as the title character, Carrie is a trick-or-treat for horror fans. Stream Carrie on Prime.

Based on John Steinbeck's pillar of Western literature, East of Eden follows three generations of the hardscrabble Hamilton family and the upscale Trask family, farming and ranching clans in California's Salinas Valley. The show's production is a multigenerational story too: It was written and created by Zoe Kazan, whose grandpa Elia directed the 1955 film version of East of Eden. All respect to Elia Kazan, but Steinbeck's story is so massive, it needs a seven-part mini-series. East of Eden is the kind of sprawling, melodramatic story that episodic television was made for. Stream East of Eden on Netflix.

Like Carrie, Crystal Lake reimagines a horror classic—in this case, Friday the 13th—and expands the lore even beyond the 12 films in the franchise. If you've ever wondered how Pamela Voorhees, played here by Linda Cardellini, became a serial murderer, and how her son Jason ended up a relentless, camp-counselor-killing-machine who lives at the bottom of a lake, Crystal Lake has all the answers. In a lot of ways, this show is better than all of the movies. Stream Crystal Lake on Peacock.

Apple TV's Slow Horses delivers a realistic, nuanced take on espionage by detailing the lives of the losers of British Intelligence. Instead of chiseled good guys and gals saving the world, the agents of Slough House are a team of dysfunctional, troubled souls trying to do the right thing (usually) in a morally gray world, just like real agents. Their leader, gruff, obnoxious Jackson Lamb, is played to perfection by Gary Oldman. Slow Horses has an almost perfect Rotten Tomatoes score over its first five seasons, and season 6 is setting new records. Stream Slow Horses on Apple TV+.

DC's TV revamp of Green Lantern details what happens when experienced Lantern Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler) trains the new guy, John Stewart (Aaron Pierre), on how to wield the mysterious and powerful Green Lantern Ring. It's a reserved, neo-noir style take on the comic mythos, as the heroes investigate a series of murders tied to an extraterrestrial threat. Lanterns is pulling in a better than 90% fresh ratings from Rotten Tomatoes, so it's definitely worth a stream. Stream Lanterns on HBO Max.

Created by Jesse McKeown and starring Josh Hartnett, Charlie Heaton, and Mackenzie Davis, Below is set in a Newfoundland fishing village beset with aquatic horror. When the Canadian government offers the residents of Snooks Arm a ton of money to relocate, no one really knows why, but ice fisherman Calvin Penney (Hartnett) suspects it has something to do with the monster he saw under the ice when he was a child. If you like taut creature feature style horror, check out Below. Stream Below on Netflix.

Season four of Ted Lasso sees the title character, played by Jason Sudeikis, returning to the UK to take on a new challenge: coaching the Lady Greyhounds, AFC Richmond's second-division women's football team. This multiple Emmy Award-winning series still has all the heart, humor, and positivity of the original run. Stream Ted Lasso on Apple TV+.

The mystery that drives creepy coming-of-age drama Phony is killer: Sonny Cooke, played by Sam Nivola, is a teenager with a very close relationship to his devoted single mother Ellen, played by Connie Britton. After a freak car accident, he wakes up convinced that his mom is an impostor. She looks the same, but there's something off about her in a way that Sonny can't describe, so he sets out to solve the mystery. Phony is rated over 90% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes. Stream Phony on Hulu.

In season four of political thriller series The Diplomat, the Kate Wyler, played by Keri Russell, finds that diplomatic relations between the U.S. and the UK are starting to crumble, and so is her marriage. Meanwhile, U.S. president Grace Penn, played by Allison Janney, and VP Hal Wyler, played by Rufus Sewell, continue their conspiracy to steal a Russian super-weapon, nudging the nation toward war with our longtime adversary. In other words, it's an international mess, with a few powerful people keeping the world from descending into chaos. If you like political intrigue, this is the series for you. Stream The Diplomat on Netflix.

Who doesn't love a sprawling organized crime drama? In Mobland, the crime is being organized in Great Britain, where two warring London crime families, the Harrigans and Stevensons, are locked in a battle for underworld power. In the middle of the crossfire is Harry Da Souza, a gritty fixer played to gruff perfection by Tom Hardy. Season 2 finds Da Souza in the unenviable position of holding together the Harrigan family on the verge of civil war. If you like backstabbing, scheming, murder, and other tropes of high-stakes crime thrillers, you'll like Mobland. Stream Mobland on Paramount+.

Young farmboy Christophe starts tilting his head unintentionally, which eventually leads to a scoliosis diagnosis and an iron corset he has to wear everywhere.
