#3499. This New Chrome AI Feature Reads Your Gmail to Make Filling Out Web Forms Easier

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Google Chrome is making it easier to autofill online forms with more than just contact information and credit card numbers. For users with Personal Intelligence enabled, Gemini will now suggest items like order numbers, tracking information, membership IDs, and booking confirmations from Gmail messages when completing forms in Chrome.

Chrome's expanded autofill capabilities use Gemini to read your emails and surface suggestions, meaning you don't have to click back and forth between tabs or manually search for codes or confirmations in your inbox. When you click a form field that has a corresponding piece of data, a pop-up menu appears and indicates that an item is "Suggested by Gemini." You can click this to autofill the suggestion as well as open an additional menu to see the specific source (the original email) or remove the suggestion. The latter doesn't delete anything from Gmail; it simply dismisses the suggestion in Chrome.

As Android Police reports, Google started testing enhanced autofill in Chrome this summer using data from other connected apps like Google Photos. The feature currently rolling out is specific to Gmail and is coming first to U.S. users who have Personal Intelligence enabled on desktop as well as in the Android and iOS apps when using Gemini in Chrome.

In the blog post announcing the enhanced autofill feature, Google states that "sensitive data is encrypted" and that users can manage autofill, including enabling or disabling enhanced suggestions, via Chrome's settings.

#3498. Legend of Zelda Officially Returns to The Wilds Era in December

It’s been a long time for Tears of the Kingdom fans

All eyes are on The Legend of Zelda right now — and for good reason. The franchise is currently in the midst of celebrating its 40th anniversary and the long-awaited remake of Ocarina of Time was released on Nov. 5, 2026, becoming the second best-selling game on the Nintendo Switch 2 less than a week after its release. But, even amid all the Ocarina excitement, it's hard to forget just how memorable earlier Switch-era Zelda titles were — particularly Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom.

Breath of the Wild came out on the Nintendo Switch in 2017, and Tears of the Kingdom followed in 2023. Both games are considered part of the franchise's Wilds era, marked by open-world exploration and non-linear gameplay. The titles are loved by critics and fans alike, with each holding a Metacritic score higher than 95. While there's been no official word yet on when Zelda fans might see a new Wilds era title built for the Nintendo Switch 2, there is a project in the works that will be sure to appeal to any Tears of the Kingdom fan.

A new statue of Link designed by FIGURIZMa is being released in December 2026. The statue, replicating Link's look and pose from official Tears of the Kingdom artwork, features Link kneeling on a floating island with the Master Sword strapped to his back. It is listed on the Sega Plaza website as being approximately 10 cm x 23 cm (roughly 4 in x 9 in), and a description of the product reads: "Pay attention to the meticulously crafted costumes and the sculpting of the master sword. We paid special attention to the texture of the pants. The rock pedestal reminiscent of the original Great Sky Island was crafted with special attention to recreating unique patterns."

The statue is a re-release of a 2024 FIGURIZMa figurine that could only be won in Sega Plaza crane games in Japan. It never quite made its way to the United States, and the statue currently sells for between $40 and $60 on resale markets. No price for the 2026 version has been confirmed on the Sega Plaza website, but the release date is listed as Dec. 25, 2026. The re-release is looking likely to be a Japanese exclusive once again, but there's good news for Zelda fans worldwide — the re-release should drive down resale prices, so more people can get their hands on this Tears of the Kingdom collectible.

The statue is the latest in a line of releases coinciding with The Legend of Zelda's 40th anniversary. Other items that have been released this year include a lineup of Hasbro action figures and a limited-edition Nintendo Switch 2 console.

#3497. Lauren Graham's 2026 Colleen Hoover Movie Is Officially Netflix's Biggest Streaming Hit

Is there anyone more representative of the recent romance novel adaptation trend than Colleen Hoover? Hollywood loves a BookTok phenomenon, and Hoover's novels seem designed in a lab to appeal to the "crying, screaming, throwing up" crowds on social media, who simply cannot resist what The Guardian called Hoover's "normcore thrillers."

But the film also has some other things working in its favor. For one it stars the talented Maika Monroe, and it also features Lauren Graham, who's best known for playing Lorelai Gilmore on "Gilmore Girls." Graham does a decent job with the material in "Reminders of Him," and regardless of how you feel about the film as a whole, it's nice to see her in a modern-day melodrama.

"Reminders of Him" is directed by British director Vanessa Caswill, who oversaw Netflix's 2023 romantic comedy "Love at First Sight," after honing her chops on BBC series such as "Little Women," "Gold Digger," and "Thirteen." This was another romance movie based on a popular book, and wouldn't you know, the movie went straight to the top of the Netflix charts upon its release. Now, Caswill has done it again with "Reminders of Him," though this one had a successful box office run under its belt before taking over Netflix.

The film stars Maika Monroe as Kenna Rowan, who made a tragic mistake years earlier that landed her in prison. After serving her sentence, Kenna returns to her Wyoming hometown, where she hopes to finally meet her young daughter, Diem Landry (Zoe Kosovic). Sadly, Diem's grandparents Grace and Patrick Landry (Lauren Graham and Bradley Whitford) are completely opposed to the idea. But there's also a strapping young bar owner standing between her and her daughter in the form of Ledger Ward (Tyriq Withers). Turns out Ledger has been helping take care of Diem, and he's similarly concerned about Kenna's return. But as the two get to know each other, romance blossoms, and Kenna finally gets a chance at redemption.

"Reminders of Him" hit Netflix U.S. on November 10, 2026, and according to streaming viewership tracker FlixPatrol, became an instant hit. The film shot to number one on November 11, 2026, proving these Colleen Hoover adaptations remain perennially popular. No doubt we'll see plenty more Hoover books being adapted in the near future.

There are plenty of movies to avoid on Netflix, and "Reminders of Him" is right on the borderline. The film managed a 56% critic score on Rotten Tomatoes, which is higher than any other Colleen Hoover adaptation. But it also has an 87% audience score, which ties it with "It Ends With Us" for most popular among viewers on the site. Now it has managed to earn the endorsement of Netflixers, does this mean you should watch it?

Well, the movie has a few plus points. For one, it stars the Maika Monroe, who's able to shift from scream queen to swoon queen with ease. Meanwhile, Lauren Graham is given some of the more emotional scenes and does a solid job of bringing them to life. Otherwise, it's sort of okay for the first half? Monroe and her co-star, Tyriq Withers, manage to wring some believable emotion out of the script. Once they throw caution to the wind and just go for it, despite their previous reluctance to besmirch Monroe's deceased husband, everything starts to get a little ridiculous.

Joey Shapiro summed things up quite aptly in his review for the Chicago Reader, when he called "Reminders of Him" a "corny TV movie" that's "made with so much sincerity and conviction by all involved that it becomes watchable, if rarely 'good' by any stretch." If that appeals, or if you simply can't get enough of these romance movies that verge on providing some sort of interesting insight into human emotion only to fall short, then why not give this lesser-known Hoover adaptation a go.

#3496. I tested the Google Pixel Tag and it’s the most findable tracker for Android phones — plus it does something Apple AirTag can't

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Pixel Tag delivers an outstanding tracking experience for Android users, matching the AirTag’s $29 price point while beating it out with superior Precision Finding range and persistent alerts when the batter level gets low.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Over the past few years, I’ve tested my fair share of Bluetooth trackers — ranging from wallet-thin cards like the Statik SmartCard Incognito to the Pebblebee Halo, which can potentially help elderly individuals in emergency situations. Google has expanded its Find Hub network, finally giving Android users plenty of options, but many of these trackers share one glaring limitation: pinpoint proximity tracking.

While iPhone users have long enjoyed the superb performance of Precision Finding — leaning on Ultra Wideband (UWB) for pinpoint accuracy — most Android trackers don’t have that luxury. Instead, they rely on basic Bluetooth proximity that only shows broad geographic circles on a map.

Google’s Pixel Tag is one of the few Android trackers that packages Ultra Wideband (UWB) and Bluetooth Channel Sounding directly into Google’s native ecosystem. As a result, the Pixel Tag delivers true visual Precision Finding to Android devices. After putting it to the test, I found it holds one distinct advantage over the AirTag and one of the best Bluetooth trackers you can get.

Ultra-Wideband (UWB) + Bluetooth Channel Sounding

Easily the best feature of the Pixel Tag is its ability to lock down an exact position with outstanding Precision Finding range, which actually managed to outperform even Apple's AirTag 2 in my testing. Using the Find My Device app on an Android phone, you get intuitive on-screen visual guidance, complete with compass-like directional arrows and real-time distance readouts that point you right where you need to go.

While the AirTag 2 tapped out around 74 feet in my testing before dropping its Ultra Wideband connection, the Pixel Tag held on slightly farther, reaching roughly 82 feet. That extra reach eliminates the guesswork of tracking down misplaced gear, like my keys when I've completely forgotten where I left them. Plus, you can still trigger a loud audio chime if the tag slips deep between couch cushions and you can't spot it right away.

The AirTag has an unmistakable look, but Google has delivered an equally compelling design — especially when it comes to size. At just 5.4mm thick, the Pixel Tag is significantly sleeker than the AirTag, making it far less conspicuous when slipped into a standard wallet. With its minimalist, matte-finished polycarbonate body, I really dig the pebble-like aesthetic, which does a far better job of masking smudges and fingerprints than the AirTag's scratch-prone stainless steel back.

Even with that slimmed-down profile, Google didn’t cut corners on durability, outfitting it with a rugged IP67 dust- and water-resistance rating. Plus, swapping out the CR2032 coin-cell battery is painless — all it takes is a quick twist of the back cover.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Beyond tracking down my keys, wallet, backpack, or other gear, the Pixel Tag offers another standout feature you won’t find on the AirTag: the ability to ring your phone. With a simple double-press of the physical button on the front, you can instantly trigger your phone to ring at full volume — even if it's set to silent or vibrate. This reverse-finding capability is a lifesaver in a crunch when you're rushing out the door and can't find your phone anywhere.

One of the biggest annoyances I have with the AirTag is discovering weeks or even months later that it's dead. Sure, my iPhone might have sent a low-battery notification, but those alerts are easy to forget. That’s why I’m stoked about the Pixel Tag’s persistent automated reminders, which offer huge peace of mind if I overlook that initial heads-up.

Google rates the user-replaceable CR2032 coin-cell battery for up to a full year of typical use. While I haven’t had the Pixel Tag long enough to drain it down and trigger an alert firsthand, knowing Find Hub will send a notification “every 2 weeks until it’s replaced” ensures it won't quietly drop off my radar. Usually, I’m not a fan of that level of notification nagging, but in this case, it's a welcome safety net.

Despite having some key advantages over the AirTag, there’s one area where the Pixel Tag falls behind its rival: accessory availability. You can find an AirTag mount, leather loop, rugged clip, or pet collar attachment with a quick search online. The Pixel Tag, however, launches with very few options.

In fact, Google doesn't even offer any official accessories right out of the gate. The only ones I’ve been able to track down so far are basic silicone cases from Walmart. Because the Pixel Tag’s design doesn't include a built-in lanyard hole or keyring cutout, you'll need a dedicated case or adhesive mount just to attach it to your keys or backpack. For early adopters, finding the exact style or mount you want right now will require some patience while third-party makers ramp up production.

Considering how long the Pixel line has been around, you’d think Google would’ve come out with its own AirTag rival sooner. Even so, the Pixel Tag is a long-overdue addition — and it’s easily one of the most capable and well-rounded Bluetooth trackers on the market.

Between its class-leading Precision Finding range, compact design, and reverse-phone-ringing feature, it addresses the pinpoint tracking compromises that have long plagued the Android ecosystem. The only other real alternatives with Ultra Wideband support are Motorola’s Moto Tag and Samsung’s SmartTag3. You still get all the essential safeguards expected from a flagship tracker, too, including left-behind alerts and a dedicated Lost Mode that allows anyone who finds your gear to scan it and get in touch.

At $29 for a single one (or $99 for a four-pack), Google matches Apple dollar for dollar — but delivers greater range and features the AirTag simply can’t match.

The Film Independent Spirit Awards are returning to the Hollywood Palladium with a new pair of hosts in tow.

Film Independent, the nonprofit organization dedicated to championing independent storytelling and supporting artists, announced on Wednesday, December 10 that “Maddie’s Secret” stars Kate Berlant and John Early will co-host the 2027 Film Independent Spirit Awards.

The acclaimed comedians, actors and longtime creative collaborators, who have written and/or starred together in other projects like Emmy-nominated variety special “Would It Kill You to Laugh?,” and cult comedy series “Search Party” will bring their comedic sensibilities to the 42nd annual Spirit Awards. We’re excited to shake things up, break a few rules and have some fun along the way.”

#3493. This Handheld Vacuum Fixed My Biggest Problem With Cleaning

We're highlighting the small changes—from useful new gadgets, to fresh productivity techniques, to efficient hacks—that are improving our lives on a weekly basis.

I may not be “messy,” exactly, but no one would describe me as “neat,” either. One of my biggest issues is that I tend to wait for a mess to get big enough to justify dragging out a full-size vacuum before I deal with it, because a full-size vacuum means finding the cord or the charger, wrestling it out of the closet, going room to room, and then putting it all away again. When the mess in question is still only a few cracker crumbs? Forget it—I'm just too lazy.

The solution to my laziness has been removing all the friction and hassle of my full-size vacuum, and instead keeping a handheld vacuum always within reach.

Though there are many handheld vacuums out there, I use the Sharper Image Dual Air Slim, which I got from Target. It's great for quickly sucking up crumbs and everyday messes, and that's exactly the job I need it to handle. The "dual air" part is what makes it more interesting than your average handheld: It's both a vacuum and a blower, so it can pull debris in or push it out, depending on what you're dealing with. I didn’t expect to need the blower at all, but I’m surprised how handy it is for blasting crumbs out of keyboard keys or loosening up stubborn debris before I suck it up.

The result is that my apartment is simply cleaner. Not because I'm spending more time cleaning overall, but because I'm no longer letting small messes pile up into big ones. When my monthly (or quarterly) deep clean does roll around, it's far less painful, because there's so much less to deal with. Perhaps this is the real upgrade: cleaning up messes the moment they happen instead of saving them up.

I love the Sharper Image Dual Air Slim, but there are plenty of similar cordless handheld vacuum and air duster combos out there, and they tend to land in a pretty similar price range. If another one catches your eye, or goes on sale, or has a design you prefer, go for it.

When comparing models, here are my handheld vacuum musts:

It should offer both vacuum and blower modes.

It should be both cordless and rechargeable. If it needs an outlet, you'll have another barrier to using it, and that defeats the purpose.

It should be lightweight and slim. You want something you can grab and use one-handed without thinking about it.

The dust cup should be easy to empty. If emptying it is a hassle, you'll use it less.

You should be able to keep it in plain sight. The closer it lives to where messes happen (the kitchen, the entryway), the more you'll use it.

I used to think a clean apartment meant big, scheduled cleaning sessions. Now I think it's mostly about making the small stuff effortless. A handheld vacuum and blower won't replace your regular vacuum, but it will make you far less likely to need it as often. If you've been waiting for the next big mess, or the next big clean, to get things tidy, consider changing the system instead.

#3492. Henry Cavill Officially Reveals His Superman Future Following James Gunn’s Exit

This has been a roller coaster of a week for DC fans now that the company is once again under new leadership and seemingly headed in a different creative direction. News broke on Monday that James Gunn and Peter Safran are out as the co-CEOs of DC Studios, with former Marvel Studios producer Jeremy Latcham in line to take their place as the new creative head of the studio. This news comes while Gunn is still hard at work in the post-production phase of his first Superman sequel, Man of Tomorrow, which is due in theaters on July 9, 2027. In addition to David Corenswet, who was back as Superman for the third time during his DCU tenure, the film is also set to star Nicholas Hoult as Lex Luthor, Aaron Pierre as John Stewart, Milly Alcock as Supergirl, and Adria Arjona.

David Corenswet took over the role of Clark Kent from Henry Cavill, who last played the character in the 2022 Dwayne Johnson-led blockbuster, Black Adam. Fans were led to believe after the ending of Black Adam that Henry Cavill was returning as Superman for at least another project, but when Gunn and Safran took over, one of their first announcements was that a new actor would take over the role. Cavill has been busy in the last few years with other movies like Enola Holmes 3 and In The Grey, but fans would still welcome him back into the DCU as Superman with open arms. During a recent sit down with Inverse, Cavill was asked about the potential of coming back to play Superman in the future now that the DCU is under new leadership, and his answer might surprise you:

Four teams, four completely different reasons to put yourself in danger for strangers. This is the roster you actually belong on, what they would want from you, and what it would cost you to stay.

You belong where the stakes are largest and the personalities are loudest. This is a team of people who are all used to being the most important person in the room, which is exactly why it works and exactly why it keeps nearly falling apart.

You have never had the luxury of being thanked for this. The X-Men protect a world that has never once been comfortable with them existing, and something in you understands exactly why they keep doing it anyway.

You do not want colleagues, you want your people. The Titans are the team where the friendship came first and the world-saving turned up afterwards as an inconvenient side effect.

You are not asking who to trust. You worked out the answer a while ago and it was nobody in a cape. This is where you go once you have decided the people in charge need watching, and that nobody else is going to do it.

"Look, there's lots of fantastic storylines. There's always a lot of opportunity... I’ve had such a wonderful time playing Superman in the past. I would never say never now."

The reality is that, right now, we don't know much about what the future of the DCU is going to look like. There are reports that Gunn will continue to write and direct movies at DC, but also reports that the studio is looking to take things in a different direction. It won't be until Skydance, the new name for the merged company formed by Warner Bros and Paramount, comes out with a public statement that we'll have some idea of what the future at DC holds.

Stay tuned to Collider for more updates and coverage of the DCU and Henry Cavill's future projects.

#3491. ‘Paper Tiger’ Review: Adam Driver Gives a Career-Best Performance in James Gray’s Devastating Tragedy

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on May 16, 2026 during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. Neon will release the film in theaters Friday, November 13.]

It’s the final weekend of summer in 1986, upwardly aspirant Jewish families across Queens are still crowding around country club pools to make sure they get their annual money’s worth, and — in a little less than two months — the Mets are going to win the World Series for what might be the last time in team history. But nebbishy engineer Irwin Pearl (Miles Teller) doesn’t know that yet. He doesn’t know that this is his golden age. He doesn’t know that this is as good as it’s ever going to get.  Related Stories Kate Berlant and John Early to Host the 2027 Film Independent Spirit Awards ‘Iron Boy’ Trailer: Beloved Animated Feature Oscar Contender Throws a Whole Watercolor World Out of Whack

What Irwin knows is that greed is good. That the income gap is widening at an unprecedented rate, that economic mobility is slowing to a crawl, and that his giant older brother Gary (Adam Driver) — a divorced ex-police officer who swans around the city like a majestic bird in a blue Mercedes — has started to make him feel even smaller than usual. What Irwin knows is that his mother-in-law wants him to move the family to Great Neck, that the older of his two bickering teenage sons wants an expensive party for his 18th birthday, and that his beautiful wife Hester (Scarlett Johansson) wants fewer things to worry about. Irwin isn’t the overly ambitious sort, but a man can only live in the suburbs of Mt. Olympus for so long before it starts to feel like the gods are taunting him to claim a small piece of it for himself.

And so the stage is set for James Gray’s deft and devastating “Paper Tiger,” a Jewish-American tragedy in a teapot that — like all of the writer/director’s best films — is both sweepingly mythic and hauntingly personal all at once. That double effect, once a magic trick that Gray’s movies would manage to pull off by the time they ended, has since become the de facto starting condition of his singular auto-cinema, which continues to pick at his formative wounds by processing them through the classics.

As indebted to Aeschylus as “Ad Astra” was to Joseph Campbell, or “The Lost City of Z” was to Henri Rousseau, “Paper Tiger” begins with a telling quote from the ancient playwright’s most famous text: “Let there be wealth without tears; enough for the wise man who will ask no further.” Even more telling, however, is the opening shot that follows, which surveys the same reedy marshland — or at least one identical to it — from the end of “We Own the Night.” It’s no surprise that a project first conceived as a direct sequel to 2022’s “Armageddon Time” should point back to Gray’s previous work, but never before has it been so clear, so fast, that he’s trying to process his own, highly specific experience by assimilating it into the curriculum that first taught him how to make sense of the world. The more acutely self-referential his films get, the more broadly they speak to the soft and immortal agony that propels their characters forward.

It’s an agony that goes by many (sur)names, but is colloquially referred to as “family.” “Paper Tiger” is many things, chief among them a textbook parable about the American Dream, a breathless thriller about a working-class schmuck who gets mixed up with the Russian mafiya, and a pleasantly open question about why Miles Teller has rededicated his career to cosplaying as “Lost in America”-era Albert Brooks (to my mind, a canny, convincing way of aging up the nonconformist spunk that first defined his screen image in the days of “Whiplash” and “The Spectacular Now”). But, at its most nuclear level, “Paper Tiger” is — to an even more explicit degree than “Little Odessa,” “The Yards,” and any of the other James Gray movies that it hungrily mulches into something all its own — a remarkably knowing and perceptive film about how family is, and has always been, the ultimate devil’s bargain. Our greatest strength and our heaviest cross to bear. The reason our most dangerous risks can seem worth taking, and the most valuable thing we risk by taking them.

Irwin gives “Paper Tiger” its shape, but it’s how Gary navigates those dilemmas that gives the film its soul. Heartbreakingly portrayed by Adam Driver in a career-best performance that stretches across flash, menace, and pure sincerity like a foot stepping down on a bed of nails without drawing blood, Gary is a vintage ’80s showboat who only knows how to show affection by offering to share in his apparent success. He strides into Irwin and Hester’s living room — after months of radio silence — with the razzle dazzle of a local celebrity and a fully catered feast from Peter Luger’s Steak House in tow for good measure. Irwin’s sons marvel at the gun their uncle still keeps holstered around his ankle (cool!), and his wide-eyed wife looks across the kitchen table and imagines what her life might have been like had she held out for the shinier Pearl.

At least, that’s what Irwin seems to imagine that his wife is imagining, though he’d sooner let such fears fester inside of him for the rest of his natural life than to speak them aloud. For all of the character’s frustrated aspirations for a better life, Teller endows him with the wizened humility of a second-generation Jewish immigrant who knows that it would be gauche to forsake what his late father-in-law — tempting to picture as Anthony Hopkins for continuity’s sake — sacrificed to make possible for their family. Irwin might even be smart enough to recognize that his brother is an empty promise in a tailored suit, but, in a less literal expression of the double vision that will soon cause his wife to crash her car into a tree, being smart isn’t the same as seeing things clearly.

Whatever the case, Irwin is powerless to resist his brother’s sales pitch when Gary lures him into the basement to reveal the reason purpose of his visit: An ambitious new business venture is seeping its way into the Gowanus Canal, and it could use a sharp engineer to help facilitate their plans for the waterway. Still connected to the gills after getting rich in the private sector, Gary doesn’t tell his naive kid brother that said venture is the Russian mob, but the beauty of it is that he doesn’t have to. It can just be another one of the many different things that Irwin doesn’t know. He’ll go down there, sketch a few diagrams for some bald and scary men straight out of central casting, and take home a healthy paycheck to his family (“Paper Tiger” won’t score any points for bucking mafia stereotypes, as Gray plays up their ruthlessness in order to stress how far Irwin is out of his depth).

The only problem is that Irwin takes the job as seriously as he would any other, and — to his profound regret — takes his two sons to go scope out the canal one night, where they see the Russians illegally dumping their waste into the water. The Russians don’t like that. They don’t know what he’s doing there. And, in the aftermath of a stomach-churning stick-up that twisted my guts with the queasy horror of a repressed memory, Gary is given a week to make the problem go away. Spoiler alert: Appeasing the leader of an organized crime ring isn’t as simple as cutting a check, and wouldn’t be even if Gary had access to $125,000.

It doesn’t take long for things to spiral out of control from there, as Irwin and his boys soon find themselves in the crosshairs of a turf war they are comically ill-prepared to survive, while Hester — kept in the dark for her own protection — is thrust into a different crucible that she chooses to keep secret from her husband for similar reasons. (Despite being heavily affected by period drag, Johansson’s performance is too limpid to be mistaken for caricature, growing more hollowed out and heartsick with every scene until it assumes the same void-like power that Brad Pitt once found in the farthest reaches of outer space.) Plotted with a fatalistic velocity that would make Aeschylus proud, Gray’s script corkscrews towards ruin at a sickening pace, its slick road to hell paved with a well-textured mixture of imperfect intentions.

For all of the red meat that “Paper Tiger” gets to chew off the bone, this is still a small and maybe slightly underfunded movie, its outsized impact only made possible because of the micro-details that Gray traces within and between his characters. And I’m not talking about the assortment of beepers and TaB cans, or the load-bearing shots of ’80s New York, which are all Joaquín Baca-Asay’s 35mm cinematography needs to complete the illusion of time travel. While the film is buttressed by a handful of exquisite setpieces (including a nightmarish home invasion sequence that transposes the film’s title into a piece of shadowplay, and a climactic shoutout that binds it even closer to the rest of Gray’s body of work), it’s ultimately fueled by the atomic frictions inside Driver’s performance.

To that point, the real tragedy of “Paper Tiger” isn’t that messing with the mob tears these brothers apart, but rather that it brings them together. There’s not a lot of time for fun and games, but it’s never lost on Gray that this is the most time Gary and Irwin have spent with each other in years — maybe even since they were kids. “We’ve never played in the dirt,” Gary tells Irwin as he lies to his brother about how everything  about the Gowanus deal is above board. But they’re playing together now. The worse things get, the more they expose the extraordinary bond that allowed things to get so fucked up in the first place (a dynamic that becomes all the more wrenching because of how Gray transposes it onto Irwin’s sons). The worse things get, the more this movie sympathizes with Gary and Irwin for their parts in it.

It’s not that Gary is trying to do something nice for his brother, or that he’s shamelessly using Irwin to broker a lucrative deal with the Russians, but rather that everything that happens after that fateful offer stems from an inextricable braid of love and leverage. Gray is no stranger to saga about fraternal strains, but never has he so forcefully tugged at the ties that bind, or more sensitively observed how they can suffocate an entire family when a certain force pulls on them hard enough.

“Paper Tiger” is a story about a household gripped by a self-inflicted event that chokes the life out of its lungs, and precious few films have better conveyed what it feels like when the oxygen gets sucked out of a home without any hope of coming back. “We already had everything,” Irwin will eventually mutter under his breath. The deepest cut of this unshakeable tragedy is that, for the very first time, it leaves him begging for more.

“Paper Tiger” premiered in Competition at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. NEON will release it in theaters later this year.

StackSocial has a refurbished, factory-unlocked iPhone 16e with 128GB of storage on sale for $354.99 right now, down from a $599 list price. The catch, and it's one worth understanding before you click buy, is that this particular unit carries a Grade C refurbished rating, meaning that it may arrive with visible scratches or dents on the housing. If that matters to you, you can get a Grade B-rated model for $399.99 for a B- grade or $434.99 for a B+ grade.

Cosmetic wear aside, the hardware is recent, and the 16e launched in 2025 as Apple's lower-cost entry with much of the same internals as the standard iPhone 16. That means you still get the A18 chip, 8GB of RAM, and a 16-core Neural Engine—enough to run Apple Intelligence features and handle games without feeling like an entry-level phone. Its 6.1-inch OLED screen is similarly well suited to everyday use, whether you’re reading, browsing, or streaming, with a sharp 2532 x 1170 resolution and up to 1,200 nits of brightness. The battery should also be able to keep up with a full day of typical use, with Apple rating it for up to 26 hours of video playback, while charging is handled through USB-C or a Qi wireless pad.

The potential downside shows up around back, where a single 48MP camera with optical image stabilization and a 2x telephoto option covers everyday photos and closer shots—though you lose the ultrawide lens that makes group shots and landscapes easier on the regular iPhone 16. Wi-Fi 6 and Bluetooth 5.3 also put it a step behind newer models on wireless, and while its IP68 rating covers immersion up to six meters for half an hour (so spills and rain aren't a worry), it isn't a dust-proofing guarantee. But for this sale price, it's a great opportunity to upgrade your older iPhone.

#3489. DC Studios’ Latest Reboot: James Gunn and Peter Safran’s Exit Is About Cost-Cutting, Not Just Creative Issues

When they were hired to run DC Studios, James Gunn and Peter Safran were tasked with turning the struggling comic book company into a true rival to Marvel. Four years later, the two have been handed their walking papers before they were able to accomplish their task.

Skydance, which recently bought Warner Bros. Discovery and with it the rights to heroes like Superman, Batman, and the other DC staples that Gunn and Safran were trying to reinvigorate, opted to go in another, cheaper direction. They brought in Jeremy Latcham, a low-profile executive who, like Gunn, had spent years working for Marvel, to oversee DC’s latest reboot. Related Stories ‘Paper Tiger’ Review: Adam Driver Gives a Career-Best Performance in James Gray’s Devastating Tragedy ‘Iron Boy’ Trailer: Beloved Animated Feature Oscar Contender Throws a Whole Watercolor World Out of Whack

There have been mutterings that the change was because of the commercial performance of DC’s films, and the track record has been a mixed bag. “Superman” did what it needed to do, earning $618.7 million worldwide on a $225 million budget, but it wasn’t a blockbuster on the level of Christopher Nolan’s “Dark Knight” films or “Aquaman.”

But “Supergirl” was an unmitigated disaster, earning $126.5 million against a $170 million budget, resulting in losses of roughly $100 million. And “Clayface,” a body horror film produced for $44 million, has been a modest success, earning approximately $110 million. So no, Gunn and Safran had yet to produce a “Guardians of the Galaxy”-style smash that taps the zeitgeist. Though, to be fair, Marvel hasn’t made as many of those lately either. Tastes have changed, and comic book movies, at least ones not starring Spider-Man, aren’t as popular as they once were.

But look closer, and Gunn and Safran’s ouster is about something more than their films’ commercial performances. It’s about cost-cutting too, something that Skydance, with its $80 billion in net debt, needs to start chipping away at if it’s going to realize the $6 billion in savings it’s promised to find.

The duo’s deal, which was set to expire in 2027, was unusually generous. Safran not only got paid to run the comic book label, he was also allowed to run The Safran Company, the wildly successful production company behind “The Conjuring” franchise (former Netflix film chief Dan Lin, in contrast, divested from his company Rideback when he went over to the streamer). Then there was Gunn, who commanded fees for producing films like “Supergirl” and “Clayface,” as well as fees for those DC films that he wrote and directed, such as “Superman” and “Man of Tomorrow.” Gunn’s total haul for a DC film could be as high as $10 million for all his various duties, according to insiders.

When Warner Bros. Discovery chief David Zaslav offered the pair such a sweet deal, comic book movies looked more durable and he needed to make a splash after DC produced flops like “Aquaman and the Lost Kingdom” and “The Flash.” To sweeten the offer, Zaslav also allowed Gunn and Safran to be relatively autonomous, reporting directly to him, whereas Skydance wanted the DC leadership to be under Skydance Motion Picture Group chiefs Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein.

Skydance has also been stunned by the financial picture of Warner Bros.’ film unit since taking over. The studio has suffered a devastating wave of flops this year, losing hundreds of millions on a slate that included bombs such as “Digger,” “The Bride!,” and last weekend’s “The Cat in the Hat.” One insider put the estimated losses at nearing $1 billion. Of course, most of those films were greenlit under Michael De Luca and Pam Abdy, who were let go as soon as David Ellison got the keys to the Warner lot, and have nothing to do with Gunn or Safran. But it does put pressure on Skydance to turn things around and improve the film division’s margins, fast. On an earnings call this week, Ellison acknowledged the film division faces “headwinds” and “has underperformed this year.” He went on to pledge to “apply the same playbook we did at Paramount: greenlighting more selectively.”

Safran remains widely respected on the lot for his stewardship of DC, and is praised for trying to keep budgets in line and for cleaning up the company’s byzantine production practices so that its films, shows, and comic books had a unifying creative voice. Gunn, though a gifted filmmaker, had a harder time adjusting to life in the c-suite, something he admitted to this week in a lengthy post on X. “What only the closest people to me have known over the past four years is my time at DC Studios has been trying, to say the least,” Gunn wrote. “I dislike the at-times corporate nature of the job (thanks to Peter for taking the brunt of that). I’m always a very hard worker, but as a filmmaker I would at least get to take short breaks to unwind, and I’ve stolen even that time from both myself and my loved ones over the past four years.” He closed by saying that he was excited to return to working purely as a creator.

Gunn’s habit of engaging with fans directly on social media raised eyebrows at Warner Bros. and, later, at Skydance. But it cut both ways, with Gunn often using his vast following to promote upcoming projects and to engage more directly with fans in a way that inspired loyalty. Insiders also credit Safran and Gunn with not only reinvigorating Superman on screen, but also backing critically acclaimed shows such as “Lanterns” and “Peacemaker.” And the pair handled a delicate situation with the production of “The Batman: Part II,” which was delayed because of personal issues involving its writer and director Matt Reeves, a situation that ultimately required Steven Soderbergh to step in to finish the sequel under Reeves’ guidance. It is expected to wrap production in the next few weeks.

Insiders also note that Gunn and Safran didn’t have a chance to fully realize their vision of making superhero films featuring a wider variety of characters across a greater diversity of genres made for a broader range of budgets. Gunn was already plotting his next move even as he edited “Man of Tomorrow,” which features a team-up of Lex Luthor and Superman. He had outlined a third “Superman” film and was working on a “Justice League” and a “Batman” film, either one of which was expected to be his next project.

In Hollywood, however, timing is everything. And Gunn and Safran had the misfortune of trying to build their own MCU just as comic book movies were declining in popularity. Will Latcham have more success? He’s widely liked and boasts ties to the Christian community that could broaden DC’s core audience. But he also doesn’t come with the kind of pedigree and profile that Gunn did.

As for DC’s fans, they are bracing for yet another reboot having seen the comic book brand they love go through three different regimes over the last decade. Will Latcham provide the kind of consistency the company so desperately needs, or will he be just the latest in a long line of executives asked to pull off a miracle without being granted much of a runway?

#3488. K-Pop Demon Hunter Fans Can't Miss Out On This League Of Legends/Netflix Pop Drop

If you're a fan of KPop Demon Hunters, then you can't miss this new collection from the teams behind Arcane. The two-season animated show is among the more critically acclaimed pieces of animation from the streamer. Expanding on the characters and lore of League of Legends, Arcane was a massive critical hit for the streamer. However, there have been few updates on a prospective third season.

Fans have also embraced some of the more unexpected League of Legends collaborations, most notably three pop bands inspired by the game's staggering roster. Collected as the League of Legends: Music Video Collection - K-pop & More, it's a chance for Netflix and Riot (the studio behind League of Legends) to cement their connection and a perfect way to tide over K-Pop fans dying for more music.

Available on Netflix as of November 12, the League of Legends: Music Video Collection highlights just how important music has become to the franchise. The music videos feature one of the three bands that have been inspired by League of Legends characters, although they take more liberties than shows like Arcane.

The music videos recast some of the champions as music stars, with three distinct groups serving as the bedrock of the collection: the K-pop-inspired K/DA, the hip-hop-influenced True Damage, and the boy band-coded Heartsteel. Each of the three has its own band energy as a group that reflects their respective genres while taking cues from their game inspirations, like unique powers and distinct aesthetics.

Miyeon (as Ahri), Soyeon (as Akali), Sophie Powers (as Evelynn), Mimi Webb (as Kai'Sa)

Madison Beer (Evelynn), Jaira Burns (as Kai'Sa)

Soyeon (as Akali), Vic Mensa (as Ekko and Yasuo), Coco Jones (as Senna) Sofia Reyes (as Qiyana)

Thutmose and Duckworth (as Ekko), Keke Palmer (as Senna), Becky G (Qiyana)

Connor Price (as Sett), Anderson .Paak (as K'Sante), Baekhyun (as Ezreal), Cal Scruby (as Kayn)

ØZI (as Sett), Tobi Lou (as K'Sante), Nic D (as Kayn)

The music videos are all animated by Fortiche, the same company that worked with League of Legends and Netflix on the award-winning Arcane. That show featured plenty of musical interludes and asides, which should efficiently tease how well the group and the characters adjust to the music video aesthetic.

While most of the music videos are done in a style similar to Arcane, there are some tweaks and experimentation with visuals that make the videos pop -- especially K/DA, who have become the biggest breakout of the three bands featured in the shorts. "POP/STARS," the debut single for K/DA, hit platinum when it debuted. It helps that the bands consist of stars in their own right, each of whom brings their own energy to the roles and the music.

There's an inherent shared DNA between KPop Demon Hunters and the League of Legends music videos that makes the latter a must-watch for fans of the former. For one thing, they share a genuine connection to the music industry, with real craft and care put into each of the band's music and visual aesthetic.

The bandmates all have big, distinct personalities even just in the music videos, an attribute that the animated format lends itself well to. Those showcases of powers make them a fun contrast to the members of HUNTR/X, given their own clear personas and unique power sets that add unique visual flourish to the music videos.

The animation styles are largely similar, even if KPop Demon Hunters takes more cues from anime and animated films while League of Legends visuals prefer showy settings. The biggest connection, though, is the quality of the music. If you're a fan of the blend of rap, pop, and ballad that made up the KPop Demon Hunters soundtrack, there's a lot to love about the League bands.

All of those elements make for a really fun watch, especially if you like to imagine the three bands co-existing in the same space. The idea of HUNTR/X having a friendly rivalry with K/DA, a bit of history with Heartsteel, or admiration for True Damage is a fun way to imagine how KPop Demon Hunters will expand their universe.

With KPop Demon Hunters 2 in active production, fans are going to have to wait a while for brand new content from the band. In the meantime, though, the League of Legends collection boasts some truly great music and could be the gateway for fans of KPop Demon Hunters to discover stuff like Arcane.

#3487. 8 Greatest Thriller Books of the Last 15 Years, Ranked

The world has changed a lot over the past decade and a half. With the dramatic evolution of the internet economy, massive cultural shifts, and the exponential development of technology, our present day would be unrecognizable to someone from the early 2010s. And just as the world has changed, literature has changed with it, and not always in the ways we might have expected.

In the thriller genre, cyberthrillers and cutting-edge modern narrative styles have been growing in popularity for a good while now, but the 2010s also gave us some great works that build on classic forms and traditions, revisiting older sub-genres with greater sensitivity and depth. And as these trends have grown and developed, we’ve been treated to some brilliant books that have earned critical and commercial success, with some even becoming pop culture landmarks. With that in mind, here’s our ranked selection of some of the greatest thriller books of the last 15 years.

Written by Liz Moore, The God of the Woods is a thriller novel with a classic setting: a summer camp. Set in 1975, the book explores the search for Barbara Van Laar, a 13-year-old girl and the daughter of the family that owns the summer camp, who goes missing 14 years after her older brother similarly vanished. As the search unfolds, it brings up long-buried secrets of both the wealthy Van Laars and the local people they employ, revealing a dark history.

It would have been very easy for The God of the Woods to be cliché, considering how common the summer camp setting and missing child premise are in thriller fiction. However, Moore crafts an ambitious, well-written story that’s suspenseful, gripping, and full of fascinating complexities. It’s partly a story of class, partly one of parents and children and the divide between them, and it’s a great read in every aspect. The novel became a bestseller at the time of its publication and has been widely hailed as one of the best thriller novels of the 21st century.

Written by Todd Ritter under the pen name Riley Sager, Final Girls is a slasher-thriller that explores the titular horror movie trope. The book follows Quincy Carpenter, one of three young women who share a tragic connection: each of them has been the sole survivor of a massacre. Ten years after surviving a vacation gone horribly wrong, Quincy is unable and unwilling to recall that night, but she is forced to confront her past when one of the first Final Girls is murdered, with another Final Girl looking more and more like the most likely culprit.

If you’re a fan of slasher movies like Halloween and Scream, Final Girls is going to be an amazingly fun experience for you. Channeling the energy, tropes, and narrative style of classic slasher cinema, the novel is a highly entertaining read that will not disappoint any thriller fan. The book was quite well-received by critics and readers when it was first published in 2017, and it went on to win the International Thriller Writers Award for Best Hard Cover Novel.

Bridging the romance and psychological thriller genres, Verity is a thriller novel written by Colleen Hoover that follows struggling writer Lowen Ashleigh, who gets a job ghostwriting a bestselling book series after the original author, Verity Crawford, is rendered comatose by a car accident. At the Crawford family home, Lowen navigates her growing attraction to Verity’s husband while learning about the tragic events that led to her accident. Things get even more complicated when she stumbles on an unfinished manuscript that reveals dark secrets about Verity.

Originally self-published before being picked up by Grand Central Publishing, Verity is a departure from Hoover’s previous work, which is primarily in the romance and YA genres, but it draws on her romance work to create a fascinating thriller narrative that’s perfect for fans of books like Gone Girl. With plenty of unexpected twists and a haunting ending, it’s a memorable thriller that explores themes of obsession and deception in fascinating ways. A movie adaptation starring Anne Hathaway and Dakota Johnson was released in 2026.

A great detective is really just a personality with a method attached, which is why we keep remaking the same four of them. Here is yours, what it says about you, and the case for them being the best in the business.

You let people think you are not a threat and then you simply never go away. Columbo is the only major detective show that tells you who did it in the first ten minutes, because the pleasure was never the puzzle, it was watching a rich man slowly realise he is in trouble.

You are the most interesting person in the room and you know exactly how to use it. Rian Johnson built Blanc as a gentleman detective who is also an outsider everywhere he goes, which lets him be charming at people who would never otherwise talk to him.

Everybody tells you everything, and you have never once asked them to. Jessica Fletcher is a crime novelist from a small town in Maine who is so warm and so obviously trustworthy that suspects confess to her essentially as a social courtesy.

You expect to be lied to and you are almost never disappointed. Chandler wrote Marlowe as a man with a rigid private code in a city that has none, which is why he takes the case, solves it, gets nothing out of it and takes the next one.

Written by S. A. Cosby, Razorblade Tears is a crime novel that centers on the brutal murder of a gay couple, one of whom is Black and one white. When the police investigation stalls, the aging ex-con fathers of the two men join forces to seek revenge, using their underworld connections to track down their sons’ killers. Simultaneously, they are also forced to face up to their own homophobia, racial prejudice, and personal shame.

Published in July 2021, Razorblade Tears was a New York Times bestseller and earned rave reviews from critics. Anchored by its relatable anti-heroes, the book takes readers on a journey that’s both thrilling and thoughtful in equal measure, with violence balanced by emotion. Exploring sensitive and timely themes through the eyes of its less-than-perfect protagonists, the book is a thriller masterpiece that’s pulpy yet literary, melodramatic yet grounded, and thoroughly engaging from start to finish.

English author Stuart Turton’s debut novel, The 7½ Deaths of Evelyn Hardcastle (originally published in the UK as The Seven Deaths of Evelyn Hardcastle), is a murder mystery book with a unique, experimental narrative structure. The story takes place at Blackheath Manor, where Evelyn Hardcastle will die at precisely 11:00 pm. We see the plot unfold from the perspective of Aiden Bishop, who is stuck in a time loop, waking up in the body of one of eight party guests and reliving the same day over and over again, unless he can discover the name of Evelyn’s killer.

The 7½ Deaths of Evelyn Hardcastle is, first and foremost, a fascinating literary experience. The inventive narrative allows the reader to experience the murder mystery in a truly immersive way, transforming it into a sort of escape room. The book was a bestseller at the time of its publication, earned high acclaim from critics, and won several awards, including the Costa Book Award for Best First Novel.

A modern epistolary mystery novel, The Killer Question is the fifth mystery novel written by Janice Hallett. Presented through text messages, emails, quiz transcripts, and local reports, the book begins with a pitch for a Netflix true-crime documentary about a once-loved country pub, The Case is Altered, its mysterious owners, Mal and Sue Eastwood, and the events that led to its closing. Through the various documents we are presented with, we learn of the pub’s popular trivia nights, which take an unexpectedly dark turn when a suspicious new team starts winning every game.

Arguably Hallett’s best book yet, The Killer Question is wicked, clever, and deliciously meta. All of Hallett’s mysteries utilize the non-linear, mixed-media format, but The Killer Question is the most accomplished execution of that narrative style so far, painting a fully realized world, down to the smallest details. The novel has earned high praise from critics and readers for its brilliant storytelling and pacing, as well as its shocking twists.

Written by Anthony Horowitz, Magpie Murders is the first book of the Susan Ryeland series. The novel explores the murder of a mystery author through a story-within-a-story structure. Susan, an editor working for a publishing company, searches for the missing final chapter of the deceased author’s new unpublished novel, Magpie Murders, and begins to suspect foul play. Simultaneously, we learn the story of Magpie Murders, a classic detective mystery set in the English countryside in the 1950s.

Anthony Horowitz has a long-established reputation as a great mystery and thriller writer, but Magpie Murders is easily one of the author’s best books, a true masterpiece of detective fiction. The inventive structure and Golden Age homages have earned the novel great praise from critics and fans alike, and it was followed by two sequels, Moonflower Murders and Marble Hall Murders, with a third in the works. All three books in the series so far have also been adapted into TV shows, the latest released in 2026.

Gillian Flynn’s third and most successful novel, Gone Girl is a crime thriller that follows the story of husband and wife Nick and Amy Dunne. When Amy mysteriously vanishes on their fifth anniversary, the investigation reveals evidence of a possible murder and a diary that points to Nick as the prime suspect, sparking a media circus and revealing shocking truths about both of them. The story is told in three parts, exploring competing narratives on the same events as seen from both Nick and Amy’s POVs.

Gone Girl makes exceptionally good use of the unreliable narrator trope, creating a gripping psychological thriller about a turbulent, complicated marriage and toxic codependency. Dark and twisted, with a major mid-story surprise that throws the reader off course momentarily, the book has been widely acclaimed ever since it was first published in 2012, and it’s had a significant influence on the thriller genre. A film adaptation directed by David Fincher from a screenplay written by Flynn was released in 2014, which also earned critical acclaim and commercial success.

You can get thousands of free e-books over the course of 2026 if you know where—and when—to look. All year long, Amazon is offering free Kindle e-books to readers, with new opportunities popping up every month. In November, Prime members can get two free Kindle e-books from Amazon's First Reads program.

Amazon First Reads is a program aimed at Prime members that offers early access to new e-books across many genres, as curated by First Reads editors (one of many Prime Member benefits). Prime members can choose to download one free e-book every month from a rotating list—though some months that number is bumped up to two, usually with a free short novel—and non-members get them for a discounted price. These e-books can be read on any compatible Kindle device or via the free Kindle app.

Go to the First Reads landing page to see the full list of e-books available this month. Once you find a book that seems interesting, click the "Shop Now" button from the First Reads landing page. Make sure you’re not being redirected to the Kindle or Amazon mobile application, because you won't see the free book option there; instead, use your internet browser on your phone or computer.

Make sure you’re not clicking the ”Pre-order for...” button, as that will direct you to pay. Instead, click the “Read for Free” or the "Buy Now with 1-Click" button under the "First Reads" banner on the book's Amazon page (don't worry, you won't be charged). This will send the e-book directly to the Kindle linked to your Amazon account. You can see what it should look like from the screenshot below.

#3485. Attend, the First Marketplace Connecting Filmmakers Directly to Theater Owners, Finally Launches Today

Way back in October 2024, The Fithian Group, led by former NATO chief John Fithian and founding partner Patrick Corcoran, announced plans for an ambitious new marketplace, one that would help connect filmmakers and their projects directly to theater owners looking to book their movies and effectively cut out the distribution middleman. Today, that vision is now a reality.

The Fithian Group on Wednesday at the American Film Market announced the formal launch of Attend Theatrical Marketplace, the group’s online platform and marketplace for filmmakers and exhibitors that is now live and ready for business.

Attend launches with today just a curated selection of four films, all of whose filmmakers will now be doing the legwork to connect with theaters and find venues at which to exhibit their work. But the platform is already loaded with exhibition partners who will be able to browse available films, with more to be added soon, and Attend will eventually be a fully open platform to any filmmaker who wishes to do outreach directly to theater owners. Related Stories DC Studios’ Latest Reboot: James Gunn and Peter Safran’s Exit Is About Cost-Cutting, Not Just Creative Issues ‘Paper Tiger’ Review: Adam Driver Gives a Career-Best Performance in James Gray’s Devastating Tragedy

IndieWire got an early demo of Attend and how it aims to simplify the work that distributors do every day in putting movies into theaters, as well as the work exhibitors have to do in booking movies, paying invoices, and more. And IndieWire will on Wednesday lead a panel discussion at AFM with Corcoran, Charles Beale of the site’s designer Titlepool, and filmmaker Lilian T. Mehrel, whose Tribeca award-winning film “Honeyjoon” will be one of the four inaugural films shopping for theaters.

Beyond “Honeyjoon,” the other three films available on Attend at launch are Kenny Riches’ crime drama “Mouse”; “Spoke,” which is a documentary about firefighters and the trauma they deal with after the fires; and “Censurada,” an LGBTQ+ drama from Marco Garza about forbidden love in 1969 Spain.

The vision of Attend was outlined to IndieWire over a year ago with an indie rom-com called “You, Me, and Her” serving as an early guinea pig for the idea. The thinking was, if you had a film that could demonstrate it already had an audience and you had a clear sense of where your audience was and how to target them, all you needed were the screens to showcase your movie and the means to get your movie into the hands of those theaters.

That was and remains the tricky part. Few people have the connections with theater owners to be able to reach them and get a film out in any meaningful capacity. This year has produced a number of examples in which enterprising filmmakers have done without distributors and found the audience they already knew was there to release their movies. YouTuber Markiplier went directly to theaters and made $50 million with his horror movie “Iron Lung.” The documentary “NAZA” skipped a distributor in order to get its story about the IDF out with urgency. Even an AI movie called “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” is next month releasing without the aid of a distributor.

Attend seeks to use technology to simplify that process, to get your film out to an even wider audience and a more targeted one. For filmmakers, the platform is designed to eliminate the guesswork of who you need to talk to, how you reach them, and what attributes a given exhibitor is looking for in a film. For exhibitors, it filters all your titles and screens into one place, and it makes the receiving of deliverables or the payment of invoices more automated than the often tedious work it is for most exhibitors today. It’s exciting to see the whole vision come into fruition.

On the filmmaker end, the way Attend works is you as an individual can upload details and assets about your film, from simple details like its runtime, logline, and genre, to much more granular details about the aspect ratio, the available formats, the awards it has won and festivals it has played, the social networking reach of talent, and many more data points. There may be assets you don’t realize will be significant to a given exhibitor but will jump out as they browse your profile. You can then identify themes that speak to the film’s target audience and narrow the demographics for which your film is intended.

From there, you can filter and browse theaters to identify which theaters would be the best fit for your movie. For instance, Attend has data that can show a theater is within walking distance of a firehouse or that the theater has ties to a local advocacy group that aligns with the themes of the film’s story, and Attend’s predictive AI engine can recommend those theaters that would be available and the best fit for your film. Then, instead of reaching out to each of those theaters individually, filmmakers can easily select all the relevant theaters they want to message and have the option to manually add or subtract more beyond the recommended targets. You can even modify proposed theatrical terms for individual theaters or personalize messages, and as theaters come in, Attend can dynamically estimate P&A spend for those locations.

When theater owners are contacted, they’ll receive push notifications about films that are available for them to review, and they can further browse any available films in the marketplace and do their own outreach. Exhibitors can create tabs and info on any number of their circuit’s screens or locations and can upload in spreadsheets specs like screen size, audio, and seat count that filmmakers can view themselves to better get a sense of which theaters are the best fit. Exhibitors can specify rental prices for individual screens, you can mark your theater as being willing to offer simple four-walling options or that it’s capable of hosting big premieres, whether you want to offer “split screens” or “clean screens,” or you can set terms for how long you’re able to hold a movie. And not only does it also itemize marketing costs, Attend clearly indicates what the share of a film’s box office would be if they were to accept it and program it.

This helps theater owners in a number of ways. It takes the busy work out of things like paying numerous individual vendors or distribution partners, and it lets you download and easily generate a W9 form based on that film’s booking, being able to do so across multiple locations. But for theater owners that generally don’t know what they’re playing until the Monday before, this gives theaters far more advanced leeway and awareness to then be able to do the necessary marketing, put tickets on sale, and actually get butts in seats. All that is especially important for the smaller indies that need that word of mouth.

For now, theaters haven’t linked their loyalty data or other point of sales or scheduling tools to Attend, but that could come with time, and as people actually begin to use the platform, the predictive functionality will improve in the long run.

Corcoran and Fithian see Attend being useful for smaller distributors themselves in the long run, not just individual filmmakers who want to cut out the middleman. Distributors can use it to plan the campaigns of multiple titles and use its automation features to save time and costs. And while today Attend just supports new releases, there’s no reason why older library titles couldn’t be marketed here to exhibitors as well.

Time will tell if filmmakers find Attend an effective form of reaching theaters or if exhibitors adopt the platform widely to make it a useful tool for all parties. But it’s an ambitious vision that if implemented properly could have enormous impacts for the independent film world. And after two years of effort and hype, that day could finally be here.

The investigation brings her to the darker side of Nashville. She finds secrets and lies will keep her from figuring out everyone's true intentions.

Chastain will also star in The Retrievals, an upcoming Netflix drama series based on the real-life scandal at Yale Fertility Center. It's an adaptation of Susan Burton's podcast of the same name, and explores how nurse Carla Russo (Amy Ryan) stole fentanyl intended for patients and replaced it with saline. Because of this, nearly 100 women were left to undergo egg retrieval procedures without anesthesia.

Chastain plays Kaitlyn Langford, a former art historian and Yale patient who becomes the key plaintiff in the historic lawsuit against the clinic. It also stars Emilia Jones, Fabien Frankel, Will Harrison, Arian Moayed, and Adepero Oduye.

The series also stars Richard Gere, Arian Moayed, Zoë Winters, Annaleigh Ashford, Will Yun Lee, Ravi V. Patel, and John Cho.

The six main characters are: A fallen television news anchor, her unfaithful televangelist husband, a rising country music star, two small-time criminals, and an ex-convict. All who face life-changing consequences of the incident.

Chastain appears alongside a star-studded cast including Chris Evans, Chris Pine, Mikey Madison, Don Cheadle, and Daniel Zolghadri.

Chastain flexes her Shakespeare muscles with Lear Rex. Based on the classic tragedy King Lear, this film stars Al Pacino as the titular character, who divides his kingdom among his three daughters. Filming wrapped back in October 2024, but a release date for this project has not yet been confirmed.

#3483. All the Health and Fitness Products You Didn't Realize You Could Buy With HSA Funds

If you have a flexible spending account (FSA), it's that time of year: Use those funds, or you'll lose them. Luckily, there are plenty of clever ways to spend your remaining FSA funds on qualifying healthcare costs—some that you may never have considered as "qualifying."

For instance, you can use your FSA or HSA funds to get yourself a sweet new fitness tracker or smartwatch (even the latest Fitbit Air). At least, that's what plenty of brands like Whoop, Oura, and even Nike want you to think. Is the process really as straightforward as the marketing suggests? Here's what to know about all the unexpected ways you can spend your FSA funds before the end of the year.

Right off the bat, when it comes to most of these fitness trackers and smartwatches, your HSA/FSA dollars won't be able to cover the entire purchase; instead, you'll save an average of 30% on eligible health purchases.

There is some more fine print, although it’s not as tricky as you might think. For the most part, if a device is necessary for treating or monitoring a specific medical condition—and not just “general wellness”—it could be eligible to purchase with those pre-tax health dollars.

The main “catch” here (as I’ve previously explained) is proving that device is in fact necessary, which requires you to obtain a Letter of Medical Necessity (LMN). Your LMN is basically a doctor's note required to classify certain purchases as qualified medical expenses under IRS guidelines, proving that the device will be used to treat a legitimate medical condition, such as obesity or a heart condition. Let’s take a look at what you can actually expect if you want to get a fitness wearable approved as a medical necessity.

When it comes to securing your LMN, you might not even need to make a doctor's appointment, thanks to third-party players like Truemed. When you browse sites like Coros, Amazfit, and more, you'll see the option to “Pay With Truemed” at checkout. From there, you'll be asked a few questions about your health circumstances, and you’ll be matched with a provider to determine your eligibility. If you qualify, you’ll get an LMN that will allow you to use your HSA or FSA funds to complete your purchase—all without ever having to meet with your primary doctor.

Truemed is one of the most popular payment platforms in this space, with the company claiming on its site that “90% of LMNs are issued within seven hours.” I spoke with Truemed’s co-founder and CEO Justin Mares to find out how it works behind the scenes. After you take that short survey about your health, an independent licensed provider reviews your answers before deciding whether the purchase looks medically necessary. If it doesn't, Truemed won't bother forwarding the request at all. Because Truemed screens your case before it has a chance of getting denied, those approval numbers get to stay mighty high. And the reality is, most Americans will have at least one health marker—like weight or cholesterol levels—that they can self-report to prove that, say, a Fitbit Air is necessary tool for prevention and maintenance.

For the purchases that do go through to a medical professional, approval turns out to be surprisingly straightforward. It comes down to the idea of "standard of care" in general. “If you go into a doctor's office and say your family has a history of high blood pressure,” Mares says, “your doctor probably is not going to ask for lab work before they'll talk to you about it. They simply take you at your word and help you manage the risk.” Proving HSA/FSA eligibility works on that same standard fairly often, according to Mares. You're not submitting a stack of medical records; you're answering a simple intake form about your health history, and a licensed clinician uses that, plus their own judgment, to decide whether a given product is appropriate for you.

Before you get your hopes up too high, FSA/HSA eligibility for wearables is still far from a free-for-all. An LMN only covers you, personally, for a specific product from a specific merchant, and it's usually tied to a specific condition, like cardiovascular risk, pre-diabetes, sleep issues, chronic pain, and so on. Some employers' FSA administrators scrutinize wearable purchases more closely than others, and even a fully compliant LMN doesn't guarantee your plan will approve the claim. Some companies (like Coros, for one) are more transparent about walking customers through the required medical consultation at checkout, while other brands market "HSA/FSA eligible" prominently without explaining that the LMN step is what actually makes that true. Luckily, I’ve saved you some time and rounded up some of the major wearables—and other unexpected items—that you might be able to prove as FSA/HSA eligible.

Screenless recovery trackers like Whoop, Amazfit Helio Strap, and the Oura Ring can usually be justified as HSA/FSA eligible around sleep quality, HRV-based stress monitoring, or recovery tracking tied to a chronic condition. These tend to draw more scrutiny from plan administrators simply because they're marketed as lifestyle products first, so the strength of your intake answers matters more here than it does for something obviously medical, like a blood pressure cuff.

If cardiovascular monitoring, training load tracking, or heart rate accuracy is relevant to a documented health concern, these watches can qualify the same way a basic tracker does. For instance, Coros offers FSA/HSA eligibility for all its watches and heart rate monitors through its partnership with Truemed. Amazfit similarly lets you filter by HSA/FSA eligibility for its smartwatches. Sadly, no Garmin watches are HSA/FSA-eligible. Still, the following Garmin-brand products are eligible for an HSA/FSA purchase:

You can filter by HSA/FSA eligibility and browse all eligible Garmin items here.

Think adjustable dumbbells, rowing machines, and connected bikes. It's the same logic doctors use when they tell a patient with pre-diabetes or high cholesterol to start exercising regularly; if a clinician is willing to attest that structured exercise is part of your treatment plan, equipment that enables that can qualify. For instance, here are some HSA/FSA eligible products from Nike Strength:

The common thread across all of these is that the product itself doesn't determine eligibility—your health history does. A Whoop band might be an easy approval for someone managing a cardiac condition, but it'll get more pushback for someone with no relevant health history at all. If you're curious whether something on your wish list might qualify, it's worth filling out the intake process just to see how creatively you can spend those pre-tax health dollars. However you choose to spend your FSA funds, don’t let that money go to waste.
