#3481. 10 Greatest Football Movies of All Time to Watch Before Thanksgiving, Ranked

Ben Brewster is a filmmaker, critic, screenwriter, and actor whose work sits at the intersection of film culture, craft analysis, and storytelling.

He is a movie list contributing writer at Collider and a contributing writer for High on Films, where he covers contemporary cinema, independent film, and festival releases with an eye toward narrative structure, performance, and visual language.

Ben is an active film festival participant, having worked with Newport Film, the Nantucket Film Festival and as a screener for the Austin, Boston & Woodstock film festivals.  He brings to that work a programming instinct shaped by years of close engagement with independent and documentary cinema. This comes with a deep investment in the kinds of films that rarely find their way into the mainstream conversation without someone willing to advocate for them.

His background spans documentary and narrative filmmaking, film marketing, and production, including work with award-winning directors. This as well as developing his own indie production company, Lilac Creative Studio, through which he develops and produces original work across fiction and nonfiction forms.  His debut documentary, Diamond in the Rust, is an examination of economic redevelopment and displacement in the Queens area of New York City. The film was recently accepted to the Unisphere Film Festival, the Defense of Democracy Film Festival, and the Urbanite Arts & Film Festival. This would mark his first festival recognition as a director.  In addition to his writing and programming work, Ben hosts Beneath the Bloom, a film podcast exploring the work behind the scenes in cinema, and the struggles one can face to make a movie become a reality. The show reflects the same sensibility that runs through all of his work. A conviction that film is not merely entertainment but one of the most powerful tools human beings have for understanding each other.

Across mediums, his work is driven by a deep belief in film as a communal, transformative art form.

Thanksgiving week is stacked with a football slate, as it seemingly has always been. The NFL has scheduled five games in three days for the first time ever. The eventful holiday weekend begins with the Packers at Rams on Netflix on Wednesday the 25th, and ends with the Broncos at Steelers on Black Friday. The Thursday triple-header brings the Bears at Lions, Eagles at Cowboys and Chiefs at Bills. It's a lot of downtime with family, and a lot of time for football and movies. So I decided to combine the two.

The ten movies below cover pretty much every flavor of football, from prison yard scrappy comedy to a Superbowl terror plot. They span 1971 to 2014, and include true stories, a literary thriller adaptation and a TV movie that made an entire sports generation cry. I ranked them by how well they hold up on a rewatch, which rewards the stronger character work over box office value and the flashier trophy-like blockbusters of the football film.

A few notes on the edges. Jerry Maguire spends most of its time with an agent, but football runs through every scene. Several connect to this week's games, from the Bears in Brian's Song to the Cowboys and Steelers in Black Sunday. The Longest Yard is the 1974 original with Burt Reynolds, while the Sandler 2005 remake takes a seat on the bench. So, in between kickoffs, here are some iconic football flicks to put on while the turkey rests and the stuffing settles.

Picture a prison yard in the sun, a warden with a plan, and a disgraced quarterback who knows he is being used. Robert Aldrich directed The Longest Yard, and Burt Reynolds built a movie star persona on Paul Crewe, a former pro quarterback with a sneer and a bruised ego. He was thrown out for shaving points, and the warden wants him to now put together an inmate team for a game against the guards. He pressures Crewe into organizing it, and he ends up getting the strongest and angriest convicts he can find.

The inmates call themselves the Mean Machine, and they relish every chance they get to hit a guard. The training sequences give the movie a fun and rowdy charm. Ed Lauter plays the head guard, Captain Knauer, with a snarl and menacing grin. Aldrich keeps the camera very close to the action, so the audience feels up tight with the game's most violent hits. The warden expects his guards to win and Crewe's early willingness to go along puts him at odds with his own teammates. Michael Conrad, an old football coach in the yard, gives the team a crusty voice of experience. Ray Nitschke, the Green Bay Packers linebacker, appears as an inmate for those Packer fans gearing up for Wednesday night.

Rudy Ruettiger grows up in a big family in a steel town, where the normal trajectory is to work at the local mill and keep your head down. His father and brothers do so, but Rudy's less inclined. He fully wakes up when a close friend's death at work makes him bolt for South Bend on a bus with little more than a dream. Sean Astin plays him with a squint of determination, a kid who stands about five foot six and keeps a Notre Dame pennant on his wall. He naturally cannot get in right away, so he enrolls at nearby Holy Cross Junior College, where a priest helps him with his grades. David Anspaugh directs from Angelo Pizzo's script, and the two had already made Hoosiers together, which should tell you everything about their creative tone of voice.

Charles S. Dutton is warm and gruff as the Notre Dame groundskeeper who gives Rudy a job. He gives him some of the best advice in the movie amidst the scout team practices, where Rudy keeps getting knocked around daily. Vince Vaughn, in an early role, appears as one of the Notre Dame players. Late in the story, the players lay their jerseys on the coach's desk, so Rudy can dress for the final game, and the chants begin from there. Rudy finally dresses for the last game, gets in for a few plays, and sacks the quarterback to end it, just as the real Ruettiger did. The crowd chants his name some more as his teammates carry him off, and Jerry Goldsmith's music swells to match every emotional beat.

Bobby Boucher has the world's strangest job. He hauls water for a college football program, and Adam Sandler plays him with a squeaky voice and a heart full of passion. Bobby lives in the Louisiana bayou with his Mama, played by Kathy Bates, who is convinced that football is a sin and girls are traps. He promptly loses his job and lands at South Central Louisiana State University, where Henry Winkler's Coach Klein is in desperate need of a spark. A locker room tease turns Bobby into a human wrecking ball, and the Mud Dogs have finally gotten their defense back. Frank Coraci directs and lets the jokes run wild, from the over-the-top swamp accents to the oddly specific rules Mama sets down.

Fairuza Balk plays Vicki, a childhood friend with a bad reputation but whose loyalty to Bobby never wavers. The movie grossed more than $160 million domestically on a fairly modest budget. Its quotes spread through schoolyards and dorm rooms for years after its release. The Mud Dogs' games get bigger and louder as the season goes on, and Bobby's anger becomes the biggest laugh. The movie pokes fun at college football's culture of worshiping its stars, and it shows little mercy in doing so.

Reacher just pulled 66 million viewers, and Fallout is back in 2027.

Black Sunday starts with a raid in Beirut, then moves to the Superbowl. John Frankenheimer (The Manchurian Candidate) adapted the novel for the screen, and Robert Shaw, fresh off of Jaws, plays Mossad agent David Kabakov. Kabrakov is opposite Bruce Dern's Michael Lander, a Goodyear blimp pilot and Vietnam veteran who has lost faith in everything. Dern plays Lander as a bitter man who has been passed over and ignored. Marthe Keller is chilling as a Black September operative who recruits Lander for the mission and convinces him of its justification.

Their target is Super Bowl X in Miami, and the weapon is the blimp itself. Frankenheimer directs it like a procedural, with stakeouts, tips and a countdown. He shot the climax inside the Orange Bowl during the real Super Bowl X between the Steelers and Cowboys. The crowd of over 80,000 is one of the more elaborate stunts of that era and gives the finale a scale most thrillers cannot come close to. The legendary John Williams wrote the score, and its brass swells over the blimp's final approach. Black Sunday asks its audience to imagine the worst day in sports, and it takes the question with a deep seriousness.

Ivan Reitman, best known for Ghostbusters, directed Draft Day, and Kevin Costner plays Sonny Weaver Jr., the Cleveland Browns general manager. The movie takes course over one day, as Weaver hopes to make the biggest trade of his career. Sonny's father, the former Browns coach, has just passed, and the weight of that loss colors every decision. Costner has a long sports resume, with Bull Durham, Field of Dreams and Tin Cup, and he is comfortable living in the psyche of these kinds of men. Frank Langella plays the owner who pushes for a flashy move, and Denis Leary plays Coach Penn, who wants Sonny to stay out of his way.

Reitman uses split screens and a ticking clock to foster the tension in the room. Jennifer Garner plays Ali, whose news about their personal life complicates a stressful day. Sonny trades the Browns' future picks to move up to the top of the draft. He then quickly second guesses himself when he takes a closer look at the quarterback everyone loves. He is drawn to linebacker Vontae Mack (Chadwick Boseman), whose character impresses Weaver more than the scouting report. Terry Crews plays running back Earl Penn, and Tom Welling is the incumbent quarterback, Brian Drew. Real NFL figures, including Commissioner Roger Goodell, appear as well, and the draft's logos are everywhere.

John Lee Hancock adapted Michael Lewis's book, with Quinton Aaron starring as Michael Oher, a gentle giant who has spent his life moving from home to home. The Blind Side uses the famous Lawrence Taylor hit on Joe Theismann to explain why the left tackle is such a crucial position to a football team's success. Sandra Bullock is Leigh Anne Tuohy, a Memphis interior designer with a Southern drawl and a steel spine. She spots Michael walking in the cold on Thanksgiving night and brings him home.

Tim Mcgraw plays her husband, a fast food franchise owner with a soft spot for Ole Miss football, and Kathy Bates is his school tutor. Bullock netted an Oscar for Best Actress and the movie got a nomination for Best Picture. It ended up grossing more than $300 million, making it one of the biggest sports movies ever. Michael Oher became a first round pick of the Baltimore Ravens in 2009. Real college coaches such as Nick Saban appear while they recruit Michael. The real Michael filed a court petition in 2023 claiming he was never formally adopted by the Tuohys, while the family fully disputes the account.

Cameron Crowe's script starts with a sports agent typing a mission statement in the middle of the night about caring for clients. He's fired the next day and nearly everyone abandons him. Tom Cruise plays Jerry as a charming man whose honesty ends up costing him his lifestyle. Cuba Gooding Jr. plays Rod Tidwell, the Arizona Cardinals receiver who becomes Jerry's last client and demands to be shown the money. Jonathan Lipnicki's Ray famously tells Jerry that the human head weighs eight pounds. Kelly Preston plays Jerry's fiancée and Jay Mohr plays the rival agent who smiles while he steals away his clients.

Football appears around the edges, with Rod's Cardinals playing on Monday night and a college quarterback prospect named Frank Cushman anchoring the early scenes. The movie runs on lines people still quote, including "You had me at hello," and Rod's celebration after a big touchdown catch gets a huge laugh. Gooding won the Oscar for Best Supporting Actor, Cruise earned a Best Actor nomination and the movie itself got a nomination for Best Picture. Jerry Maguire grossed more than $270 million, and is engrained in pop culture for all of its quotable moments.

In 1971, Alexandria, Virginia, integrated its high schools, and the T.C. Williams football team became front page news. Denzel Washington is new head coach Herman Boone, a stern black man hired over the beloved white coach Bill Yoast (Will Patton). Yoast agrees to stay on as an assistant, and the two fight before they learn to respect each other. Wood Harris is defensive end Julius Campbell, and Ryan Hurst stars as All-American Gerry Bertier, two teammates who start out at odds and end up as brothers. Ethan Suplee, Donald Faison, Kip Pardue, and Ryan Gosling round out the young but remarkably talented cast.

The training camp at Gettysburg College in Remember the Titans is a focal point. Coach Boone puts the players through rigorous drills till the early hours of the morning and gives a memorable speech about the historical battlefield beneath them and the men involved who sacrificed their lives. The team's chants, including the famous call of "left side, strong side," give it an emotional depth and tonal richness. The soundtrack mixes 1970s hits with a stirring score by Trevor Rabin that keeps the energy high. Real events were reshaped for the screen, but the 1971 team did go undefeated and win the state championship. The movie ended up grossing more than $136 million and stands the test of time as a classroom and football season favorite.

Brian's Song aired on ABC on November 30th 1971, marking this year as its 55th anniversary right after Thanksgiving. It is a TV movie that people still talk about like a theatrical classic. James Caan plays Brian Piccolo, a bold, slightly resentful undrafted free agent out of Wake Forest who plays his way onto the Chicago Bears. Billy Dee Williams is Gale Sayers, a quiet yet gifted star. The two begin as fierce rivals playing the same position and grow into good friends after Sayers tears up his knee.

Piccolo helps him rehab, and their unlikely friendship becomes the story's center. When Piccolo is diagnosed with cancer, the movie follows his decline with a restraint that surprised audiences at the time. Sayer's speech for the George Halas Award is dedicated to Piccolo, and it's a moment that audiences remember decades later. Brian's Song won multiple Emmys and a Peabody Award. The Bears of the movie travel to Detroit on Thanksgiving Day, which gives the classic a timely connection. A 2001 remake starred Sean Maher and Mekhi Phifer, but most fans still talk about the original.

Friday Night Lights starts in Odessa, Texas, where the high school football team is the town's biggest event. Billy Bob Thornton is coach Gary Gaines, a man who gets called out at the grocery store when the team loses. Derek Luke plays running back Boobie Miles, a talented kid whose knee injury changes the course of the season. Lucas Black is the quarterback and Garrett Hundland is a kid whose father (Tim McGraw) pushes him a little too hard and wears his old championship glory like a warrior's armor. Peter Berg directs with handheld cameras that put you on the sideline.

The score by Explosions in the Sky and David Torn gives the movie a dreamy, restless sound. H.G. Bissinger's book about the 1988 Permian Panthers supplies the story, and Berg keeps the film close to its real people. Connie Britton stars as Sharon Gaines, the coach's wife, and she would later become famous as Tami Taylor on the TV series. The season ends at Texas Stadium, and Gaines's pregame speech about being perfect is regarded as the movie's most recognized sequence. The TV series premiered on NBC in 2006, and a Peacock reboot is currently on pause.

#3480. Democrats Won. When Do Hollywood Crews Get Back to Work?

Tom Curley is happy about the election results. Whether they’ll help him get back to work is another matter. The production sound mixer, who won an Oscar for “Whiplash,” told IndieWire he has struggled to find consistent employment since his last gig, “CSI: Vegas,” was canceled in 2024.

He’s picked up some work here and there, but nothing has restored the professional footing Curley said he had just two years ago: a loss that has felt “humiliating.”

“I kind of feel like I was in a car accident almost, and I’m just here staring at the aftermath, wondering how I’m going to pick up the pieces, if I’m ever going to pick up the pieces,” he said. “It’s a very destabilizing thing.” Related Stories DC Studios’ Latest Reboot: James Gunn and Peter Safran’s Exit Is About Cost-Cutting, Not Just Creative Issues Attend, the First Marketplace Connecting Filmmakers Directly to Theater Owners, Finally Launches Today

Before last week’s midterms, Curley was cautiously optimistic about a proposed federal tax credit designed to keep more film and TV production work inside the U.S. Now, he’s worried the blue wave could inadvertently slow a bill that had been gaining momentum on both sides.

With Republicans meeting such dramatic electoral losses on November 3, Curley fears President Trump could withdraw his support for the proposed tax credit as a kind of punishment.

“All it takes is some hurt feelings to get in the way,” he said.

But the election was mostly good news for Hollywood, right? Democrats won back both chambers of Congress, and Xavier Becerra (also a Democrat) will soon succeed Gavin Newsom as governor of California — still home to the country’s largest film and TV production workforce.

Meanwhile in LA, Nithya Raman beat incumbent Mayor Karen Bass after explicitly campaigning to make it easier to shoot here. Raman’s victory was widely seen as a rebuke of the status quo in a city where production jobs have become increasingly difficult to find. It’s also part of a broader Democratic promise to make the economy work better for the people who actually depend on it, crews included.

Yet for the scads of film and TV workers IndieWire spoke to in Los Angeles, being pleased with the election results politically didn’t necessarily mean expecting more work to come their way.

Hollywood is a state of mind, sure. But it’s also a literal place where residents have rent due even when the industry isn’t thriving — and inflation, gig-economy restrictions, SAG-AFTRA contract uncertainty, permitting headaches, artificial intelligence, inaccessible healthcare, corporate consolidation, and, yes, productions increasingly leaving town are making the gaps between paychecks harder to survive.

Legislation can support crews in theory, but film and TV executives still decide what gets made, where it gets made, and who gets hired in the end. For someone like Curley, even one more gig might ease his anxiety and help with the bills. The harder question is what comes after that opportunity wraps, and whether today’s labor market can still offer the people who make movie magic enough for a real living.

The first test for this new establishment comes even before the majority takes office.

In the first quarter of 2025, roughly 46 percent of scripted American projects tracked by Luminate were filmed entirely abroad. That’s part of a broader trend toward international production that has drawn bipartisan concern in the U.S. since the late ‘90s.

Right now, Sen. Adam Schiff and Rep. Laura Friedman, both Democrats from California, are trying to pass a federal production tax credit through the outgoing Congress during the lame-duck session. The bill was introduced in September with bipartisan backing — including from South Carolina Sen. Tim Scott and Texas Rep. Nathaniel Moran, both Republicans returning to Congress next year.

The proposed Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act would lower the cost of hiring film and TV workers in the U.S. by giving eligible productions a national tax credit covering 20 percent of qualifying pay. Bonuses could bring that up to 30 percent, although qualifying projects would generally need to cost over $1 million and spend at least 75 percent of their principal photography days in the U.S.

Some domestic post-production and visual effects work would qualify for federal tax breaks, too, and paired with the right state incentives, film producers could reliably use those savings to motivate new work. In fact, Curley said the people who’d hired him before were explicitly waiting for a federal incentive along those lines. That made the proposal feel like a possible job, not just another bill.

“I’ve been in a survival state of mind for the past couple of years, and I would say my nerves are pretty frayed,” he said. “So I’m extra sensitive to potential downfalls to this whole plan that we’re hoping goes through.”

Still, legislators say there’s cause for hope. Rep. Friedman told IndieWire on November 9 that the House bill had 54 cosponsors, evenly split between Democrats and Republicans.

“I’m working to get this done as soon as possible because film and television workers need these jobs back now, not in a few months or a couple of years,” she said.

With weeks left in the current Congress, attaching the credit to a larger bill already headed for a vote might speed things up. But responding to IndieWire, Friedman didn’t identify a specific legislative package that could carry the measure to a scheduled floor date right now. If the proposal doesn’t become law before this session ends, lawmakers will have to reintroduce the initiative next year.

“It will take both parties working together to get this across the finish line, and we are pushing hard to make this much-needed incentive a reality,” Sen. Schiff told IndieWire in a statement.

Friedman noted that, as written, the credit could possibly take effect as early as January 1 — again, if the bill is signed before 2027. That could establish when production could qualify, but it doesn’t tell us when out-of-work crews might actually start getting calls. What’s more, when those job offers finally do come through? They could be far from old creative hubs like Los Angeles.

Richard Sanchez has a production job in California right now, and he knows how much that counts.

“I’m one of the very lucky folks who is working at the moment,” the visual effects editor told IndieWire by email. “But admittedly it’s lean and has been lean for quite a while.”

Tax credits have put states in fierce competition for film and TV jobs, from the first day of shooting to the final edit. And in September, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed AB 2319 — specifically creating a separate California tax credit for post-production work. The state is scheduled to start allocating those credits on July 1, 2027, and the yearly budget will ultimately determine how much is available to give out.

“It’s a start, it needs more funding but I hope that brings work in,” Sanchez told IndieWire.

California already makes up to $750 million a year available through its broader film and TV production credit. That previously expanded program began in July 2025 and generally covers 35 percent of qualifying spending, with a higher initial rate for TV series that relocate here. That can help California land a show, but it doesn’t guarantee steady employment for crew members. Studios still decide how many episodes to order and where to send the post-production work.

In the third quarter of 2026, projects in the program accounted for 40.3 percent of scripted on-location filming in Greater Los Angeles (nearly double their share a year earlier), according to FilmLA’s quarterly report. But over the same period, total on-location filming across the region fell 4.8 percent.

“Where the tax credit applies, it’s working to bring productions back to Los Angeles and put local crews to work,” FilmLA CEO Denise Gutches said in a statement to IndieWire. “Still, overall production remains far below where Los Angeles needs it to be, and crews and businesses across the region are feeling it.”

FilmLA also counts shoot days, not jobs or paychecks. So, those figures can’t tell us how many people were hired, how much they made, or whether they worked enough to qualify for benefits. One person who responded to IndieWire’s Reddit callout and identified themselves as a Bay Area camera operator said they were working on a union production but doubted they’d log enough hours for health coverage.

Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra called the current program “the floor” during his campaign and pledged to expand. Newsom’s proposal would raise the annual cap to at least $1 billion, make expenses such as actors’ pay eligible, and set aside $100 million a year for indie productions. Those changes still need legislative approval, but Becerra’s first budget will give crews a better idea of what he’s prepared to seek.

As for Curley, he got a brief stint with the U.S. main unit of “Artificial,” which shot partly in San Francisco, but most of the shoot, he said, took place in Italy. A federal credit might make a U.S. production more attractive to filmmakers facing such a choice, but then there’s the question of which state they’ll choose.

Georgia, for example, offers a 20 percent base credit plus another 10 percentage points for productions that promote the state, with no annual cap on how much productions can earn in credits. California and Georgia count different expenses, so the percentages are only part of the calculation.

And a producer weighing L.A. and Atlanta gets to run the numbers both ways — while a crew member who’s spent years building a career in one city has a different calculation to make. If the next show goes across the country, can they afford to follow it? Can they afford to stay put and wait? Either way, more American projects won’t necessarily mean more openings for the crews Hollywood has left behind.

“We can’t always be the cheapest, so we need to be the easiest.” That’s how Pamala Buzick Kim, a co-founder of the production advocacy group Stay in LA, sees the city’s job supporting the industry.

A tax credit can make a shoot look good on paper. But someone still has to get the permits, pay the fees, and figure out what happens when the next location runs across a city line. Buzick Kim said mayor-elect Nithya Raman’s office regularly talked with Stay in L.A. about what was getting in the way of filming and what the city could practically do about it. Those conversations made her optimistic.

“Everybody’s looking after their small piece of the pie, which is what their job is,” Buzick Kim said. “But we have not instituted any infrastructure to look out for our business in Los Angeles as a whole.”

Raman’s office did not immediately respond to IndieWire’s request for comment. But her campaign platform called for a staffed film office within the mayor’s office, clearer permit timelines, lower fees for smaller productions, and regular reviews of neighborhood filming restrictions. She also pledged to work with the county and neighboring jurisdictions so productions could move more easily.

“If we’re going to incentivize more people to roll here we need to cut down permit processing times, lower fees, and lift unnecessary restrictions on local filmmaking,” echoed film and TV editor Andy Young in an email to IndieWire. Young volunteered for Raman in the primary and worked as a paid freelance video editor for her campaign during the general election. (He said he was speaking for himself.)

“I’m excited to have a Mayor that sees LA as an industry town, sees how bleak things are right now, and has a real sense of urgency when it comes to filling sound stages and getting cameras rolling again,” Young wrote.

Some of Raman’s proposed changes will take cooperation across local groups. For example, FilmLA coordinates applications and charges for its services, but city officials approve permits and set some of the fees that FilmLA ultimately collects. A new administration at City Hall will have to work with the people already making those decisions to successfully enact changes.

Of course, for a smaller shoot, every cost makes a difference. FilmLA and the city recently extended their low-impact permit pilot through April 30, 2027, meaning qualifying productions can apply for just $350, compared with the standard $931 application fee. A few days on a commercial can pay the bills between longer jobs, and Buzick Kim wants city residents to see community when film crews take over their block.

“How do we get residents to be more favorable and optimistic about production?” she asked for Stay in LA. “How do we get them understanding that these are your neighbor’s jobs?”

Curley said he didn’t know enough about permitting to say how much a film office would practically help with the issues he’s been facing. After all, for years, the city’s reputation as the best place in the world for movies “was our film office,” he said. Still, taken together, Curley’s dry spell and the Stay in LA pitch assume that literal Hollywood, like anywhere else, must earn its place amongst national competition.

California voters chose new leadership in Washington, the state capital of Sacramento, and LA’s City Hall. But they didn’t get say on who would own two of Hollywood’s biggest studios.

On October 6, less than a month before the election, Paramount Skydance completed its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery. The deal followed a separate earlier merger in August 2025, when Skydance and Paramount Global combined.

In its November 9 investor update, Skydance said it was aiming for at least $6 billion in annual savings within three years. Those plans include combining back-office functions and using more AI in some corporate workflows.

An August analysis commissioned by L.A. County estimated that the merger could put about 4,500 local film and TV jobs at risk over the next three years. That was an estimate of potential losses, not a count of people already laid off — and it also preceded a fall settlement, which required additional production spending from Skydance. Still, investors got a number and a deadline, while crews are continually being asked to wait and see how much work the combined company will actually have for them.

California and other states did get some promises in writing. A court-approved settlement disclosed in an SEC filing requires Skydance to release a minimum number of films in theaters and bars it from selling or closing the Paramount and Warner Bros. studio lots for five years. The deal also requires the new company to spend at least $1.5 billion more on U.S. filmmaking over that period than the two companies would have spent at their combined pace in 2025. But where will that business go?

Curley, for one, can actually imagine some good coming out of an industry that’s scattered beyond Los Angeles. Maybe more people will get a shot at making something of their own. Maybe there’ll be a burst of indie filmmaking like the one he associates with the ’70s. The Academy Award-winning craftsman can also see doors closing for people who’ve spent their working lives learning how to make movies.

“Maybe this is a good thing for the young people,” he said. “I’m hoping that’s the case anyway.”

For now, Curley already has an Oscar. What he wants is a call time and a chance to create again.

#3479. Amazon's Upcoming Crime Thriller Releasing In Two Weeks Is The Perfect Black Doves Follow-Up

Black Doves season 2 has ended with major question marks over what happens next, but season 3 still hasn’t been confirmed, although show creator Joe Barton has offered hope that there will be one. Yet, even if season 3 is confirmed soon, it might still be another two-year wait before it premieres. That leaves fans of the action-packed show missing out on the spy shenanigans for quite a while.

Not if MGM+, a streamer under the Amazon umbrella, has anything to say about it, though. While every TV series involving spies is different, MGM+ is debuting a new British series on November 22, 2026, that will more than satisfy Black Doves fans. It won’t cure the anticipation of waiting for a potential Black Doves season 3, but the upcoming MGM+ show Secret Service will make the time pass a little quicker.

Adapted from the novel of the same name by news anchor Tom Bradby (who also worked on the series), the series debuted in the UK in April, but has now found its American home on MGM+. The show follows Kate Henderson, a senior spy for MI6, who, in the course of working an operation, uncovers a Russian conspiracy to infiltrate the British government at the highest levels. Henderson and MI6 begin a covert investigation into the matter after the Prime Minister decides to resign, which means Henderson must investigate even those closest to her, including her husband and best friend.

Secret Service is a bit more grounded in realism than Black Doves, but it’s equally exciting, with enough twists and turns to keep viewers on the edge of their seats. Starring former "Bond girl" Gemma Arterton as Henderson, along with Avi Nash, Mark Stanley, Rafe Spall, and Aoife Hinds, the show isn’t a carbon copy of Black Doves, but it shares similar spy and political elements that fans will enjoy.

A new five-part spy series headlined by a former star of the James Bond franchise finds an appropriate streaming home in the United States.

Both shows are women-led, and while the Black Doves and MI6 are very different organizations (in fact, MI5 is highly suspicious of Helen in Black Doves), both offer viewers the tension and high stakes of spycraft mixed with government. Like Black Doves, which is drowning in conspiracies and double (or even triple) crosses, Secret Service delivers a major conspiracy.

Henderson is in a race against time to find the Russian assets hidden within the British government before it's too late. Helen and Henderson both have husbands in government, too, as Henderson’s husband is the chief aide to the Chancellor. Ideally, though, Secret Service won't leave viewers with as many lingering questions as Black Doves season 2 did.

Secret Service makes the perfect replacement for Black Doves fans who enjoy female spies, vast conspiracies, and storylines that keep you guessing. Plus, the show is a quick watch, so it won’t be long before all the secrets (or at least most of them) are revealed.

Secret Service only has five episodes, so it’s entirely bingeable. It appears that MGM+ will drop the show's first episode on November 22, and then release the others weekly into December, on Sundays at 10 pm EST.

With this release schedule, Secret Service will make a fantastic thriller to watch over the holiday season. Even better, Black Doves fans can wait until all the episodes have aired and enjoy a Christmas Day binge after all the gifts have been exchanged.

Hopefully, whether Black Doves season 3 is happening will be officially confirmed (or denied) sooner rather than later. For now, though, fans of that show can ease themselves through the pain of season 2 ending (and on a cliffhanger) with MGM+’s Secret Service. After all, there’s always room for more badass women taking down the bad guys in the TV schedule.

#3478. Apple Is About to Release a Touchscreen MacBook Pro (Plus Four More Devices)

Apple has had a busy fall. Head to the company's website, and you'll immediately be greeted by a sea of new products: the foldable iPhone Duo; the iPhone 18 Pro; HomePod mini 2; Apple Watch Series 12; the list goes on. It seems, under new Apple CEO Jon Ternus, the company is ready for a refresh of just about every product it sells. To that point, the company seems far from finished. Just this week, Apple is planning to release five brand new products, each launching on Friday. While four of these are Macs, Apple does have a new iPad in the works, as well. Here's everything new Apple is releasing this week.

Finally. For the first time, the iPad mini is about to ship with an OLED display. Apple's smallest tablet has always come with a standard screen. Despite its price tag, the iPad mini has never come with an OLED display, or even a mini-LED screen, until now. With this new model, there is no backlight. As such, each individual pixel on the iPad's display will be able to shut itself off when displaying dark content. That will benefit the content you watch on this device, as well as the overall contrast of the screen.

Beyond the new OLED panel, the new iPad mini is thinner and lighter than the previous model. It also comes with Apple's newest A20 Pro chip, the same processor the company put in its iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo smartphones. The new device starts at $699 for 128GB of storage, though there are various upgrades, including nano-texture glass (add $100) and cellular (add $150).

Good news: There's a new iMac. Bad news: Not much is different here from the previous model. The biggest change here is the new M6 chip, which Apple says is up to five times faster than the iMac with M4 and up to 12 times faster than the iMac with M1. With that M6 chip, the iMac now supports Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. Other than that, this is the same iMac you may already know: It comes with a 24-inch LED display (no OLED, unfortunately), two or four USB-C ports (depending on the configuration), and a built-in 12MP webcam. If you're looking for a new all-in-one computer, or you've been considering upgrading your older iMac, this is likely a great choice. But if you already have an M-series iMac, it's not such an obvious upgrade. (My M1 iMac may be up to 12 times slower, but it's still plenty fast for me.) Apple didn't change the price here: The M6 iMac still starts at $1,499 for two ports, 16GB of RAM, and 256GB of storage.

Similarly, Apple's newest 14-inch MacBook Pro isn't much different from the previous model—save for the new processor. This model also comes with Apple's M6 chip, which Apple says is up to 13 times faster for AI processing than the M1 MacBook Pro. (Apple seems keen on convincing stubborn M1 users to upgrade this cycle.) Now, the company is offering this model of MacBook Pro in three chipsets, depending on use case: M6 for "entry-level" pro work; M5 Pro for mid-tier pro work; and M5 Max for the most demanding situations.

But, like the M6 iMac, this is the same MacBook Pro Apple sold before. It has a 14-inch mini-LED display with a refresh rate up to 120Hz. It comes with three Thunderbolt 4 (USB-C) ports, an HDMI port, and an SDXC card slot. It, too, has a 12MP webcam for video calls. Apple's newest MacBook Pro starts at $1,999, but you can quickly ramp up that price tag with screen, chip, memory, or storage upgrades.

Apple's most exciting product launch this week is undoubtedly the new touchscreen MacBook Pros. Unlike the M6 MacBook Pro, which only comes in the 14-inch variant, Apple's first touchscreen laptop comes in both 14- and 16-inch options. Apple says this touchscreen lets you scroll, zoom, or draw on the display. That works with basic functions, like web browsing or selecting files, but also with specific workflows, like playing virtual instruments in Logic Pro, or manipulating an object in a 3D modeling app. Like the iPad mini, this laptop comes with an OLED display (Apple calls it PROLED XDR), with up to 1,000 nits of typical brightness and 2,000 nits of HDR brightness. It also brings back the backlit Apple logo, something I've missed on my last two MacBooks.

This MacBook Pro also comes with the iPhone's Dynamic Island for the first time. This replaces the "notch" that other MacBook Pros and MacBook Airs currently ship with. It can function as a basic webcam, but also as a dedicated zone for Spotlight, Live Activities, and Siri AI. This machine comes in either M5 Pro or M5 Max variants—no M6 for this model—as Apple seems to be positioning it exclusively for the most taxing situations (particularly AI). The company says the new MacBook Pro has up to 13 more hours of battery life than Intel-based MacBook Pros, and can fast charge up to 50% in 30 minutes. It's essentially a supercharged version of the existing MacBook Pro.

As such, this is Apple's most expensive laptop. The 14-inch M5 Pro version starts at $2,899, while the 16-inch starts at $3,399. However, you can configure these machines to have outrageous price tags. The maxed-out 16-inch MacBook Pro is $14,549, roughly half of which is the 16TB of RAM.

#3477. 15 Movies To Watch if You Love 'MobLand'

Guy Ritchie has long been the go-to Guy when it comes to British crime movies. Ever since his 1998 feature-length debut, Lock, Stock and Two Smoking Barrels, it has been clear that this British director has a keen eye for the wickedly violent and the devilishly funny. With the premiere of the second season of The Gentlemen and Prime Video's Young Sherlock, there's no better time to be a Ritchie fan.

This is especially true when considering the unquestionable success of his latest foray into the world of crime, MobLand (the series was created by Ronan Bennett, with Ritchie attached as a director). With the stars aligning to take on Ritchie's big-budget caper, including Tom Hardy, Pierce Brosnan, Helen Mirren, and Paddy Considine, this modern-day series has received plenty of high praise thus far, including a strong 83% approval rating on review aggregator Rotten Tomatoes. For fans craving more movies like MobLand, several films deliver the same beats. With all that in mind, here's a look at the best movies to watch if you love MobLand.

There's no better place to start when recommending a movie following MobLand than 2019's The Gentlemen, not to be confused with Ritchie's series of the same name. Directed by Ritchie, the film follows Matthew McConaughey's American expat who, while trying to find the highest bidder for his marijuana empire, ends up sparking all-out criminal chaos.

Featuring a star-studded ensemble worthy of rivaling MobLand's — including the aforementioned McConaughey, Charlie Hunnam, Jeremy Strong, Hugh Grant, and more — The Gentlemen is a fast-paced, stylish run through the best of Ritchie. Effortlessly funny and often brutal, this is a winding crime web spun to perfection.

Mobland's brilliance lies in its distinct mix of witty charm and hard-hitting crime action, making the overall experience an absolute blast to watch, a strength shared by the underrated 2000s crime comedy Smokin' Aces. The film follows a magician turned mafia informant on the run after the mob gets word of his betrayal, placing a $1 million bounty on him as well as looking to take him for their own personal reasons.

The initial setup is about as classic as crime comedies get, seeing various personalities with ties to the mob converging and facing off in an attempt to make it on a high bounty. However, as the intricacies of these crimes and an array of shocking twists come to light, it becomes largely apparent that the film is hiding a much larger web of lies, deception, and madness between intersecting parties. Similar to Mobland, the film has an absolute slam-dunk cast to help elevate its story, featuring the likes of Ben Affleck, Ray Liotta, Jeremy Piven, Ryan Reynolds, Alicia Keys, and Jason Bateman. —Robert Lee

For those who like Hardy in MobLand, Legend is the next port of call. The man behind fixer Harry Da Souza takes on not one but two of the most infamous criminals in British history, portraying both of the Kray twins in this journey through their lavish, tragic lives in 1960s London.

Perhaps Hardy's best performance to date, his ability to switch between both twins, offering evolving and nuanced perspectives on both their lives, is nothing short of remarkable. Add to that a stellar supporting cast, a neat script, and several action scenes that live long in the memory, and a recipe for British crime movie success is born.

Mobland doesn't simply follow a singular mob family, but instead the infighting and squabbles that come up as a result of conflicting mob families, a facet that has consistently found strength within crime storytelling. Lucky Number Slevin takes this classic archetype and provides the engaging dark comedy of taking a completely unrelated third party, throwing him in the middle of this conflict, but having completely mistaken him for a friend who is in deep with the mob.

It covers a similarly dark comedy tone that Mobland expertly utilizes, with Lucky Number Slevin getting a lot of comedic mileage out of not just the inherent miscommunication of its concept, but all of the different moving pieces and wild characters that end up intertwined in this dilemma. The film also features a standout cast, including Josh Hartnett, Morgan Freeman, Bruce Willis, Lucy Liu, Ben Kingsley, and Stanley Tucci. —Robert Lee

Brosnan's patriarch, Conrad Harrigan, is one of the standout characters in MobLand, with Die Another Day the best next stop for the actor at his suave and stylish best. The movie follows Brosnan as the iconic James Bond as he attempts to bring down an international criminal enterprise that plans to build a world-threatening space weapon.

Brosnan is still as effortlessly cool as ever in MobLand, but rewind 23 years to 2002, and his portrayal of 007 marks the actor's peak. An action-packed Bond entry that also marked the end of an era for the series, Die Another Day might usher in an even greater period for the franchise, but let that take nothing away from just how impressive it is on its own.

While Mobland was undeniably the standout gangster story worth watching in 2025, one other gangster film from the year that parallels its strengths in distinct ways is Caught Stealing, the most recent film from Darren Aronofsky. Similar to Lucky Number Slevin, the film follows an unaffiliated third party who finds himself at the center of an ongoing feud between a bunch of different criminal groups. From Russian mobsters to Hasidic brothers to corrupt police, all of the different moving pieces prove to make the film that much more of a striking watch.

Leading star Austin Butler is one of the key selling points of the film; he exceptionally navigates the chaos and death that constantly follow him both as a result of these criminals and the guilt of his past haunting him. The aesthetic of '90s New York also does wonders for the feel and look of the film, harkening back to iconic New York crime movies of the '90s like A Bronx Tale and Carlito's Way. —Robert Lee

For many, Snatch is Ritchie's magnum opus. Featuring a cast that includes a young Stephen Graham and Brad Pitt at the peak of his powers, Snatch follows the theft of a priceless diamond and the many invested criminal minds attempting to beat the competition and track it down.

Snatch feels like Ritchie let loose. Packed from start to finish with iconic one-liners, unapologetically violent action, and even a terrifying Irish action from Pitt for good measure, Snatch is an enigmatic, bloody imprint on Ritchie's wonderful legacy. MobLand might show Ritchie at his most mature, but Snatch will showcase him at his best.

Four criminal masterminds. One of them was always going to be yours. Here is who comes for you, why they picked you out of everyone available, and what they want from the encounter.

Your nemesis does not want to beat you. He wants to know you completely, and he is patient enough to wait for it. The frightening part is how good the conversation is.

Your nemesis is not after money, territory or revenge. He is after a demonstration, and you are the person he has chosen to prove his point on.

Your nemesis respects you, which sounds flattering until you work out what it means. He chose you because nobody else was worth his time.

Your nemesis has no personal interest in you whatsoever, and that is precisely what makes him unsurvivable. You are not a rival. You are a stop on the way.

While this crime comedy certainly leans more toward comedy than crime in its tone, the overwhelming amount of violence and dark humor present in Seven Psychopaths helps the film never stray away from its roots as an unrestrained story of crime. The setup is about as goofy as a crime story gets, with a screenwriter getting into hot water with the Los Angeles criminal underworld after his friends kidnap a gangster's beloved Shih Tzu. However, the pain and carnage that this kidnapping sets in motion is very real, emphasized by the immaculate directing of Martin McDonagh.

This strange blend of killers, blackmail, and extravagant personalities at times feels like a distillation of classic gangster films down into an absurdist satire on crime culture, Hollywood, and everything in between. The film was largely celebrated when it first released, but has largely been lost in the shadows due to McDonagh's career being elevated to Academy prestige in his subsequent films. Still, there is a charm and brilliance within Seven Psychopaths that makes it still worth watching almost 15 years later. —Robert Lee

MobLand boasts an extremely talented cast, with one of the more underrated performances in the series coming from Considine. Back in 2004, Considine once again put in a highly underrated supporting turn as Phil in Paweł Pawlikowski's My Summer of Love. Two young women from either end of the class spectrum end up entwined in a burning romance across a hot British summer, only for the reality of their situation to rear its ugly head.

Considine's performance as the reformed criminal Phil in My Summer of Love underpins almost every emotional beat in the story. Perhaps underrated due to this movie marking the breakout of one Emily Blunt, experiencing Considine's skin-crawling turn with knowledge of his impeccable career that followed certainly makes this a worthy follow-up to MobLand.

MobLand is seen as this glorious collaboration between English filmmaking talent, most notably with director Guy Ritchie and A-list leading star Tom Hardy. However, this actually isn't the first time that these two have collaborated on a creative work, as Hardy appears as one of many icons of English cinema in RocknRolla, one of Ritchie's most often forgotten crime comedy films. The film sees various members of London's criminal underworld pursuing their share of a lucrative fortune brought about by a Russian mobster's real estate scam.

Hardy's role in the film isn't front and center, as it is largely balanced with its prominent cast of other English talent, including Gerard Butler, Mark Strong, Idris Elba, and Thandiwe Newton. Still, even in this side role, released 17 years before they would collaborate again in MobLand, Hardy fits into Ritchie's signature style of directing perfectly. It certainly also helps that MobLand and RocknRolla are both crime stories that act as a workaround for exceptional English ensembles. —Robert Lee

#3476. How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Dominated the Box Office: GKIDS Chief on IMAX’s Impact and the Growing Market for Foreign-Language Movies

“Godzilla Minus Zero” almost pulled of a Godzilla-times-three on its opening weekend, earning $31.6 million in North America to nearly triple the domestic debut of its 2023 predecessor “Godzilla Minus One.” With that Godzilla math, it destroyed the record for the biggest North American debut for a live-action foreign language film.

It was a crowning moment for the speciality distributor GKIDS. Founded in 2008, the label primarily built itself as a distributor of foreign language animated features, most notably with its acquisition of the North American distribution rights to the Studio Ghibli library. As a day-one employee of GKIDS, and its president since 2017, Dave Jesteadt has helped expand the stateside audience for subtitled features. After a 2025 acquisition by Toho, the Japanese film industry giant behind “Godzilla,” the reach of GKIDS is wider than ever with “Minus Zero,” which drew a box office debut that some studio tentpoles this year would envy. Related Stories Democrats Won. When Do Hollywood Crews Get Back to Work? Attend, the First Marketplace Connecting Filmmakers Directly to Theater Owners, Finally Launches Today

“Anecdotally, so many people I know are like, ‘I took my dad this movie and he doesn’t go to any subtitle movies,'” Jesteadt told IndieWire. “Godzilla brings us together. If we’re spreading the gospel of foreign cinema, and Godzilla is a vehicle to get people to engage with great films and deep themes, then I’m all for it.”

After a flashy premiere at the New York Film Festival and a historic cume from IMAX and other premium large-format auditoriums, Jesteadt digs into how GKIDS helped “Minus Zero” come to America.

The following interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and length.

IndieWire: “Godzilla Minus One” was seen as a breakout success in 2023, with $57 million in North America. What lessons did GKIDS take away from Toho‘s release of “Minus One” in building toward this big opening for “Minus Zero”?

Dave Jesteadt: GKIDS joined the Toho Group in October 2024, but our story of working together on this began before that, back in 2023. GKIDS had “The Boy and the Heron” from Hayao Miyazaki and Studio Ghibli in theaters just a week after “Godzilla Minus One” opened, which was being handled by Toho’s L.A. office at the time. We got to know that team because we had these two films in theaters, sort of competing for similar audience profiles.

In terms of lessons that both sides took, it’s that you can really drive conversation with theaters as a source of celebration and community. When we joined the Toho Group, we took in the team that worked on “Minus One.” We re-released “Shin Godzilla” in 2025 as a test for bringing modern Japanese “Godzilla” films to theaters. Then the planning for “Minus Zero” really began in terms of how we could build and improve on the audience that “Minus One” already found.

Did “Minus Zero” get a bigger marketing spend stateside? How did you consider which people to reach to expand the audience for a Japanese “Godzilla” film?

I can’t give a specific number, but I’d say that we’re very efficient and very mindful of how we can reach the audience in the most direct way possible. For this film, we have the great benefit of our colleagues at Toho International owning and operating Godzilla.com, overseeing merchandise licensing. They have direct communication with the “Godzilla” fan as they exist in America.

But the other goal is to reach, as “Minus One” did, an audience that hadn’t engaged in Japanese “Godzilla” films. We also balanced reaching that core “Godzilla” fan and making sure that they turn out with this desire to continue the story from “Minus One,” reminding people that these films from director Takashi Yamazaki really speak to broader feelings today. They have prestigious bona fides through playing film festivals and great critical reviews. We’re leading with the quality of the film, making people feel that this is a very safe choice — not just if you like spectacle, but that this is going to be one of the best films of the year.

The New York Film Festival premiere played as a flex, especially after a stretch where Hollywood would premiere summer blockbusters at Cannes, draw mediocre reviews, and then have to weather weeks of bad buzz for their expensive tentpoles. With the NYFF premiere, “Minus Zero” was positioned as a prestige object. Is that the aura you were trying to cultivate around it?

I think so. Godzilla has been one of the most famous characters in the world. There’s a big audience that you can potentially address. But the “Minus” franchise takes it into more realistic, human-centered stories. That differentiates it. It is a risk to go to a film festival; I think that has been pretty well-argued. It is a risk anytime you want to share something with the world early before you open, especially when you have such high hopes about how it’s going to go. On the other hand, this was a really important way to demonstrate confidence.

“Minus Zero” opened in more than 3,200 theaters, roughly 1,000 more theaters than “Minus One.” How much did you expand its presence in premium large-format auditoriums?

“Minus Zero” was the first Japanese production filmed for IMAX. That was a central part of the very first announcement and it was a defining part of the marketing campaign. IMAX mentioned it was the highest-indexed opening gross on IMAX screens for an opening weekend in the U.S. We had Godzilla Day on November 3, with IMAX early access screenings globally. So, PLFs definitely played a big presence: Imax, 4DX, Dbox, and others. That’s very unusual for a subtitled foreign film.

It speaks to the expectations for high quality that audiences brought. The PLF story is a way to reinforce production quality. Everyone is saying, “You have to see it in the biggest screen possible with the best sound.” I’ve seen many, many beautiful foreign films. They often end up playing circuits to audiences that are very passionate, but don’t have access to those kind of screens. So it’s a privilege to be able to play a film on the kind of screen that’s typically reserved for the biggest mainstream titles.

How long are you staying in IMAX and PLFs?

It depends on the market. We’re definitely here for the rest of this week. But as “The Odyssey” and other titles have demonstrated, there’s such draw to these moments. It can even create this quest to see something in multiple formats. But as we head into the Thanksgiving frame, the Hollywood competition is obviously huge. We’re realistic about that, even while we’re trying to encourage people to see it as soon and as often as they can.

The reported statistic that more than 70 percent of grosses came from PLFs seems a bit of a double-edged sword to me. It speaks to a high regard for the film among consumers, but it also might indicate that it has a specialized audience that may only want to see the movie in a premium format. Is that a consideration GKIDS takes in, particularly when other titles are taking those auditoriums in the coming weeks?

Obviously, PLFs are time-sensitive. It’s not just about performance, but also about new titles coming in. We’re up against the biggest studios in the world. I’m obviously thrilled that we were able to get so many and I’m thrilled that people saw it that way. I also encourage everyone to just see it in regular theaters too. The way that it was mastered and the way that director Yamazaki made the film is so you won’t have a bad experience in any house watching it. But with any of these core fandoms, there’s a lot of interest in seeing something “the right way.” I’m happy for that, but then the hope is they tell their friends and we continue the growth from there.

You’ve been with GKIDS since its inception and have played a major part in growing the American audience for foreign language cinema. What do you think has changed in the marketplace that has allowed a Japanese “Godzilla” film to now find a much broader audience in the West than it could find before?

There’s no doubt that the quality of the films really helps. “Minus One” was a fantastic film. It won the Oscar for visual effects and became an audience darling. But really, the thing that’s changed the most is that younger generations are much more open to subtitled and foreign cinema than they would have been 10 or 20 years ago. We’ve entered an age of opportunity where what can constitute a hit film is really broadening. That gives me a lot of optimism compared to negative stories about the overall economics of the industry. GKIDS has been bringing subtitled animated movies and anime to audiences for almost 20 years and seeing that audience grow naturally. At first, dubs were essential; now, they’re not.

Though GKIDS isn’t producing these films, I’m curious if, as a distributor, you think that Japanese productions like “Minus Zero” are now being developed and produced with more of a global audience in mind.

The films are still intrinsically Japanese and are basically impossible to separate from the cultural tradition of “Godzilla” in Japan, as well as the overall Japanese film industry. On the other hand, there’s no doubt that the property has the ability to reach a global audience. The popularity with the “Minus” series is really a focus on quality, and how its storytelling is rooted in a time and a place that feels authentically Japanese. Although it deals with a post-war moment in Japanese history, it is incredibly contemporary in terms of the thoughts and preoccupations of a global audience.

So I don’t think there’s necessarily a change in focus. I would say that the audience and the director are in a much more direct conversation. On social media now, everything is auto-translated. You can see real-time active conversation between Japanese fans and viewers commenting about the film with American or Spanish or European audience. Everyone is able to share their thoughts or opinions about some of these themes in a way that brings local perspective to the table. By creating something that feel like it’s created for a specific audience, ironically, you end up making it feel more universal, just because it feels more lived in.

Do you think we are headed to a world where a Japanese “Godzilla” film can outgross a Western “Godzilla” film in North America?

I don’t really think about that. I’m very competitive against a lot of people, but the “Godzilla” franchise has benefited from having a lot of flavors to it. By building that big tent, it ends up being a character that has endured.

“Godzilla Minus Zero” is now in theaters.

#3475. Six Fitness 'Rules' That Don't Actually Matter

I’ve learned a lot in my many years in the gym, and beginner-me would be shocked and appalled by the things present-me does during workouts. With the benefit of experience, I now do exercises I used to think one should “never” do, and I’ve broken pretty much every other rule besides.

I've already explained a bunch of things you can stop worrying about as a beginner, but I’d like to expand on that list with a few more rules that even intermediate-level exercisers can ditch without consequence.

If you can theoretically do 13 bicep curls with a certain weight, how many curls should you actually do? One common misconception is that if you don’t do all 13, you’re leaving gains on the table. The rule kind of makes sense if you have truly no clue where to start; if you go until you can’t do a single rep more, then at least you know you’re not slacking off.

But the downside is that going to failure for every set of every lift is just going to make you exhausted. On bicep curls, maybe not so much, but once you’re squatting pretty heavy weights, you’re going to feel spent if you do every single set to failure, and that fatigue will get in the way of getting a good workout in consistently. What’s better is to follow a program that advises you on when to hold back and when it’s a good time to really push your limits. You’ll find that most of the time, you stop a set at least 2-3 reps shy of failure, and sometimes even more.

Rest days are a convenient tool for making sure you’re not overworking yourself, but that’s all. Organizations like the American College of Sports Medicine recommend leaving 48 hours between intense strength-training sessions for a given muscle, but if you look at where they get that number, it’s meant to be a general recommendation for beginners and for people who are exercising just to stay healthy. Once you’re talking about athletes or enthusiasts, the ACSM acknowledges that training most days of the week is fine if your program manages fatigue effectively. That may mean alternating between heavier and lighter days, rather than taking complete rest days.

The “10% rule” is a not-terrible guideline for figuring out how quickly to ramp up your training. But like many of these other myths, it’s a suggestion, not a commandment to be strictly obeyed.

As running coach Jason Fitzgerald told Lifehacker, “While the adage is to only increase weekly mileage by 10%, this may be either too conservative or even too aggressive depending on where you start from.” When you’re coming back from a short layoff, you can probably increase mileage a lot faster. Same goes if you’re a beginner and your mileage is overall very low; if you took the rule literally, you wouldn’t be able to increase from zero to any other number.

Meanwhile, serious running programs—once again, a program is a wonderful thing—may give you a bigger increase for a few weeks in a row, then cut back and decrease your mileage temporarily before ramping up again. Or they may keep you at the same mileage for weeks at a time before venturing a larger increase. If you were to stick to the 10% rule, you would miss out on the advantages of programs that work this way.

There are pros and cons to lifting before cardio, and to doing cardio before lifting. It’s more of an “it depends” than a rule. So here are some of the ways to decide which makes sense.

Your lifts tend to suffer when you’re fatigued, and doing them fresh is important to you

Cardio is your top priority, and you want to have more energy for it

Your lifts are the kind of thing that can get done even when you’re fatigued

Or you only intend to do a small amount of cardio before lifting

So a cyclist may prefer to do a strength workout after hopping off the bike, but a powerlifter would probably rather get their conditioning in after finishing squats for the day. Either is fine if you don’t care, or if you prefer to mix it up.

There are a few supplements that can help you in your fitness journey, but none of them are necessary. Creatine is one of the best-known muscle-building supplements. It’s understood to be effective, but here’s the thing: Just because it does something for most people doesn’t mean it does very much. If you decide it’s too expensive or just that you would rather not have another thing to remember to take every day, you’re not missing out on any substantial amount of gains.

Likewise, protein powder is a helpful way to get more protein in your diet, but you don’t need to use a supplement; you can just eat more protein-containing foods.

And finally, pre-workout drinks can give you more energy in the gym (it’s mostly caffeine), but the idea that you need it is a very recent development. Even ten years ago, it wasn’t really a thing. People showed up to the gym with a coffee or a coke or with no caffeine at all in their stomach, and worked out just fine.

Look, people have been exercising successfully for millennia, but all of our apps and devices weren't even a thing until the 2000s. Tracking every minute, every step, or every mile of your routine is not actually necessary. You’re still a runner even if you don’t have an app that knows how many miles you ran. You don’t even have to track your sets and reps in your lifting journal if you don’t want to. Your body is what knows how much work you put in, even if your phone were to get wiped overnight.

#3474. Godzilla's Gigantic New 'Kingzilla' Form Explained

Whatever humanity throws at the King of Monsters, Godzilla only gets stronger. Now, he's getting much, much taller too. Godzilla just adopted one of his tallest forms of all time, with a new name to go with it - 'Kingzilla.'

While Godzilla is always gigantic, the character's height varies radically depending on the appearance. While Godzilla Minus One and Godzilla Minus Zero depict Godzilla at over 150 feet, Godzilla: Planet of the Monsters shows him closer to 950.

Now, Godzilla is even bigger, depicted at over 1,400 feet tall and truly unstoppable. Here's what you need to know about 'Kingzilla.'

In the recent 'Kingzilla' from Godzilla vs America: Godzilla vs New York City #1, Frank Tieri, Mark Texeira, Tom Napolitano and Brian Kolek present a story inspired by 1933's King Kong. The comic story imagines what would have happened if, instead of discovering a giant ape, filmmaker Carl Denham had discovered the King of Monsters.

Seeking to make the ultimate monster movie, Denham leads an expedition to a mysterious island that is rumored to be the home of "a giant that was simian in nature." Sadly for the group, King Kong has been unseated and replaced by Godzilla, who is worshiped by cultists who address the monster as their king.

Godzilla promptly kills Ann Darrow and chases the expedition back to New York, laying waste to the city. At the end of the story, Godzilla recreates King Kong climbing the Empire State Building. Except 'Kingzilla' is so gigantic it towers over the building, destroying it with its razor-sharp claws then gnawing on the Chrysler Building for good measure.

As the story ends, the biplanes that killed King Kong arrive, only to be swatted out of the air by Kingzilla. The whole story is told in sepia-tinted black and white, recreating the aesthetic of King Kong even as the narrative disastrously diverges.

As fun as it is to see Godzilla and King Kong work together in the Monsterverse, this is the crossover fans really deserved. Ultimately, the original King Kong and Godzilla tell very different stories with very different metaphors for their monsters.

Putting Godzilla in King Kong's place results in an explosive new story that still touches on hubris, but with humanity as the losers rather than the subjugators of nature. Of course, now fans need to see the other side of the equation - King Kong running rampant in 1950s Japan.

Very mild spoilers for Godzilla Minus Zero follow.

As fun as 'Kingzilla' is, it's just one story in this anthology issue that imagines different versions of Godzilla attacking New York. Indeed, the larger series sees Godzilla take on a variety of US locales, including Los Angeles, Portland, Texas and more.

The series is a particular balm for fans of Godzilla Minus Zero, who were led to believe the movie would see Godzilla attack the United States. Unfortunately, the trailer tease of Godzilla crushing the Statue of Liberty is actually a short fantasy scene in the movie, albeit one of the movie's most awe-inspiring and disturbing, as everyday Americans are incinerated in slow motion.

For anyone who actually wanted to see Godzilla running wild in America, Godzilla vs America delivers again and again, with a variety of creative teams tackling different iconic locations. 'Kingzilla' shows how creative new ideas can emerge from the prompt of Godzilla conquering different US cities, not just using the imagery of these real-world settings but their pop culture legacies.

Godzilla vs America: Godzilla vs New York City #1 is available now from IDW Publishing.

#3472. This New Sci-Fi Novel From a Pulitzer Prize Winner Could Be the Next Hunger Games

For only having three books under his belt, author Hernan Diaz has added an impressive number of literary prizes to his trophy case. The Argentine and American writer won the New American Voices Award for his 2017 debut novel In the Distance, and was also a finalist for both the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction and the PEN/Faulkner Award for Fiction for the same book. Later, his follow-up novel, Trust, won both the 2022 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction and the Kirkus Prize. This year, Diaz has made a triumphant return to the page – except this time, he’s playing in the science fiction sandbox.

Diaz's newest novel, Ply, came out in September 2026. This refreshing book takes a sharp detour from the author's usual route. Usually, Diaz writes historical fiction novels. Ply tackles Diaz's usual themes – power, wealth, American mythology, loneliness – except, this time, in a futuristic, hardscrabble world. The novel takes place centuries from now in a ruined American city, where citizens have to struggle for even the most basic necessities, including food, shelter, and, most importantly, electricity. Overall, Ply is a dark dystopian take on America’s future, featuring a savant female protagonist whose great intellect and razor-sharp edge might just pull her out of obscurity. Sound familiar? This surprising sci-fi take from an award-winning literary novelist will remind readers of The Hunger Games series by Suzanne Collins and Station Eleven by Emily St. John Mandel – and it just might be the next big thing in dystopian fiction.

Like many dystopian epics, Ply begins with a girl. The book’s unnamed protagonist is introduced to readers simply as “the Pincher.” She is an orphan, hustling her way through life in a derelict cityscape. Set centuries from now, the Pincher’s world is one of decay, pollution, and rugged individualism. Citizens of this crumbling America are left to fend for themselves; they scavenge for food and trade wares with their neighbors, all the while living in fear of the powerful corporations that control society’s water and electricity output – simply called Flow and Tensor.

There’s also the terrorizing group known as CTS, a blurry security conglomerate that polices the city’s streets with hawk-like eyes. This is the context in which readers are introduced to the Pincher. As the book unfolds, readers soon learn more about her world. She lives in a deteriorating building on the wrong side of the city’s heavily polluted river, and makes her living by stealing electricity from the grid and selling it secretly on the black market – this is where her title of “Pincher” comes from.

While the Pincher has many clients, one of her passions is fueling the city’s underground music concerts. Over the years, she has earned a reputation for being exceptionally good at her job; she is both swift and undetectable. However, while surreptitiously delivering a brick of power to a concert one night, the Pincher gets the eerie feeling that she is being followed. But who is following her, and what do they want? It’s not long before the Pincher finds herself pulled into a complicated web of tinkerers, power players, and black market dealers – all of whom are scrambling to get their hands on a groundbreaking experiment. If the Pincher is able to provide the electricity to power this new machine, she could revolutionize the world as she knows it.

Like The Hunger Games and the Divergent series before it, Ply is the story of a spiky female lead who is forging not only a new path for herself but is also breaking new ground for society as a whole. While Katniss Everdeen changes the world through her physical prowess in the arena and her political cunning, and Tris challenges the status quo with her very brain functions (by being naturally immune to mind-control serum, of course), the Pincher in Ply stands out from the rest thanks to her technological genius. Diaz’s novel may be a portrait of a dystopian America, but the star of the show is, undeniably, this electrician whiz; readers will care about her character's evolution first and foremost.

Looking at these books, sci-fi is in great hands.

Hernan Diaz is anything but a newcomer to the literary scene. When his debut novel, In the Distance, was released in 2017, it quickly became the talk of the proverbial town. The prestigious publication, The Paris Review, listed it as one of the top books of the year, while Literary Hub listed it as one of “The 20 Best Novels of the Decade.” He followed up his success with Trust – Diaz’s second book published in 2022. This sophomore release upped the ante, earning the Argentine-American writer a spot on the longlist for the 2022 Booker Prize and taking home the 2023 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction. It, too, found its way on many “best of” lists – including the New York Times’s “10 Best Books of 2022” list.

With such a sterling reputation, fans of Diaz may have been expecting more of the same with his third release. After all, why depart from a winning model? However, Ply marks new territory for Diaz and sees him dipping his toes into the sci-fi genre, which comes with its own unique conventions and history. Did Diaz stick the landing? Both In the Distance and Trust are historical fiction novels that look to the past to help make sense of the present.

Set in the 1800s, In the Distance tells the story of a Swedish emigrant named Håkan who is searching for his brother across the American West. Along the way, he faces poverty, hardship, and discrimination. Likewise, Trust is a puzzle-like novel that takes place in the early 1900s, examining the world of extreme wealth in New York City before and after the cataclysmic event that was the Great Depression. By setting his third novel in the future, in an unspecified year, Diaz expands his toolkit, bringing in techno-thriller elements to craft a dystopian setting.

While Daniel Kraus took home the 2026 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction with his World War I novel Angel Down, Diaz and his team could potentially be eyeing up next year's competition. According to the Pulitzer committee, any book published in the 2026 calendar year is eligible to be considered for the 2027 award. Having hit US shelves on September 29 of this year, Diaz’s name is sure to be thrown into the ring for his experimental third novel.

If Diaz were to take home the 2027 Pulitzer Prize, he would join an elite club of writers who have two Pulitzer Prizes under their belt, including Booth Tarkington, William Faulkner, John Updike, and, most recently, Colson Whitehead, who won for The Underground Railroad in 2017 and The Nickel Boys in 2020.

Fans of Ply will have to bide their time, though, as the 2027 Pulitzer Prize winners won’t be announced until May of next year. If Ply does take home any big literary awards in the coming season, it may herald a new exciting era for sci-fi novels. Announced on November 9, 2026, the 2026 Booker Prize winner, The End of Everything by M. John Harrison, has been celebrated as the first winner in Booker history to come from the science fiction world. Could Ply be the next big sci-fi literary champion? Only time will tell.
