#3471. Sandra Wollner’s ‘Everytime’ Is a Stunning Film About Grief Like You’ve Never Seen Before

Few human emotions are as fathomable as grief. Someone (or something) was here, had meaning and value and presence, and is now gone. There is a hole, a gap, an empty space. The pain that accompanies that void may manifest in different people in different ways, but its very existence is understandable. What makes people happy? What makes them sad? What makes them angry? Grief, well, that’s an easier question with a tougher answer.

For her third feature film, German filmmaker Sandra Wollner tackles the most tangible of dramatic genres — the grief tale — and turns it on its head in a way that our own David Ehrlich called “infinitely beguiling.” Mostly, the film shows how infinitely elastic and malleable this genre is, and the emotions that power it. Related Stories How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Dominated the Box Office: GKIDS Chief on IMAX’s Impact and the Growing Market for Foreign-Language Movies Democrats Won. When Do Hollywood Crews Get Back to Work?

The logline for the Un Certain Regard winner is simple enough: after the death of teenager Jessie (Carla Hüttermann), her mother Ella (Birgit Minichmayr), her little sister Melli (Lotte Shirin Keiling), and her boyfriend Lux (Tristán López) form an unlikely family unit as they attempt to move on. To say much else is spoiler-y in the truest of senses: It would detract from the joy and wonder of watching this story unfold.

That Wollner’s film is doing something different with seemingly well-trod material is obvious from the start, as “Everytime” layers on cut scenes from the video game “Vintage Story” — not “Minecraft,” though Wollner understands why the audience might think it’s the more well-known game — long before the real drama kicks in.

A familiarity with “Vintage Story” is not required to understand her film, Wollner promised during a recent interview with IndieWire. “Maybe if someone hears the dialogue of Melli and Lux, then maybe they would feel they have to know more about it, because they’re talking about how you can basically cut trees to harvest stuff and to get that, but I don’t feel that you have to know anything,” she said.

Wollner herself isn’t even a “hardcore gamer,” but she admires video games for their world-building and how they can encourage exploration. Her early forays into both “Vintage Story” and “Minecraft” tickled that. “It felt like the ‘Backrooms’ phenomenon, but before the ‘Backrooms’ phenomenon,” she said. “You’re walking through infinite worlds that feel so big, but minimalistic in a way. And the sounds; a very ambient sound feels eerie and soothing at the same time. I was just very compelled and inspired by that.”

The idea that Jessie would leave behind her own video game world that Melli could then play in was one of the film’s first seeds. “I thought, it’s a way of a memorial I haven’t seen so far,” she said. “[We have this] whole world of avatars and gaming communities where people meet online and then if someone really goes out, their avatar might live forever in there and create a life on its own in a way. I just found that very intriguing, and this is why I wanted in there.”

While the film is unique in how it handles digital mementos — avatars, literally — Wollner also pays close attention to real-world details that can make grief feel even bigger.

“One of the first scenes [I thought of] was Ella lying down on the couch and hearing how her daughter would come back [into their apartment],” the filmmaker said. “It’s something I think also everybody can relate to, even with a more natural loss and not such a tragic one. For example, when I was a kid, my aunt would always run down the stairs [in the apartment complex where we lived], and I would always hear her in the morning, running down in the morning. The noise was very specific to this person. I didn’t want it to be full on, but to let us think, it couldn’t be Jessie.”

Wollner was also intrigued early on by the “constellation of people” impacted by the loss of one. “The boy, the little girl, and the mother, it’s people I’ve met in my life in several decades, I would say, variations of them, but somehow similar constellations,” she said. “They seemed very clear to me. Three people who, especially the mother and the boy, really tried to do the right thing in a way. But there is a big conflict in there. They are having a weird dependent relationship. She needs him to grieve. He needs her to forgive. Of course, I could have made this conflict much bigger, but I really was interested in ordinary people who just try to do the right thing and just try to go along with that.”

Having her own child added a new dimension to the film, even for Wollner. The filmmaker was editing the film when her daughter was born (her longtime partner is writer and cinematographer Timm Kröger, who also worked on the digital imaging in “Everytime”), an experience that deepened her understanding of her own work.

In the film’s second half, the trio travel to Tenerife, Spain on holiday, a place that baby Jessie (who we’ve seen in home videos) once visited. There, they discover another baby, who looks just like Jessie, playing happily in the same quiet space that baby Jessie once occupied.

“We watched the scene again of baby Jessie sitting there, and we looked at each other,” she said. “I always understood what [that scene] means for me, but there, we really felt it for the first time, being a parent. And I felt, oh, I really nailed it! I mean, that sounds so stupid, but when I had the baby, I think, as many people feel, you still sometimes have the feeling, oh, where does it come from? It’s suddenly here. Suddenly there’s a person there. It’s like with that moment when she walks around the corner, and baby’s sitting there.”

Wollner was also compelled by the way we memorize different places and the unpredictability of memory. The odd little space, located in the far reaches of the resort’s clubhouse, comes to haunt Ella, Melli, and Lux in different ways, forever linked to Jessie and her absence.

“When my dad died, I was with him, and I suddenly had this image of him standing somewhere in this bend on the river and fishing, and it felt so familiar,” the filmmaker said. “This memory intruded on my present. We cannot control when we get a memory. They’re just coming. Sometimes we can make them happen to come. But we never know if maybe the weird place where we saw our baby sitting or the weird moment is the one that haunts us the most. It’s this weird banal little room with this weird banal kitschy toy that is playing this music. And this is the thing that then comes back.”

Those “banal little” details pack immense emotional power. So do turns from Minichmayr and López, who never turn to over-the-top histrionics to convey their grief. Wollner’s choice to set the majority of the film a year after Jessie’s death helped, giving the characters some distance from the immediate stab of loss.

“It was a conscious choice to pick some time after the death [to mostly focus the film on],” she said. “As a writer, we need to know what happened in the time between, and so I wrote that as well, but it honestly felt not depictable. I feel I can only fail to show that. I wasn’t interested in these big emotions. That just felt too overwhelming. And sometimes we are made to believe that grief comes in these neat boxes to check: Now you’re sad, now you’re angry, now you accept. Maybe you can be angry again, then you accept. It’s just this messy thing that you can feel for a very long time.”

Keiling also offers a nuanced performance, built more on a kid’s curiosity than on saddling the young actress with big, showy scenes. There’s no screaming and crying here, no sobbing or yelling. But that doesn’t mean that Keiling wasn’t accessing some major emotions.

“I love to work with kids,” Wollner said. “And even having a kid, I think I still am a kid in a way. For this one, I met Lotte, I had not met another kid, I only met her, I did not do any other castings. I just fell in love and thought, oh, she’s exactly what I thought of Melli could be and even better, so I trusted the script to her.”

Wollner worked with fellow filmmaker Juli Neuhaus, who served as a “kids’ coach” for the younger members of the cast. Wollner and Neuhaus were eager to meet Keiling where she was. The young performer loves to draw, so she would draw the scenes before performing them, to better understand what they were about, which allowed her to access a full spectrum of feeling.

“With Melli, there was no scene where she really had to act her grief,” she said. “I always felt that the film itself, the editing and the framing, the absence, we see her doing her homework, and then we see the same room behind her, but now we know that the sister is not there anymore, I always felt that this will tell us the grief, so she doesn’t need to act it. If she holds her phone and is texting her sister, it will already make us feel the grief. She doesn’t need to feel the heavy weight of that. So, actually for her, it was, I would say, like a very light shoot. Playful. It was really playful.”

Still, for all its sense of fantasy and play, “Everytime” is about a terrible heartbreak. Yet, as ever, Wollner chose to depict Jessie’s sudden, shocking death in a unique way, tracking her fall from a tall building while out with Lux from a great distance away. We can see it. We can do nothing about it. That’s grief, too.

“This was one that really was clear to me in the writing process already, that we’re going to have this lens and that we have this weird perspective of the universe itself looking at it, being so far away and still not able to do something about it, but still witnessing so intimate,” she said.

The actors were on one high-rise building, while Wollner and her crew were on another, about half a mile away. “And we had this insane lens. I had a 3,000-millimeter consumer camera, which is an insane lens,” she said. “It’s really like you don’t want to point it on people. It feels really not OK. But I was sure that I wanted to work with exactly that length or something similar to that, that feels kind of forbidden to be so close and too far away at the same time.”

While the scene is shot as if Jessie and Lux are very close to the edge of the building, the actors were not. (Hüttermann later told Wollner that she still had the feeling she might fall, even with myriad safety measures in place. That’s just how immersive the entire thing felt.) Hüttermann’s actual fall was shot in a studio, and their visual effects supervisor Kariem Saleh combined that footage with the outdoor shots.

Because they needed a certain kind of light, Wollner estimated they had only about five takes to get it right, though she knew they would likely only get one shot with the “perfect” light. Her script also called for the camera to follow a bird after the fall, but she said with a laugh, “Unfortunately, no bird came in exactly that moment.” (They lensed other birds, though, and those also ended up in the final composite shot.)

“We worked so many hours just on the sounds, just to get the right level of there is a little sound, and there is a little tink when she falls down, a little bit,” she said. “Just to realize, given how far away we had to be, how does the sound have to be? We worked the whole time on that, and I never really felt it until I sat at Cannes in the audience. And I heard the gasps for the first time and really it went through my bones. I mean, it’s weird to say that, but I was happy, but I felt the first time that it actually worked.”

Wollner remains very emotionally connected to the film, constantly talking about the way certain scenes make her feel, either while making them or editing them or even seeing them with an audience. Of course, such a deep-feeling filmmaker crafted such a beguiling film, one that invites all sorts of responses and theories. Since Cannes, audiences have been talking about its genuinely thrilling third act and the implications of its final scenes. And while we won’t spoil them here, we had to ask: What did Wollner want her viewers to feel in those moments?

“The feeling that I wanted to have is that [this film that is] grounded or hopefully grounded in the beginning, then suddenly you walk around the corner and you feel still some ground, but it’s such an odd place now and you don’t know,” she said. “I always hoped it doesn’t feel just dreamy, but there is some groundedness to it and that the people still react in a way that made sense for them, the characters, but that you don’t know what room you entered now, some kind of back room. That was clear from the beginning.”

And, as fantastical as it might sound, she’s clear: it’s all real. “I mean, it’s such a cliché to say that, but everything we see at the end is true at the same time,” she said.

A 1-2 Special release, the film is in limited theaters now, with a wide release to come in February 2027.

Amazon has cut the price of its latest Fire TV Stick 4K, dropping it to $24.99 from $59.99 and bringing it to its lowest price ever, according to price trackers. There's also no support for Apple AirPlay or Google Cast, so sharing content directly from your phone isn't particularly convenient. #3469. John Wick Director’s New Heist Thriller Sets All-Time Career Rotten Tomatoes Record

David Leitch's new heist thriller has set an all-time career Rotten Tomatoes record.

The former stuntman made his uncredited directorial debut on John Wick (2014) alongside Chad Stahelski and went on to become one of Hollywood's go-to action directors, helming crowd-pleasers like Atomic Blonde (2017), Marvel's Deadpool 2 (2018), Fast & Furious Presents: Hobbs & Shaw (2019), Bullet Train (2022), and The Fall Guy (2024) – many of which received mostly positive reviews from critics.

Now, ahead of its release on November 13, How to Rob a Bank has debuted with a 44% score from critics on Rotten Tomatoes, David Leitch's lowest ever. The movie has 34 reviews at the time of writing, so its score could change as more are published.

Its audience score should also start to take shape once the film releases in theaters this Friday. See how its critics' score compares to Leitch's past movies below:

Directed by David Leitch, with a script written by Mark Bianculli, the new film follows a crew of bank robbers who broadcast their heists on social media, which become viral sensations and attract the attention of a seasoned FBI agent and a brilliant software engineer determined to bring them down. With the net closing in, the robbers attempt one final high-stakes score.

The movie stars Nicholas Hoult, Zoë Kravitz, Emmy winner Anna Sawai (Shōgun), Rhenzy Feliz, Pete Davidson, John C. Reilly, Christian Slater, Tati Gabrielle, Paul Sparks, Emmy nominee Young Mazino (Beef), and Alessandra Frugoli.

Choose the movie with the higher Rotten Tomatoes score.

Sign in to claim your place on the leaderboard!

Sign in to claim your place on the leaderboard!

In ScreenRant's review of How to Rob a Bank, George Bate rated it six out of 10 stars and writes, "David Leitch delivers [a] timely, flashy thriller with thin characters... Leitch brings his kinetic style to a timely heist thriller that has plenty of energy and style, but lacks compelling characters." He continues:

Though it falls short of becoming one of the greats, this heist thriller is still a breezy, diverting time at the movies.

Overall, critics are divided on How to Rob a Bank, but the consensus leans negative. On one hand, David Leitch delivers energetic action, flashy visuals, and a timely premise about wealth inequality and internet-fueled rebellion. However, many feel the film mistakes noise for substance. Its political commentary comes across as shallow, and it struggles to make its heists feel compelling.

Still, there are some bright spots. Critics praise its lively performances, infectious punk-rock attitude, bursts of entertaining action, and willingness to tackle anti-capitalist themes. Unfortunately, an undercooked script, thin character development, excessive silliness, and an inconsistent tone keep the film from reaching its full potential. The verdict is that How to Rob a Bank is a fun but forgettable ride.

Let's dive into what's available and which devices support these new features.

Amazon has knocked $100 off the latest Google Pixel Watch 5 (45mm, LTE), bringing it down to $429.99 from $529.99, its lowest price yet, according to price trackers. If you can do without cellular connectivity, the 45mm wifi model is also down by $100, now selling for a record-low $329.99 (down from $429.99). PCMag calls the Pixel Watch 5 the best smartwatch for Android users, largely because Gemini is built in so deeply—the assistant works proactively, so it can surface your flight details on the way to the airport or suggest a contact's number while you text about dinner plans, and a new AI-powered Health Coach reviews your workouts with tailored feedback, though some of its fitness advice sits behind a paid subscription.

Helping all of those AI features along is a faster Qualcomm processor that Google says improves the overall performance of this smartwatch by 20%, while RAM increases from 2GB to 3GB and storage doubles to 64GB compared with the Pixel Watch 4. #3466. All 8 Episodes of 'VisionQuest,' Ranked

Spoiler Alert: This list contains spoilers for the VisionQuest finale.With VisionQuest finally finishing up its limited series run, Marvel fans are extremely happy. The finale to the trilogy that began with WandaVision is making its rounds as a fan-favorite Disney+ series. This is all thanks to the fact that the show has all the makings of a good superhero television series, while still staying extremely true to itself.

The character of Vision (Paul Bettany) has been through the ringer since his birth in Avengers: Age of Ultron, and while many had thought his story ended with his death in Avengers: Infinity War, the likes of WandaVision revived him (in a way). While, at first, there were lots of people who weren't happy about this new Vision being introduced, VisionQuest's eight awesome episodes have given them ample reason to be.

VisionQuest Episode 5, "Firewall" is a bit more of a sit-down-and-breathe episode, so it takes itself a tad slower than the rest of the others. This doesn't mean it's any kind of snooze-fest, though. Episode 5 is a lot more character-driven, especially when it comes to the likes of antagonists Jocasta (T'Nia Miller) and Ultron (James Spader). This fifth entry does quite a bit of legwork to make them more understandable as characters moving into the latter half of the season.

Having good, relatable, and sympathetic characters as antagonists is wildly important, and the Marvel Cinematic Universe can either be really good at this, or quite bad. Episode 5 makes it so VisionQuest truly succeeds on the antagonist front (even though the true villain of the series had yet to be truly introduced). It's not a perfect episode, and sometimes the pacing really keeps it from being everything it could be. But, all-in-all, it's still a decent episode that develops the characters effectively.

The first few episodes of a new show are extremely important. If the audiences are hooked by the first or second episode, the crew behind the series needs to make sure that hook stays and that was the important job that VisionQuest Episode 3, "Reboot" had. Thankfully, things are really kicking into high gear by this point in the plot, with Tommy Shepherd/Maximoff (Ruaridh Mollica) and Vision finally paired up and working together in full force.

The third entry also further develops the mystery behind whom the so-called "Butcherbird" is, and why they have been killing so specifically. This mystery truly engages viewers and keeps them guessing. This, combined with the great character work written between Tommy and Vision, makes Episode 3 a great continuation to the borderline perfect introduction that was in the first two episodes (which dropped together).

A good pilot for a television show is everything. If a pilot fails, the potential continued viewership of the show drops drastically. While the MCU has pre-installed fans that will watch whatever they put out, a bad pilot can still crash the plane and detract even the most dedicated viewer. Thankfully, director Christopher J. Byrne did a wonderful job bringing this new story to viewers.

Byrne reintroduces the audience to Vision and where he's been in the time since WandaVision with prowess and grace. Not to mention, it wastes no time introducing all the main players and the conflict. This faster pacing doesn't keep it from feeling too fast, though, and it still takes ample time to slow down and establish these characters, where they're at in their journeys, and what's to come. VisionQuest Episode 1, "No Strings" is a great example of an effective beginning.

The truth of Tommy's past is a mystery (to him) that lingers over his entire character arc. That presence is very prominent in VisionQuest Episode 6, "Deadlock" as they head to Madripoor to meet with Paladin (Todd Stashwick) for a tense alliance. If it isn't obvious from online discussion, the son of Vision is a fan-favorite character in the series, and this is a big episode for his character arc.

VisionQuest does a great job making reveals while still maintaining as much mystery as they can, and it doesn't just do that with Tommy's past in the sixth installment, but regarding the mysterious man behind all the shenanigans thus far. Not to mention, it's got a wonderful MCU callback cameo in Faran Tahir returning as Raza for the first time since Iron Man in 2008. A super fun inclusion that awards MCU fans who have been here since the beginning and still made it this far into such an expansive universe.

Four villains, and four arguments the films were honest enough to actually let them make. Here is the one you lean towards, the part of it that holds up, and the exact point where it stops holding up.

You align with the one who was right about the problem and wrong about the solution. Killmonger is the most persuasive villain Marvel has produced because the film never pretends his anger came from nowhere.

You align with the protector, which is the most understandable and most dangerous position on this list. Namor is not chasing power or revenge, he is doing whatever keeps his people hidden, and he has been doing it for centuries.

You align with the patient one, the only man on this list with no powers, no army and no hurry. Zemo lost his family in Sokovia and then spent years working out that you do not fight the Avengers, you introduce them to each other's secrets.

You align with the one who decided the answer was arithmetic. Thanos is not angry and not grieving in any way he will admit to, he simply reached a conclusion and never once revisited it, which is precisely what makes him frightening.

Just as a good pilot is important, a good finale is just as important—if not more so. VisionQuest had a lot it needed to accomplish by the end of the runtime of VisionQuest Episode 8, "Forever" and, thankfully, it managed to execute on it. MCU Disney+ finales have definitely struggled in the past, so this story had a lot to prove, with high stakes. There was a lot to be screwed up here, and, if everyone on the team—cast and crew alike—didn't give their A game, it could have turned out catastrophically. A bad finale can tarnish how people view a series as a whole forever, unfortunately.

The show's first seven episodes are incredibly strong, so to fumble in the final hour would have been horrific for the show's reputation and overall quality. "Forever" wraps up every plot thread relatively well, being able to weave the plots together into one cohesively. Everyone's character arcs feel like they've reached a natural conclusion, and the way that Vision finally bests Ultron is quite creative, as it doesn't rely on just action to wrap the conflict up. Plus, it gets huge points for finally bringing the Maximoff boys together, with Billy Maximoff (Joe Locke) making an appearance to help Tommy revive their father.

VisionQuest Episode 1, "No Strings" focuses mainly on introducing Vision and his AI crew, but they're not the only protagonists of this show. On the other hand, VisionQuest Episode 2, "Theseus", takes its entire runtime to introduce the character of Tommy and develop his side of this world and his character arc. Ever since WandaVision and Agatha All Along, people have been wondering where he's at. Is he alive? Where did he end up? What does he even look like?

This second episode answers all those questions. So, in a way, this is a bit of a "second pilot"—a job that it wonderfully succeeds at. The young man was always going to be one of the most important characters of this show, so giving him an entire episode to be introduced and established was an incredible call on the VisionQuest team's part. This is especially true with the great direction, as per usual, from Christopher J. Byrne.

Comic book fans were abundantly excited when it was announced that the awesome villain, Jocasta, was going to be making her MCU debut in VisionQuest. If there's an episode to consider the "Jocasta Episode," it would be VisionQuest Episode 4, "Malware" as it's her big introduction and the reveal of her major plans for the future. This episode also throws a bit of a wrench in the father and son's relationship, as the young speedster discovers that Vision wasn't wholly honest about who resides in his mind.

With Tommy putting it together that Ultron is in Vision's mind, he's obviously not very happy with his father. Things get worse, however, when Jocasta makes her move, and Vision is forced into letting Ultron take control to stop her—which, to no one's surprise, does not go well. Tommy also gets to finally show off his true speed in the climax of this episode, which is abundantly cool to finally see on display.

A good penultimate episode needs to tee up what's to come in the big finale, and—genuinely—VisionQuest Episode 7, "Immolation" is one of the best penultimate Disney+ MCU episodes of all time. The way this seventh episode sets up what's to come and reveals such massive information to the audience is masterful in every way. It truly puts Vision and Ultron at odds, brings Jocasta one step closer to her goal, sets Tommy up for a huge arc conclusion, and so much more.

VisionQuest Episode 7, "Immolation" has everything that makes this show as great as it is. It has some of the most raw, vulnerable dialogue and character moments out there that bring these characters to where they need to be perfectly. It's got action that ups the ante with spectacle and wonder. Not to mention, the visuals continue to be astounding, thanks to Director of Photography, Neville Kidd. With this in mind, there's just no question that the penultimate entry to the VisionQuest journey is the best the show has to offer. The stakes are set, the characters are ready, and the crew executed everything they needed to with so much prowess.

#3465. 10/10 Fallout Replacement Officially Added As PlayStation Plus Free Game

There simply aren't enough games like Fallout. With Bethesda's lackadaisical approach to the series resulting in just two entries over the past 11 years, fans have been left with few ways to engage with the franchise beyond the abundance of available mods. However, even they prove to be insufficient at retaining one's interest, especially when the foundations are so old, unstable, and ill-equipped to serve a contemporary audience looking to get even more out of their gaming experiences.

Fortunately, while there are few Fallout games and fewer pretenders, there is one title that promises to be a suitable replacement for those whose apocalyptic appetites had yet to be satiated. This title, which proved to be a sleeper hit back in 2025, has finally been added to PlayStation Plus as a free title, making it so that those who've never heard of it and those who had but didn't want to buy it at full price finally have the next best Fallout replacement they've been searching for accessible at the press of a button.

Atomfall was released back in March 2025 and offered an experience that was as close to Fallout as one could have hoped for. Developed by Rebellion, the same folks behind the Sniper Elite series, Atomfall marked a rather significant departure from the studio's usual style of game. It featured a vast open world filled with towns and cultist settlements that had to be discovered rather than pinpointed on your map with markers, a mysterious narrative packed full of meaningful choices, factions, survival mechanics, and a retrofuturistic aesthetic, all of which would feel right at home under the Fallout moniker.

Atomfall proved to be a huge success for Rebellion, garnering more than enough sales to warrant the production of DLC, which expanded the game's narrative and world significantly. Now, it joins numerous other games coming to PlayStation Plus on November 17. This is the first time Atomfall has been on the platform, with it previously finding success on Xbox Game Pass when it initially launched. It has been available on PlayStation since launch, but only as a full-price title, with the occasional sale bringing down its price a tad.

Atomfall will join the pantheon of amazing games on PS Plus, of which Fallout 4 is also proudly included. It isn't clear how long Atomfall will remain on the platform, especially as PlayStation Plus titles seem to come and go at the drop of a hat, but one can reasonably expect it to be around for at least a few months. To be clear, Atomfall's two DLCs, Wicked Isle and The Red Strain, aren't included in its PlayStation Plus release, and will still need to be bought separately.

If you've been looking for a first-person, narrative-focused, survival-based shooter like Fallout, then Atomfall is absolutely the game for you. While it isn't perfect (Atomfall's initial reviews were favorable, if a little mixed), there is a lot to love about it, especially if you're already a huge fan of Fallout. Rebellion may not have referred to Atomfall as the Fallout killer at launch, but it very much feels like one, especially considering that Bethesda has yet to release a new mainline entry.

#3463. The Out of Touch Adults' Guide to Kid Culture: What Does 'Code Rot' Mean?

A weekly deep dive into the current trends, slang, and viral videos of youth culture in terms that even the squarest can understand.

This week's Out-of-Touch guide takes a look at a phenomena that's probably going to define the lives of generations of young people: Code rot—both actual computer-style code rot, and the more elusive cultural kind. I'm also taking a look at the fake controversy over the "cancellation" of Freddy Krueger, and finally, bringing things home with viral videos of boyfriends dancing.

Expect to hear young people talking about code rot for awhile, maybe for the rest of their lives. It's a concept that's going to affect them more than any previous generation. Code rot, or software rot, describes what happens to a computer program when the hardware and operating system it runs on advance. If older programs aren't updated, they become less stable and glitchy until they eventually become unusable.

The idea of code rot has really caught on in the young people's popular imagination, probably because they're going to spend a lot of their lives dealing with it. They've even taken the idea of code rot into life, and use the phrase to describe anything that is worn out or malfunctioning. If the ice cream machine isn't working at McDonald's, it's code rotted. Bad grades on a report card? Code rot.

Kids are making videos where they demonstrate actual code rot:

or point out physical things that are code rotted, like a cat:

Interestingly, a lot of the online discourse around code rotting concerns the massive video game platform Roblox. Because Roblox games there are made by users, there's often not a lot of incentive for the creators to keep the games current with the platform's changes, so a lot of Gen Z's childhood memories of playing games are sinking into code rot. Here's a video about it:

Another interesting wrinkle is the tone these videos take. Code rot is seen as apocalyptic. While it's mostly hyperbole, I think part of it is the realization that the entire world is code rotted. The old programs that used to run within the "Western Culture" operating system no longer apply and everything is starting to glitch out.

The meaning of "PDF file" depends on the context. If you're at work, it refers to a Portable Document Format file, a format created by Adobe that is famously hard for older people to open. In slang, though, PDF file is algo speak for "pedophile." Because that word is flagged by moderation software online, people say "PDF File" to skirt the censorship.

The run-up to Halloween brought a lot of online discourse about Nightmare on Elm Street villain Freddy Krueger. The supernatural serial murder/PDF File was supposedly cancelled online by overly woke, Gen-Z Tiktokers outraged that he is a child predator. The controversy started with a post from Entertainment Industry Reporter that points out how strange it is that in the '80s and '90s, Freddy Krueger, depicted in 1984's A Nightmare on Elm Street as a child murderer so driven by bloodlust he transcended death, was featured on dolls, board games, and lunchboxes aimed at children. It's a good point, but not a call for "cancellation."

Although the article does say that "Freddy Krueger lunchboxes shouldn’t exist," and that parents "shouldn’t have been buying their kids action figures of a child murderer," this is not a call to action. It's not suggesting cancellation of any kind, and it's hard to even conceive of what cancellation of a fictional character in an old horror franchise would even mean. The article is actually an observation about how merchandising (and low-quality sequels) change the meaning of art. But people online missed the point entirely and invented a scenario where "woke" young people are calling for the cancellations of a fictional villain for doing bad things.

I've been scouring TikTok, looking for even one video where someone is calling for "canceling" Freddy Krueger, and I can't find any, but there are hundreds, maybe thousands of videos like this:

In these videos, people point out how enraging it is that the woke people are calling for Krueger's cancellation and vowing that they won't let it happen. Even though it is not happening. There are even levels to the myths about woke mobs canceling Freddy. Supposedly, younger users were unaware that Krueger is depicted as a "PDF file" as well as a murderer in the 2010 reboot of the franchise, so there are online arguments about whether that's the reason he's being canceled. Even though no one is canceling anything. These anti-woke folks are, ironically, defending a fictional villain from cancellation by creating another fictional villain, the shadowy woke mob that's ruining horror movies. Meanwhile, the real villain is a lack of media literacy. Saying "wow, it's crazy that previous generations made a comedy mascot of such a terrible character and marketed him to children" is not the same as cancellation.

This week's viral videos are of boyfriends dancing. The newest thing on the TikTok is young women sharing video of their boyfriends getting down accompanied by a clip from the song "gay alligations fr. my girlfriend" by TikToker OH MICKEY. Like this:

It's a simple, silly template that maybe doesn't mean a whole lot, but this generation of young men are so messed up when it comes to relationships and masculinity, I'm always happy when a meme becomes popular that indicates that young women want goofy dudes, dudes who know how to dance, and dudes who act silly as boyfriends more than they want red-pilled, manosphere, looksmaxxing types. I don't know if these kinds of messages ever really "break through" to the underground of internet incels, but I like to hope they do, because a lot of young men are not OK.

#3462. Dwayne Johnson's Hercules (2014) Is Now Streaming For Free On Tubi

Dwayne Johnson has a remarkable filmography spanning decades. He successfully transitioned from full-time wrestling in 2004. Since then, he has starred in dozens of movies across multiple genres, one of which being a Hercules adaptation. His first movie appearance was as the Scorpion King in The Mummy Returns. He didn't feature prominently, though he was instantly recognizable in the movie's climactic battle. Johnson then starred in The Scorpion King spinoff movie in 2002.

The Scorpion King was set in Ancient Egypt, providing a backstory for the character before his campaign to conquer the world. Since then, Johnson has gone from strength to strength on the silver screen, playing numerous beloved characters across several franchises.

Agent Hobbs from Fast and Furious is one of his fan-favorite roles. He was an antagonist of sorts in Fast Five, relentlessly pursuing Dom (Vin Diesel) and his team as they plan a daring heist in Brazil. Hobbs' relationship with Dom's crew has changed in newer installments, and he's now a franchise mainstay.

Johnson also starred in the successful Jumanji reboot, Welcome to the Jungle, as Dr. Smolder Bravestone. The movie pays homage to the Robin Williams original and expands on the story with a modernized spin that fits the source material.

Even casual moviegoers know Johnson's more famous movies, but some still slip under the radar. A lack of hype doesn't necessarily mean a movie is bad, and one of Johnson's lesser-known films is now available to stream for free.

Hercules premiered in 2014 and stars Dwayne Johnson as the son of Zeus himself. The movie is now available to watch for free on Tubi. It's a streaming platform similar to Netflix or Prime Video. However, it's funded by ads, and no subscription is required.

Tubi is less well known than some other streaming services, but it does have a solid selection that is frequently refreshed. The platform also boasts some exclusives under its Tubi Originals label, such as Lowlifes in 2024.

Hercules offers a fun spin on the Greek legend. Most notably, Hercules is a mercenary in the 2014 movie, and we're not even sure if he's truly a demigod. Ergenia (Rebecca Ferguson) approaches Hercules with a proposal. She wants him to help her father, Lord Cotys (John Hurt), fend off Rhesus (Tobias Santelmann), a brutal warlord. He agrees to help when he learns that Rhesus has burned down villages, even though it's an uphill struggle.

Lord Cotys' soldiers lack training. Hercules and his crew attempt to make them battle-ready, but will he succeed before Rhesus's forces close in?

2014's Hercules rarely comes up in conversation today, which is surprising, considering its performance at the box office. The movie reportedly made $243.3 million worldwide, not including physical sales. Financials vary by project, but movies typically need to make 2.5x their production budget to be considered a success. Hercules was very close to that target, with an estimated production cost of $100 million.

The movie itself tells an entertaining dark fantasy adventure story. Hercules is famous across Ancient Greece, and his legendary 12 labors are known across the land. Interestingly, during his first fight, we notice that his teammates contribute far more than the stories may suggest. Hercules is supported by several fighters, including Atalanta (Ingrid Bolsø Berdal), a skilled archer, and Amphiaraus (Ian McShane), a seer.

Iolaus (Reece Ritchie) is a unique member of the team, as he's Hercules' nephew. He's not a fabled warrior like his uncle, but he is a storyteller who can inspire others, even if he embellishes the truth. Hercules' group is just as important as the legendary warrior himself, and the movie offers a multilayered take on the character. He's charismatic and strong, not unlike the Scorpion King in many ways. Hercules also has a troubled past, thoroughly explored as he tries to prepare Lord Cotys' army for battle.

#3461. Atomically Thin Materials Significantly Shrink Qubits

MIT researchers use 2D materials for capacitors in quantum circuits in an effort to scale processors

Superconducting quantum processor and its microwave packaging.

Quantum computing is a devilishly complex technology, with many technical hurdles impacting its development. Of these challenges two critical issues stand out: miniaturization and qubit quality.

IBM has adopted the superconducting qubit road map of reaching a 1,121-qubit processor by 2023, leading to the expectation that 1,000 qubits with today’s qubit form factor is feasible. However, current approaches will require very large chips (50 millimeters on a side, or larger) at the scale of small wafers, or the use of chiplets on multichip modules. While this approach will work, the aim is to attain a better path toward scalability.

Now researchers at MIT have been able to both reduce the size of the qubits and done so in a way that reduces the interference that occurs between neighboring qubits. The MIT researchers have increased the number of superconducting qubits that can be added onto a device by a factor of 100.

“We are addressing both qubit miniaturization and quality,” said William Oliver, the director for the Center for Quantum Engineering at MIT. “Unlike conventional transistor scaling, where only the number really matters, for qubits, large numbers are not sufficient, they must also be high-performance. Sacrificing performance for qubit number is not a useful trade in quantum computing. They must go hand in hand.”

The key to this big increase in qubit density and reduction of interference comes down to the use of two-dimensional materials, in particular the 2D insulator hexagonal boron nitride (hBN). The MIT researchers demonstrated that a few atomic monolayers of hBN can be stacked to form the insulator in the capacitors of a superconducting qubit.

Just like other capacitors, the capacitors in these superconducting circuits take the form of a sandwich in which an insulator material is sandwiched between two metal plates. The big difference for these capacitors is that the superconducting circuits can operate only at extremely low temperatures—less than 0.02 degrees above absolute zero (-273.15 °C).

Superconducting qubits are measured at temperatures as low as 20 millikelvin in a dilution refrigerator.Nathan Fiske/MIT

In that environment, insulating materials that are available for the job, such as PE-CVD silicon oxide or silicon nitride, have quite a few defects that are too lossy for quantum computing applications. To get around these material shortcomings, most superconducting circuits use what are called coplanar capacitors. In these capacitors, the plates are positioned laterally to one another, rather than on top of one another.

As a result, the intrinsic silicon substrate below the plates and to a smaller degree the vacuum above the plates serve as the capacitor dielectric. Intrinsic silicon is chemically pure and therefore has few defects, and the large size dilutes the electric field at the plate interfaces, all of which leads to a low-loss capacitor. The lateral size of each plate in this open-face design ends up being quite large (typically 100 by 100 micrometers) in order to achieve the required capacitance.

In an effort to move away from the large lateral configuration, the MIT researchers embarked on a search for an insulator that has very few defects and is compatible with superconducting capacitor plates.

“We chose to study hBN because it is the most widely used insulator in 2D material research due to its cleanliness and chemical inertness,” said colead author Joel Wang, a research scientist in the Engineering Quantum Systems group of the MIT Research Laboratory for Electronics.

On either side of the hBN, the MIT researchers used the 2D superconducting material, niobium diselenide. One of the trickiest aspects of fabricating the capacitors was working with the niobium diselenide, which oxidizes in seconds when exposed to air, according to Wang. This necessitates that the assembly of the capacitor occur in a glove box filled with argon gas.

While this would seemingly complicate the scaling up of the production of these capacitors, Wang doesn’t regard this as a limiting factor.

“What determines the quality factor of the capacitor are the two interfaces between the two materials,” said Wang. “Once the sandwich is made, the two interfaces are “sealed” and we don’t see any noticeable degradation over time when exposed to the atmosphere.”

This lack of degradation is because around 90 percent of the electric field is contained within the sandwich structure, so the oxidation of the outer surface of the niobium diselenide does not play a significant role anymore. This ultimately makes the capacitor footprint much smaller, and it accounts for the reduction in cross talk between the neighboring qubits.

“The main challenge for scaling up the fabrication will be the wafer-scale growth of hBN and 2D superconductors like [niobium diselenide], and how one can do wafer-scale stacking of these films,” added Wang.

Wang believes that this research has shown 2D hBN to be a good insulator candidate for superconducting qubits. He says that the groundwork the MIT team has done will serve as a road map for using other hybrid 2D materials to build superconducting circuits.

Dexter Johnson is a contributing editor at IEEE Spectrum, with a focus on nanotechnology.

#3459. 10 Great Thriller Movies Based on Best-Selling Books, Ranked

Novels remain one of the most significant sources of cinematic inspiration, and it takes a particular type of film to stay faithful to a story. From the bone-chilling adaptation of Thomas Harris' thriller, The Silence of the Lambs, to the intelligent and masterful novel by author Stieg Larsson's, The Girl With The Dragon Tattoo, there have been many successful adaptations of incredible books.

Popular novels turned into movies create an exciting opportunity for viewers to see the story play out visually, many of which have become some of the greatest thrillers ever to hit the big screen. While some thrillers remain loyal to the author's original novel, others carry the source material into previously unforeseen places. There have been many book-to-screen thriller adaptations, but certain ones stand out as cinematic masterpieces.

Children of Men is a dystopian action thriller that works on many levels, including as a cautionary story and a trailblazing human drama about society's struggle for survival. The film unfolds in 2027 London, where humanity is on the verge of extinction, and worldwide chaos ensues. When a woman falls pregnant, cynical bureaucrat Theo Faron (Clive Owen) and his ex-wife Julian Taylor (Julianne Moore) help secretly transport a pregnant refugee to safety. At the same time, they fight to protect the world's last remaining hope from danger.

Directed by Alfonso Cuarón and based on the 1992 novel The Children of Men by author P.D. James, the film received overwhelming critical acclaim but no box-office success. However, the powerful thriller has recently enjoyed a remarkable resurgence with glowing reappraisals on both sociopolitical and artistic grounds. The movie and novel contain general similarities, including a dystopian setting, developed main characters, and a strong plot that remains relevant with each passing year.

The psychological thriller The Girl on the Train follows divorced alcoholic Rachel Watson (Emily Blunt), who obsessively watches the house belonging to her ex-husband and his new wife on her morning train commute. Along the route, she catches glimpses of their neighbors, a seemingly perfect young couple, Scott and Megan. However, when Megan suddenly goes missing, Rachel is caught between helping to investigate the disappearance and becoming a murder suspect.

Directed by Tate Taylor and based on the bestselling novel by Paula Hawkins, the movie The Girl on the Train is an excellent example of a great mystery. The book-to-movie adaptation stays primarily loyal to its original material with only a few key changes, including the film's location switching from London to New York City and the original pair of detectives in the novel becoming one complicated character. The movie unfolds in diverse, compelling ways as it plays with the timeline and the narrator while keeping viewers guessing until the end.

In the movie The Girl With The Dragon Tattoo, disgraced journalist Mikael Blomkvist (Daniel Craig) hires brilliant computer hacker Lisbeth Salander (Rooney Mara) to help solve the 40-year-old murder of Henrik Vanger's (Christopher Plummer) niece. As the two main protagonists uncover the truth, they discover more than they bargained for about the powerful Vanger family secrets.

Masterfully directed by David Fincher and based on the novel by Swedish author Stieg Larsson, The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo film is a compelling psychological thriller. In the second book-to-movie adaptation, Fincher created a masterful neo-noir thriller that unravels a genuinely captivating story and remains faithful to the novel's intricate plot.

The erotic thriller Crash is one of director David Cronenberg's most controversial and provocative films. The movie follows film producer James Ballard (James Spader) and his wife Catherine (Deborah Kara Unger), who are looking to spice up their sex life. Following a car crash, they are lured into a strange subculture and underground community of sadomasochistic car-crash fetishists.

Cronenberg adapted J.G. Ballard's highly controversial future-shock novel into an immaculately directed, vivid depiction of graphic sexual acts instigated by violence. Both the movie and book present disturbing and equally profound inquiries into human desire. With its twisted and erotic portrayal of eroticism, this drama/thriller will grip its viewers entirely.

Set in New York City in the 1980s, American Psycho follows investment banker Patrick Bateman (Christian Bale), an egotistical psychopath consumed by the social politics of the upper-class circle. By nightfall, Bateman's corporate illusion drastically changes as his sadistic desires take full effect, shifting towards a double life as a serial killer.

Filmmaker Mary Harron's adaptation of Bret Easton Ellis' American Psycho is the epitome of cult cinema. While Ellis' novel is a satire of greed and heartlessness that consumed parts of America during the 1980s, Harron's film investigates similar themes but with the addition of dark humor. Both the novel and the film have polarized their audiences with horrifying brutality as they examine the elements that make a man a monster.

The psychological thriller Shutter Island follows troubled U.S. Marshall Edward "Teddy" Daniels (Leonardo DiCaprio) as he investigates the disappearance of a woman who has escaped an asylum for the criminally insane. As the investigation deepens, Daniels, while dealing with his haunting past, begins to realize things are not as they appear.

The film Shutter Island is arguably one of the most popular thrillers of all time and a haunting adaptation of Dennis Lehane's pulpy gothic novel. Director Martin Scorsese brilliantly uses visceral horror imagery to convey the despair of Daniel's tortured psyche. The psychological components detailed in both the book and movie continue to keep audiences guessing as to what is fact and what is fiction.

In the movie Gone Girl, New York-based writer Nick Dunne (Ben Affleck) and his wife Amy (Rosamund Pike) appear to be the perfect couple. However, when Amy suddenly disappears under suspicious circumstances, Nick becomes the prime suspect. The resulting media frenzy causes the couple's image of a blissful union to fade quickly, leading to compelling questions regarding who the real Nick and Amy.

Director David Fincher's adaptation of Gillian Flynn's Gone Girl resulted in a dark and intelligent psychological thriller, receiving widespread critical acclaim. While the film appears to be a straightforward mystery, it becomes much more complex with its jaw-dropping twists and turns. The book-to-film adaptation has successfully managed to remain faithful to the novel while also introducing its own creative style.

The movie Fight Club observes a depressed office worker (Edward Norton) and a soap salesman named Tyler Durden (Brad Pitt) forming an underground fight club. The club attracts other individuals who also lead monotonous lives as they turn to express their inner anger by beating each other senselessly. However, as the group continues to grow, soon enough, anarchy reigns.

Acclaimed filmmaker David Fincher's adaptation of Chuck Palahniuk's 1996 novel is an insightful satire of masculinity and consumerism and observes how both can be equally toxic to society. While Fincher's brilliant adaptation of Palahniuk's acclaimed novel is dark and unorthodox in many ways, the beloved '90s cult classic proved remarkably faithful to the book.

The 2007 thriller No Country for Old Men tells the story of Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin), who discovers the gruesome aftermath of a drug deal. Unable to resist temptation, Moss takes off with the cash left behind. However, it is not long before a tense game of cat and mouse ensues, as merciless killer Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem) begins to pursue Moss.

The Coen brothers' adaptation of Cormac McCarthy's brilliant novel is a true masterpiece in which the filmmakers have crafted their most suspenseful and terrifying film to date. At the same time, the film adaptation has remained highly faithful to the novel regarding its primary elements, namely tone, twists, and surprises.

The cinematic masterpiece The Silence of the Lambs is an intoxicating and absorbing thriller. The film follows young FBI cadet Clarice Starling (Jodie Foster) as she seeks advice from Dr. Hannibal Lecter (Anthony Hopkins), an incarcerated cannibalistic serial killer, to track down another serial killer.

Jonathan Demme's adaptation of Thomas Harris' compelling novel The Silence of the Lambs is considered one of the most horrifying and iconic thrillers of all time. In the book-to-movie adaptation, Demme has successfully created a thrilling, thought-provoking pop-culture phenomenon close to Harris's novel in most aspects, including story and dialogue.

#3457. Prime Video's #1 Global Hit Series Takes Advantage Of Massive Streaming Trend

Although every streaming service and cable network has cashed in on one popular trend recently, Prime Video’s worldwide number one hit proves that the streaming service is at the vanguard of this particular cycle. Despite TV’s infamous reputation for chasing trends, the entertainment industry can sometimes move surprisingly slowly when it comes to riffing on popular titles thanks to the slow speed of television production.

While HBO’s Game of Thrones became a huge hit when the show debuted in 2011 and was a massive worldwide success by 2013, Netflix’s The Witcher didn’t reach screens until the HBO show’s series finale aired in 2019. Prime Video’s ambitious Lord of the Rings prequel The Rings of Power took even longer, with the fantasy adaptation only arriving in 2022 even though the series was clearly intended to act a Game of Thrones replacement or substitute.

Similarly, even though Grey’s Anatomy creator Shonda Rhimes had a massive global hit in 2020 with the alternate history romance novel adaption Bridgerton, it took almost half a decade before the rest of the industry caught onto this trend. In 2025, Heated Rivalry became a colossal success, and this hit was followed by a flurry of romance novel adaptations including Prime Video’s Off Campus, Every Year After, and, most recently, Campus Drivers.

Based on the bestselling book series by author CS Quill, Campus Drivers is a six-episode romance novel adaptation that aims to recapture the success of Prime Video’s earlier 2026 hit Off Campus. The story of the series follows Carmen Kassovitz’s Lois as she arrives at Belrose University with her love interest, Max, only to end up living with Baptiste Madeline’s Lane. Lane is famous on campus for inventing the titular ride-share app, and what starts out as awkward cohabitation soon blossoms into something else entirely.

Campus Drivers immediately proved a massive breakout hit when the series arrived on the streaming service, rocketing to number one worldwide despite stiff competition from high-profile shows like The Terminal List. This might seem surprising, but the consistent success of Bridgerton and its spinoff, Heated Rivalry, and Off Campus, as well as original romance shows not based on novels, such as Prime Video’s small-town story Sterling Point, make the development less shocking.

Much like Shonda Rhimes’s underrated political thriller Scandal was part of a massive genre resurgence that also included Designated Survivor, Madam Secretary, Veep, House of Cards, and even The Newsroom, her Bridgerton success was just the tip of the iceberg when it came to successful streaming adaptations of romance novels. Like Bridgerton, Heated Rivalry, and Off Campus, Campus Drivers is also a multi-book series, meaning there are two more seasons of material ready to go if the show is renewed.

This in-built longevity is particularly useful at a time when even the biggest streaming projects are struggling to maintain their fan bases. Wednesday season 2 saw a major drop-off in viewers when the Addams Family spinoff released its second volume in 2025, but romance novel adaptations are a safer bet for streaming services since they tend to be less expensive than flagship fantasy or sci-fi shows.

Meanwhile, the arrival of Prime Video’s upcoming romance thriller Perfect Liars proves that the genre has a winning flexibility that allows these shows to incorporate elements from other genres seamlessly. Anyone who was around for the Twilight saga’s Team Edward and Team Jacob fan wars knows that fantasy romance is big business, but the success of Campus Drivers proves that contemporary romance, romantic comedies, romantic thrillers, and historical romances clearly also have the viewing public’s heart in 2026.

#3455. How AI Will Change Chip Design

Artificial intelligence’s promise and potential for the semiconductor industry

Rina Diane Caballar is a contributing editor covering tech and its intersections with science, society, and the environment.

An array of semiconductor wafers are ready to be made into chips.

The end of Moore’s Law is looming. Engineers and designers can do only so much to miniaturize transistors and pack as many of them as possible into chips. So they’re turning to other approaches to chip design, incorporating technologies like AI into the process.

Samsung, for instance, is adding AI to its memory chips to enable processing in memory, thereby saving energy and speeding up machine learning. Speaking of speed, Google’s TPU V4 AI chip has doubled its processing power compared with that of its previous version.

But AI holds still more promise and potential for the semiconductor industry. To better understand how AI is set to revolutionize chip design, we spoke with Heather Gorr, senior product manager for MathWorks’ MATLAB platform.

How is AI currently being used to design the next generation of chips?

Heather Gorr: AI is such an important technology because it’s involved in most parts of the cycle, including the design and manufacturing process. There’s a lot of important applications here, even in the general process engineering where we want to optimize things. I think defect detection is a big one at all phases of the process, especially in manufacturing. But even thinking ahead in the design process, [AI now plays a significant role] when you’re designing the light and the sensors and all the different components. There’s a lot of anomaly detection and fault mitigation that you really want to consider.

Then, thinking about the logistical modeling that you see in any industry, there is always planned downtime that you want to mitigate; but you also end up having unplanned downtime. So, looking back at that historical data of when you’ve had those moments where maybe it took a bit longer than expected to manufacture something, you can take a look at all of that data and use AI to try to identify the proximate cause or to see something that might jump out even in the processing and design phases. We think of AI oftentimes as a predictive tool, or as a robot doing something, but a lot of times you get a lot of insight from the data through AI.

What are the benefits of using AI for chip design?

Gorr: Historically, we’ve seen a lot of physics-based modeling, which is a very intensive process. We want to do a reduced order model, where instead of solving such a computationally expensive and extensive model, we can do something a little cheaper. You could create a surrogate model, so to speak, of that physics-based model, use the data, and then do your parameter sweeps, your optimizations, your Monte Carlo simulations using the surrogate model. That takes a lot less time computationally than solving the physics-based equations directly. So, we’re seeing that benefit in many ways, including the efficiency and economy that are the results of iterating quickly on the experiments and the simulations that will really help in the design.

So it’s like having a digital twin in a sense?

Gorr: Exactly. That’s pretty much what people are doing, where you have the physical system model and the experimental data. Then, in conjunction, you have this other model that you could tweak and tune and try different parameters and experiments that let sweep through all of those different situations and come up with a better design in the end.

So, it’s going to be more efficient and, as you said, cheaper?

Gorr: Yeah, definitely. Especially in the experimentation and design phases, where you’re trying different things. That’s obviously going to yield dramatic cost savings if you’re actually manufacturing and producing [the chips]. You want to simulate, test, experiment as much as possible without making something using the actual process engineering.

We’ve talked about the benefits. How about the drawbacks?

Gorr: The [AI-based experimental models] tend to not be as accurate as physics-based models. Of course, that’s why you do many simulations and parameter sweeps. But that’s also the benefit of having that digital twin, where you can keep that in mind—it’s not going to be as accurate as that precise model that we’ve developed over the years.

Both chip design and manufacturing are system intensive; you have to consider every little part. And that can be really challenging. It’s a case where you might have models to predict something and different parts of it, but you still need to bring it all together.

One of the other things to think about too is that you need the data to build the models. You have to incorporate data from all sorts of different sensors and different sorts of teams, and so that heightens the challenge.

How can engineers use AI to better prepare and extract insights from hardware or sensor data?

Gorr: We always think about using AI to predict something or do some robot task, but you can use AI to come up with patterns and pick out things you might not have noticed before on your own. People will use AI when they have high-frequency data coming from many different sensors, and a lot of times it’s useful to explore the frequency domain and things like data synchronization or resampling. Those can be really challenging if you’re not sure where to start.

One of the things I would say is, use the tools that are available. There’s a vast community of people working on these things, and you can find lots of examples [of applications and techniques] on GitHub or MATLAB Central, where people have shared nice examples, even little apps they’ve created. I think many of us are buried in data and just not sure what to do with it, so definitely take advantage of what’s already out there in the community. You can explore and see what makes sense to you, and bring in that balance of domain knowledge and the insight you get from the tools and AI.

What should engineers and designers consider when using AI for chip design?

Gorr: Think through what problems you’re trying to solve or what insights you might hope to find, and try to be clear about that. Consider all of the different components, and document and test each of those different parts. Consider all of the people involved, and explain and hand off in a way that is sensible for the whole team.

How do you think AI will affect chip designers’ jobs?

Gorr: It’s going to free up a lot of human capital for more advanced tasks. We can use AI to reduce waste, to optimize the materials, to optimize the design, but then you still have that human involved whenever it comes to decision-making. I think it’s a great example of people and technology working hand in hand. It’s also an industry where all people involved—even on the manufacturing floor—need to have some level of understanding of what’s happening, so this is a great industry for advancing AI because of how we test things and how we think about them before we put them on the chip.

How do you envision the future of AI and chip design?

Gorr: It’s very much dependent on that human element—involving people in the process and having that interpretable model. We can do many things with the mathematical minutiae of modeling, but it comes down to how people are using it, how everybody in the process is understanding and applying it. Communication and involvement of people of all skill levels in the process are going to be really important. We’re going to see less of those superprecise predictions and more transparency of information, sharing, and that digital twin—not only using AI but also using our human knowledge and all of the work that many people have done over the years.

Rina Diane Caballar is a writer covering tech and its intersections with science, society, and the environment. An IEEE Spectrum contributing editor, she's a former software engineer based in New Zealand.

#3454. How to Try 'Audio Intelligence' on Your Apple Watch Early

It has been a big year for Apple. There's a new CEO, prices have increased across the board, and there's been a seemingly endless rollout of new devices, including two new Apple Watches: the Series 12 and the Ultra 4. All things considered, these watches offer only minor upgrades over the previous models, shipping with new heart rate monitors and the latest S11 processor. But one of the biggest new watch features, "Audio Intelligence," is also the most controversial—and it's rolling out in beta today.

Audio Intelligence is Apple's branding for a new set of features exclusive to the Series 12 and Ultra 4. These features use the new Apple Watches' hardware, along with on-device and cloud-based AI, for tasks like sound and music identification as well as dictation. "Sound Recognition" can alert you to important sounds, like alarms and doorbells, while "Music Recognition" can automatically display songs playing around you—but these aren't the features you'll hear talked about in discussions of Audio Intelligence.

Rather, everyone is up in arms about "Live Rewind" and "Siri Recap." These Audio Intelligence features passively "listen" to your conversations throughout the day, and, using AI, deliver summaries of what was said. When you double-click your Apple Watch's crown to use Live Rewind, you'll get a loose transcript of the last 15 seconds of conversation it overheard, while Siri Recap can show summaries of all your in-person chats throughout the day. You can even configure a schedule for when your watch is "listening" for recaps—e.g., only run during work hours. Apple suggests each is intended to help jog your memory; maybe you use Siri Recap to remember important discussions you had that morning, while Live Rewind is meant for moments where you forget what someone just said. (As opposed to asking them to repeat themselves, I suppose.)

Apple's claims may or may not assuage your fears, but it seems the company is pushing on ahead regardless. Apple is releasing Audio Intelligence as part of iOS 27.3, which launches in beta on Tuesday. If you have an Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4, you can try it out today, assuming you enroll in Apple's latest beta version.

To do so, you'll need to sign up for the Apple Developer program, since iOS 27.3 is rolling out first for devs. This program used to require a $99 fee, but you can skip it now if you opt for the free account. Once you enroll your Apple Account in this program, you can open your iPhone, head to Settings > General > Software Update > Beta Updates, and choose "iOS 27 Developer Beta." Go back one page, then follow the on-screen instructions to download and install iOS 27.3 when it's available.

#3453. Taika Waititi’s Next Film Officially Shelved Following Controversy

Editor's Note: The following contains descriptions of sexual misconduct that some readers may find disturbing.

It has not been a great time for Taika Waititi? It feels like everything the New Zealander touches these days is cursed, and his newest project is no exception. One of his next appearances was supposed to be in a family-friendly fantasy movie adapted from a popular children's book, with a cast that included several familiar faces. Unfortunately, the production has now found itself caught up in a controversy unrelated to its leading man, and its release plans have taken a significant hit.

Waititi's upcoming fantasy film Fing! has officially lost its UK and Ireland distributor, with Sky confirming that it intends to withdraw from the project following serious allegations against author and screenwriter David Walliams. The decision comes after a joint investigation by The Guardian and ITV News reported allegations of inappropriate behavior involving teenage girls and young women.

The film, which stars Waititi alongside Mia Wasikowska and Iona Bell, is based on Walliams' bestselling children's novel. Walliams also co-wrote the screenplay and had filmed a cameo appearance, but the producers have now confirmed that his scene has been removed and that he will have no involvement in promoting or releasing the movie. In a statement to Variety, the producers explained:

"We take the allegations reported regarding David Walliams seriously. Our thoughts are with anyone who has been affected. We have removed his cameo appearance from Fing!, and he will have no involvement in the film’s release or promotion."

Sky, which was set to release the film as one of its originals, has also announced its intention to abandon its distribution agreement. A spokesperson said:

"The allegations made against David Walliams are extremely serious. We have notified the producers of the film of our intention to exit our position as the U.K. & Ireland licensee of Fing."

#3452. Scarlet Witch’s Avengers: Doomsday Return Sets Up A Game-Changing Hulk Connection

Warning! This article contains SPOILERS for VisionQuest episode 8.Elizabeth Olsen's Scarlet Witch is back in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, setting up the character's surprise role in Avengers: Doomsday, and the franchise has just established an exciting connection between Wanda Maximoff and the Hulk. Olsen's Scarlet Witch grew to become one of the most popular characters in the Marvel Studios shared universe through the release of WandaVision, one of the MCU's best TV shows.

However, the character ended up becoming a villain again, leaving a path of destruction throughout the multiverse, and killing characters like a version of Patrick Stewart's Charles Xavier, John Krasinski's Reed Richards, and more in Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness. Then, at the end of that movie, Wanda Maximoff sacrificed herself to destroy all Darkholds across the multiverse.

The dark magic book, which she was seen reading at the end of WandaVision in hopes of finding her twin sons, had corrupted her, and by giving her life to avoid the same happening in any universe, Olsen's Scarlet Witch found a path to redemption. For years, Marvel has worked with the notion that the Scarlet witch was dead, but that has changed.

VisionQuest's secret post-credits scene brought back the Scarlet Witch, who was resurrected seemingly right after her death in Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness by none other than Robert Downey Jr.'s Doctor Doom. This directly sets Wanda to appear in December's Avengers: Doomsday, also drawing a link between her and Mark Ruffalo's Hulk, shedding light on Doom's plan.

The VisionQuest finale saw the Scarlet Witch be resurrected by Doctor Doom as he told Wanda that her power would be his, which instantly reminded me of another 2026 appearance from Downey's MCU villain. The actor previously played Doctor Doom in one of Avengers: Endgame Encore's post-credits scenes, where he came to take away Ruffalo's Bruce Banner following the events of Spider-Man: Brand New Day. Not only did Doom retrieve both the Hulk and the Scarlet Witch, but the scenes were similar, with the villain telling Banner that he came to collect him, while Doom said he wanted the Scarlet Witch's powers.

Based on those MCU post-credits scenes, Doctor Doom is clearly assembling a powerful team of his own, either through mind-control or by taking the powers of some of the Marvel Studios franchise's most powerful characters, a category both the Hulk and Wanda fall into. There is a factor that boosts the mind-control theories, as that is an ability the Scarlet Witch has famously mastered through magic, which Downey's Victor von Doom could also know how to wield, given he managed to resurrect Wanda. Additionally, there are mysterious Latverian witches in Avengers: Doomsday, with one of them wearing red robes, which could be a mind-controlled Wanda.

Avengers: Doomsday will feature several powerful Marvel characters, but looking at the upcoming MCU movie's trailers, Tom Hiddleston's Loki has not appeared in the footage nearly as much as the rest. That, added to the fact that Loki is right on Doom's path to reshape the multiverse, given how the God of Stories' role is to protect the multiversal branches of Yggdrasil, positions Hiddleston's character as a fitting addition to the villain's growing list of kidnapped heroes.

Loki could also have a darker fate, as it would make more sense for Doctor Doom to kill him and take Loki's multiversal powers than to attempt a mind-control spell on him like the existence of the Latverian witches suggests might be the case for Wanda.

That said, it would also track if Doom was simply building his own team to fight the combined might of two Avengers squads, the Fantastic Four, and Fox's X-Men, as those superhero teams have powerful characters like Thor, Sentry, Magneto, and more. With few Avengers: Doomsday details revealed a month before the film's release, Marvel's new Scarlet Witch reveal, and its Hulk connection is an exciting update.
